#1203. Brunch in pole position al Bar del ristorante Derby Grill di Monza

La proposta domenicale del brunch del Derby Bar, il locale più informale del Derby Grill dell’Hotel de la Ville di Monza, nasce da una consuetudine di altri tempi.

È credenza comune che il brunch sia un’invenzione moderna, dettata dall’esigenza di accorciare i tempi. Eppure, la tendenza a riunire colazione e pranzo in un unico pasto ha radici lontane, più precisamente nell’Inghilterra del XIX secolo. Legato in origine alle attività venatorie, il pasto consumato a metà mattina dopo le battute di caccia portava in tavola carni ripiene, uova, salumi, formaggi, frutta, marmellate e dolci di ogni tipo, in un tripudio luculliano di forme e sapori. Un’usanza informale che oggi, sempre più spesso, si sostituisce ai pranzi del weekend (e qui trovate la mappa con 70 brunch a Milano).

La formula del brunch a Monza comprende una selezione di antipasti da condividere, un piatto principale a scelta, un dolce, un cocktail e caffè. La firma è quella di Fabio Silva, Executive Chef dal 2011 del ristorante Derby Grill, di cui vi abbiamo già raccontato e di cui leggete in seguito.

Per il bistrot, lo chef napoletano ha ideato una carta di piatti semplici ma gustosi, in linea con la filosofia del ristorante adiacente, fondata sull’attenta selezione delle materie prime e dei produttori.

Il menù si muove su due direttrici: da un lato suggestioni mediterranee con fusilloni al ragù di polpo, gamberi, cozze e finocchietto (25 €) e branzino alle erbe mediterranee e ortaggi di stagione (30 €). Dall’altro, la tradizione lombarda con il risotto alla milanese (24 €) e la costoletta di vitello con patate all’origano (33 €). A queste si aggiunge ogni domenica, da settembre a giugno, anche il brunch all’italiana al costo di 70 euro a persona.

Lo chef Silva interpreta il rito conviviale di stampo british in chiave italiana, dipingendolo con i colori e i profumi mediterranei.

Il menù fisso, che cambia a seconda della stagione e della disponibilità delle materie prime, si apre con una selezioni di antipasti da condividere:

L’ultimo atto del brunch al Derby Grill chiude il percorso con un dolce a scelta tra:

Ad accompagnare, Bloody Mary, Aperol Spritz o Champagne.

Il nostro “brunch stampa” parte in quarta con una serie di antipasti da condividere. In pole position ci sono il cotto, il crudo e il salame del salumificio Villani di Modena, insieme ai formaggi del territorio, tra cui taleggio e parmigiano, accompagnati da mostarda di pere.

Al centro della tavola, i panificati – grissini, focaccia, e pane realizzato in collaborazione con il Forno del Mastro di Monza – fanno da cornice a una sequenza di assaggi che attraversano la penisola.

Dalla caponata di melanzane con olive e pinoli alla lingua di vitello in salsa tonnata, fino al pane sfogliato con salmone e le sue uova.

A chiudere la carrellata, l’uovo in camicia su crema di zucca e fonduta di casera. Morbido, setoso e avvolgente, è il piatto autunnale per eccellenza.

I piatti principali sono una tappa lusinghiera. I fusilloni trafilati al bronzo con ragù di polpo, gamberi e cozze non si oppongono al morso, mentre il sugo di pesce, fresco e generoso, ammorbidisce la pasta accompagnandone il volume extralarge.

Il branzino alle erbe mediterranee è invece un rendez-vous tra mare e orto. La carne morbida e delicata del filetto flirta con il guazzetto colorato che guida il palato tra le note verdi degli ortaggi.

L’ultimo miglio spetta al dessert. Il gelato artigianale con marron glacè e meringa dà vita a un girotondo irresistibile di temperature e consistenze. Il cremoso avvolge la castagna glassata, prolungandone le note tostate, mentre la meringa interviene con la sua texture ariosa e friabile.

Quello del Derby Bar non è il solito brunch. Lontano dalle logiche modaiole, lo chef Silva reinterpreta il pranzo della domenica con un appeal disinvolto e conviviale. Un invito alla condivisione, costruito intorno a sapori immediati e familiari, ma tutt’altro che scontati.

A renderlo ancora più piacevole contribuiscono l’ambiente e la cortesia dei ragazzi in sala, che fanno sentire gli ospiti nel posto giusto al momento giusto. Sotto la volta di vetro del dehors, ricavato dalle scuderie reali dei Savoia – da qui il nome Derby – ci si lascia coccolare da una cucina sofisticata e concreta, priva di inutili stravaganze. Mentre fuori, la vegetazione del viale Regina Margherita cede il passo ai colori caldi dell’autunno, completando il quadro di una domenica da assaporare senza fretta.

In una Monza abituata a correre veloce, il tempo all’interno del Derby Grill sembra fermarsi. Con la sua luminosa veranda e le sale intrise di storia, il ristorante dell’Hotel de la Ville è un’oasi di sofisticata eleganza nel cuore del capoluogo brianzolo. Affacciato sul parco della residenza estiva dei Savoia, il locale conquista con il suo arredamento squisitamente british, di cui le sedute in cuoio dall’aspetto vissuto, i ritratti nobiliari e la boiserie scura ne tracciano i contorni. Un ambiente affascinante e accogliente che fa da scenografia alla proposta gastronomica dello chef Fabio Silva, campano classe 1978.

Dopo una solida formazione nelle brigate di Antonino Cannavacciuolo, Claudio Sadler e i fratelli Cerea (solo per citarne alcuni), Silva approda in Brianza dove firma piatti che uniscono la luminosità mediterranea al rigore lombardo. Riletture dei classici in chiave contemporanea, accostamenti insoliti ma convincenti e texture che parlano una lingua spontanea: sono questi i pilastri della cucina del cuoco napoletano.

La qualità degli ingredienti è il denominatore comune di tutti i piatti dello chef, che cura la selezione delle materie prime e dei fornitori. Nel menù compaiono così le uova della Valtellina, il Carnaroli di Pavia, la luganega brianzola, le alici di Cetara e il cioccolato cuneese, ma la lista potrebbe continuare.

In carta spiccano grandi classici come l’ossobuco di vitello in gremolata e risotto agli stimmi di zafferano (40 €) o la costoletta alla milanese a doratura lenta nel burro chiarificato (38 €). Il raggio si amplia con il risotto al Granun, pesce persico, caffè e shiso (29 €) e il salmerino in argilla con finocchio e lattuga (45 €). Attenzione a lasciare uno spazietto per il dessert, in particolare per il gelato al fiordilatte servito al carrello (18 €) che appaga l’occhio e rinfresca il palato.

Sedersi al Derby Grill di Monza è stato molto più che piacevole. Le aspettative, già alte, sono state confermate da un servizio puntuale e preciso, ma per nulla intimidatorio. L’ambiente è curato nei minimi particolari e la proposta dello chef Silva seduce il palato a ogni boccone, con gusti complessi resi leggibili da una mano elegante e fervente.

Pranzare al Derby Grill di Monza in un sabato di fine settembre è come tornare in vacanza. Accolta dalla gentilezza del personale, mi siedo nel dehor arredato in stile coloniale, con sedie in bambù e sinuose porcellane. Luminosa, fresca e di quell’eleganza misurata, mutuata dai club inglesi, la sala invita a restare il più a lungo possibile. È per questo che scelgo il menù degustazione per questo pranzo stampa. Il territorio…secondo me! 6 portate a 120 € in cui i sapori brianzoli danzano insieme alla tradizione partenopea e a suggestioni orientali, in una coreografia ben riuscita. Stesso prezzo anche per il menù Viaggio alle Origini Alla carta spendete in media per 3 piatti 95 euro.

Si inizia con quattro amuse-bouche. Ostrica di Goro fritta con polvere di cipolla di Montoro e crema di ananas alla brace; polpetta di coda di Bruna Alpina con panatura di pane e zafferano; sedano rapa con la sua crema e misticanza; gelato alla barbabietola su crumble di cacao e ricotta salata grattugiata. Tutti gli ortaggi e le erbe utilizzati in cucina sono biologici, racconta lo chef, e provengono dall’orto della Cascina Gallina di Busnago.

Il momento dei panificati è sempre il più atteso. Arrivano grissini tirati a mano e una pagnotta ai grani antichi e lievito madre del Forno del Mastro, servita ancora calda.

Ad accompagnarla, un disco di burro paglierino con sale Maldon.

Il pranzo entra nel vivo con i due antipasti. Il capocollo con foglie di senape, cipolla all’agro, ravanello e fichi marinati nell’olio delle loro foglie. La carne è talmente morbida che non serve il coltello. Le cipolle donano al bouquet un sentore pungente, mentre il frutto spinge l’equilibrio su un versante decisamente più amabile.

La selezione di funghi della Valtellina – finferli, chanpignon e porcini – conquista con la sua consistenza spugnosa e il sentore nocciolato, amplificato dal tartufo nero estivo e dalla salsa di mirtilli. Il mais alla brace aggiunge un quid croccante e affumicato al piatto.

Si prosegue con i primi piatti del Derby Grill. Da una parte il risotto Carnaroli della Riserva San Massimo mantecato al Granun, con persico spadellato nel burro, shiso e polvere di caffè. Mentre il pesce di lago alleggerisce la composizione, l’erba aromatica ne prolunga la persistenza, aggiungendo profondità.

I ravioli ripieni di tarassaco, ortica e dragoncello seducono invece con il loro profilo verde e la tenacia della sfoglia. Le animelle di vitello alla brace creano il giusto compromesso tra la delicatezza della pasta ripiena e il gusto rotondo delle frattaglie. Il polline chiude l’ensemble con sfumature luminose e floreali.

La seconda portata è divertissement puro. Il salmerino cotto al forno viene presentato al tavolo dentro una corazza di argilla, frantumata al momento per trattenere fino all’ultimo l’umidità e i succhi della carne. Il pesce di lago, rigorosamente pescato, è servito con il suo fondo e le sue uova, che completano il quadro con un’aggiunta scoppiettante. Finocchi e lattuga alla brace fanno da contrappunto alla componente lipidica.

Per esaltare il piatto, viene servito del gin aromatizzato al finocchietto, con sciroppo di finocchio, bergamotto e qualche goccia di olio di arancia.

Il pre dessert apre l’ultimo atto al Derby Grill. Sorbetto al sedano con meringa abbrustolita e caramella al limone. Fresco, gentile, luminoso.

Il dessert è quella sana punta di esibizionismo che nel fine dining è sempre piacevole. Arriva al tavolo su uno scenografico carretto: al centro, una montagna di Fiordilatte della Fiorida e tutt’intorno colorati barattoli colmi di leccornie da aggiungere al gelato. Scelgo la composta di mirtilli selvatici e le nocciole caramellate. Che dire? Un match perfetto.

Un tris di piccole dolcezze è il saluto dello chef. Cono biscotto con pastiera liquida e agrumi canditi; pancotto con crema di cioccolato bianco. Tartufo di cioccolato fondente aromatizzato al rosmarino.

L’eleganza e la convivialità che si respirano tra le pareti del Derby Grill si ritrovano anche nell’albergo adiacente. I suoi corridoi hanno visto passare illustri personaggi, volti noti dello spettacolo e soprattutto campioni dell’automobilismo, complice la vicinanza con l’Autodromo di Monza. Fin dall’ingresso, ciò che conquista dell’hotel è l’atmosfera ricercata e familiare, per nulla abbottonata come ci si potrebbe aspettare da un quattro stelle, ma pur sempre impeccabile.

Qui, da oltre sessant’anni, la famiglia Nardi esercita l’arte dell’accoglienza. È il 1958 quando il direttore d’hotel Bartolomeo Nardi rileva quello che fino a pochi anni prima era stato l’Eden Hotel Savoia. Il palazzo ottocentesco, che prima di diventare un punto di riferimento dell’hôtellerie era una residenza privata, dal 2007 fa parte del circuito internazionale Small Luxury Hotels of the World, un riconoscimento che certifica l’eccellenza dell’ospitalità e dello spirito del luogo.

Ristorante Derby Grill. V.le Cesare Battisti, 1, 20900 Monza MB. Telefono: 339 791 3900. Instagram

Sono Rebecca, food e fashion editor. Cresciuta con un libro in mano e una penna nell’altra, ho sempre trovato nelle parole il modo migliore per raccontare ciò che mi appassiona. Amo il bello in tutte le sue forme: dai sapori che evocano emozioni alle tendenze che esprimono personalità e stile. Attraverso i miei articoli cerco di condividere storie, ispirazioni e curiosità, accompagnando i lettori alla scoperta del mondo del food e della moda con uno sguardo attento, autentico e sempre curioso.

#1206. Boeing narrows third-quarter loss as defense sales rise, but focus remains on 737 Max production

Boeing narrowed its loss in the third quarter after defense sales rose, but CEO Kelly Ortberg told staff that the manufacturer has "more work to do."

Here's what Boeing reported for the third quarter compared with what Wall Street analysts are expected, according to consensus estimates from LSEG:

For the three months ended Sept. 30, Boeing reported a net loss of $116 million, or 26 cents a share, compared with a $5.34 billion loss, or $7.14 per share, a year earlier. Adjusting for one-time items, the company reported a loss of 34 cents a share. A year earlier, Boeing had taken a nearly $5 billion charge on its long-delayed 777X aircraft program.

Revenue climbed 4% on the year to $24.19 billion. Free cash flow rose to $464 million from $238 million in the third quarter of 2025.

The company's defense unit revenue rose 15% in the third quarter from a year earlier to $7.94 billion.

Boeing delivered 161 commercial airplanes in the third quarter, one more jet than a year earlier.

Revenue in the all-important commercial aircraft business fell 3% to $10.72 billion. The unit had a negative operating margin of 6.5% because of a "less favorable delivery mix, higher projected costs associated with future production rate adjustments and higher estimated supply chain costs," Boeing said.

The plane manufacturer's executives are set to update investors on how quickly it can increase aircraft production in the coming months when it holds a quarterly earnings call on Tuesday at 10:30 a.m. ET.

Boeing has been producing about 47 of its 737 Max planes a month, but is aiming for more. CEO Kelly Ortberg told investors last month that production is taking "a little bit longer" than expected to stabilize, and the company expects to increase its output of the planes next year.

"Looking ahead, expectations are rising, and they should," Ortberg said in a note to staff on Tuesday. "That means elevating our performance through lean, productivity and efficiency improvements in our day-to-day work while upholding our high levels of safety and quality."

Aircraft production and deliveries are key to Boeing's recovery since the bulk of an aircraft's price is paid when the customer receives it.

But the manufacturer had some wins lately. The U.S. Navy tapped Boeing to develop its next-generation fighter jet.

And the Federal Aviation Administration last week signed off on the 737 Max 10, the largest in the Max family. That followed the approval of the 737 Max 7 in August and marked the final certifications for the aircraft line.

#1211. Healey's Budget needs to sustain the stronger economy through gathering clouds

Healey's Budget needs to sustain the stronger economy through gathering clouds

The chancellor's aides are using intelligence-style security measures to guard its secrets: the Budget has been split into "compartments" with very few given access to all of them. There are codenames. The IT has been locked down and ministers viewing the plans have to sign a digital promise not to brief media.

Such security is a response to the feeling that speculation around the last Budget, sometimes informed by insiders, was economically destabilising.

As a recent former defence secretary, Chancellor John Healey has embraced such strict procedures, and has approached most of his public engagements and interviews with a sturdy refusal to break the Budget omertÃ , akin to his fellow Yorkshireman Geoffrey Boycott's at times ultra-defensive stance on a cricket pitch.

The economic news has been good - growth has been better than expected and the International Monetary Fund has endorsed the UK for "standing out" among the G7 countries for at least planning to cut borrowing.

John Healey has embraced strict security procedures to keep this year's budget secret

The bond market's reverse beauty contest, in which investors single out the countries they distrust most, has moved on from Britain. Traders I occasionally hear from who were once focused on UK borrowing costs are now more preoccupied with "le spread" - the widening gap between French and German borrowing costs (the former being higher than the latter) - and with America's long-term debt outlook.

And yet there are clouds on the horizon. The inflation rate rose more than forecast to 3.5% in September, and borrowing numbers were also higher than forecast. This means an imminent Bank of England rate rise is very much on the cards, with the resultant rise in mortgage repayments for some.

Credibility with investors requires not just that Budget maths add up on Wednesday, but also belief that growth plans are realistic, and the perception that Downing Street can actually convince MPs to pass its Budget.

The question for John Healey is whether he can deliver a Budget that can sustain the revival in growth and offer the help with the cost of living that his backbenchers demand. At the same time he needs to reassure the markets that his budget will keep a check on borrowing.

"Is it resilient, or is it actually strong?" has been the tone of the debate among economists about the curious case of the UK economy ahead of what is a vital Budget.

The UK is the fastest growing G7 country so far this year, at 0.6% in Q1 and 0.5% in Q2. The widespread assumption of stagnation in the second half is being defied with Q3 heading for 0.6 to 0.8%.

Each quarter has seen growth twice as fast as predicted by the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) in March and independent forecasters. This is the fastest growth in the first eight months of a year since 2017, ignoring the post-lockdown re-opening.

It's more resilient than it was in 2022. Back then, the Ukraine war, massive energy bailouts, and Liz Truss' mini budget all culminated in the UK facing the highest borrowing costs in the G7, in what was derided in financial markets as a "moron premium".

Then last year, with constant policy u-turns, UK borrowing costs rose the most of the G7.

This year the gap has narrowed, as uncertainty about the US and France takes centre stage, but all advanced economies are feeling the heat from the Iran war energy shock.

Inflation has risen, but not just in Britain. The link between gas and electricity prices has weakened, meaning spikes in gas prices have less impact on electricity bills than they used to and helping to keep inflation lower than it otherwise might have been.

The fact that up until now the Iran war has been more of an oil shock than a gas shock (where the UK is more exposed) has been another saving grace. Meanwhile, the significant amount of AI and tech investment in the UK is another boost to the economic numbers.

The net result is that doom-mongering predictions of recession, of being hit worst by the Iran war, and, in some quarters, of imminent national bankruptcy, have been defied.

That economic defiance of the early part of 2026 has persisted in the first three months of the Burnham-Healey tenure in Downing Street, buoyed by a lull in the Iran war and the energy price shock.

Post Liz Truss' mini-budget the UK faced the highest borrowing costs in the G7

Burnham was advised upon entry to Downing Street that if consumers could at least feel more confident, they might save less and spend more and therefore help boost growth.

So far Burnham and Healey appear to be relying on a series of relatively inexpensive "feel-better" policies - such as capped bus fares and a temporary VAT cut on household energy bills - that have improved confidence without significantly increasing spending.

But there isn't a lot of spare money, which limits just how much can be offered for "temporary and targeted" measures. And come January, the clouds on the horizon could be overhead, with typical energy bills predicted to rise by 16%, interest rates potentially up and an enduring fear that the AI bubble could burst.

At a gleaming hi-tech robotics research facility in Coventry last month, John Healey sought to set out the broad contours of his approach to the economy. On a walkabout at the Manufacturing Technology Centre, I asked him if there had been too much doom-mongery.

"I know the global conditions mean that it is hardâ¦ we have huge latent potential in this country. Great talent, and deep capital markets.

"The challenge now is to make sure that we balance the books, we manage and control public spending, and the prime minister and I are in lockstep in our determination to meet the fiscal rules with a buffer," he said.

The giant orange robot arms whizzing around were being trained by AI to use lasers to carve the most intricate metal shapes for prototype parts for the jet engines of the future. The Budget manoeuvres required by Healey may require even more precision.

The essential question is whether he has chosen to impress the markets and explain himself to his MPs, or impress his MPs and explain himself to the markets. Judging by my three interviews with him in recent weeks, it is more the former than the latter.

At Labour conference Healey wore the same tie once worn by Gordon Brown

The answer may not be found in his speech at all, but in the borrowing tables that will reveal how much money the government expects to borrow over the coming years, published in the OBR's forecast released - assuming no repeat of last year's disaster - when Healey sits down in the House of Commons around 13.00.

Just after that, as Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch is delivering the Opposition's response, the real reaction the chancellor's team will be looking for is whether the markets move, particularly when the Debt Management Office publishes the "gilt remit" - the detail of any changes to its plan to sell UK government bonds to investors.

My sense is that every effort is being made to minimise this number, and help guide down medium and long-term borrowing rates for the government and for mortgages. (It was at this moment in 2022 that markets vomited at the prospect of how much extra they thought the government would need to borrow after Liz Truss' mini budget.)

From Healey's first day in office, the prudence message was practically tattooed to his head. He has spent more time working in the Treasury than any recent chancellor. He spent five years from 2002 to 2007 as a junior minister when Gordon Brown was chancellor - five finance bills, five Budgets, pre-Budget reports and two Spending Reviews.

Healey says he will take on some of the challenges Rachel Reeves found tricky to resolve

For his Labour Party conference speech, Healey sported Brown's old conference tie. But the Treasury he returned to this year is a changed place in important ways. When his predecessor wore the tie, the Treasury was running an annual surplus, not a Â£120bn deficit adding to a Â£3 trillion total national debt.

I asked him just afterwards, and just before he was whisked off to a meeting of the government's emergency COBR committee on RAF Fairford, if he was going to have another go at some of the things that proved so difficult for his predecessor, former Chancellor Rachel Reeves.

He replied: "100%. I was very clear to the conference today and the public beyond. There isn't the money that there was in the 1990s. People understand that. The public aren't daft.

"Running through the Budget I deliver must be fiscal discipline and the maintenance of control on the public finances, because otherwise we won't get on top of the debt costs."

One intriguing element of what we may see on Wednesday is that this theoretically more left-leaning Labour government appears to believe they have the political capital to save money on welfare payments.

The aim is to get some of the 1.35 million people currently off work with mental health issues back into jobs.

Some reporting suggests some affected younger people may see benefits payments cut, with the government instead investing more in getting them into jobs and keeping them in them through the offer, for example, of in-work therapy.

Back in Healey's time under Gordon Brown, there was no OBR. Back then it was not unknown for late budget maths problems to be settled with an optimistic tweak of a forecast, a date change to the economic cycle, or choosing a stronger rate of long term growth.

The OBR's verdict is crucial now - to what extent it agrees with projected welfare savings or even the importance it places on stronger GDP figures matters now.

The bigger point here is that the chancellor must be shocked by the contrast between the sheer power of the Brown Treasury to do what it wanted, and the reality of what he currently faces: the constraints of the OBR, manifesto red lines, bond markets, significant debts and an energy shock.

There are reasons to postpone some of the toughest decisions beyond this Budget, such as how to fund desired increases in spending on defence and social care. The economic outlook could improve were the Iran war to settle at some point in the next few months, and after revised statistics the OBR may also have cause to rethink last year's downgrade to long term economic growth.

There is an imaginable pathway to a forecast next year with higher growth, lower inflation and lower debt interest costs, plausibly improving the public finance projections by tens of billions.

This would be a much more agreeable basis upon which to decide the pace of those big ticket spending rises. It also may be a tempting option for anyone thinking about an election. Former Treasury officials lament: "There is always a reason for procrastination."

Expect the Chancellor to laud the resilience and strength of the UK economy and seek to sustain it, and spread growth geographically. His key judgement, however, will be a balance between extra financial and economic support and the peril of still elevated borrowing costs.

He will try to offer breathing space. It may be needed not just for households and families, but for the Exchequer itself.

#1216. Santoli: We are nearing a now-or-never moment for the AI trade to rebound

The difference between a restorative rest and unhealthy stagnation is time. Distinguishing between resilience and fatigue isn't always easy.

The S&P 500 has been sideways for months, last week dipping to levels first reached on June 1. It has spent nearly all of the last three months within the range the index traveled during a peppy two-day rally Aug. 3-4.

Along the way, the former leaders of the AI trade, captured in the iShares AI Innovation ETF, have collapsed by 35 percentage points relative to the equal-weight S&P 500, then regained half the loss, then gave up most of that bounce.

Aside from giving all of us plenty of time and room for overthinking it, this process of constant churn and testing and positioning shocks has done some good, in a tactical sense.

It has created short-term washout conditions in semiconductors and other former momentum AI-hardware plays. Meantime, the cyclical pockets of the market – from consumer discretionary to industrials to banks - have undergone double-digit setbacks as higher bond yields and elevated oil prices restrain growth expectations.

Equity investors have shown a clear preference for quality and defense, as the debt markets have begun rationing growth capital more stringently, raising hurdle rates for the more marginal AI-data-center borrowers.

Along the way, some familiar intermarket relationships have been scrambled: Treasury yields have stopped moving closely with oil, yields retreating well off their highs as crude stays above $100 a barrel. And the S&P 500's former inverse correlation with Treasury yields has loosened, as the bond market bid seems more tied to hiccups in the AI buildout, which has stymied the Big Tech players.

The Goldman Sachs equity desk over the weekend noted "trader exhaustion," in part from the momentum-factor stock basket having moved at least 5% in a day 30 times in 2026 – more often than in any other full year, including ones when there were crashes such as 2000, 2009 and 2020: "Not sure we can handle much more flipping of the thematic script(s)."

Of course, confusion and stress ultimately can reset positioning and attitudes for the good. The sentiment and positioning composite kept by Macro Risk Advisors' John Kolovos that runs here weekly is approaching a "fat pitch" for a tactical rebound, he says.  By most measures, hedge funds have radically cut their leverage and exposure to tech. Broad institutional positioning in tech is not far above the Iran-war lows, according to Deutsche Bank, which adds that "the last two reversals higher in tech coincided with strong earnings releases."

This setup takes shape as the mega-cap cloud platforms Alphabet, Amazon and Microsoft report results this week. Further, AI-funding anxiety should arguably ease a bit with the Anthropic IPO filing showing good operating metrics and $100 billion in cash before the IPO proceeds are collected, alongside Blackstone's financing for SpaceX capex and Broadcom lining up $63 billion to fund chips for Anthropic.

It's not quite a now-or-never moment for the AI trade to find some relief, but it's not far from one.

If there's a nagging outlier to the evidence of investor retrenchment and waning risk appetites, it's the ceaseless buying by retail traders of even the worst-looking tech charts.

Scott Rubner, head of equity and equity derivatives strategy at Citadel Securities, wrote on Friday after Thursday's nasty 3% tech selloff, "Despite commentary from several sell-side banks suggesting retail capitulation, our platform data showed the opposite." Namely, the retail order flow Citadel handles as a top market maker revealed extreme dip buying in the leveraged semi ETFs, Micron, Meta and other hard-hit names. This matches data from Robinhood, which according to the firm's Sherwood Media showed its traders stampeded into Bloom Energy on Friday as it fell 11% with the second-highest day ever of net buying in the stock.

While impressive on some level, and even admirable to some, this aggressive buying of severe weakness is not something that has typically coincided with important market lows. Citadel's data tell us that the late-March and late-July bottoms in the market occurred when retail traders panicked out and were net sellers for a week or two.

Not to say that retail's stubborn dip-buying precludes some relief in hard-hit parts of the market, but it likely limits how strong or durable a rally might become.

John Kolovos of Macro Risk Advisors on the latest reading: "Sentiment and breadth are finally giving us something to like, and a fat pitch may be approaching, but the macro needs to cooperate. Our studies show that improving momentum amid tight financial conditions has historically produced disappointing returns and left the market dangerously vulnerable to left-tail outcomes or market corrections."

-Sometimes assessing the weight of the evidence requires a long wait for all the evidence. I grant that the anxious churn and valuation compression of recent months has generated conditions for upside surprise and a relief trade higher.

But bigger picture, I want to stay alert to changing atmospheric conditions.

As I've noted in the weeks since this newsletter launched, I think we're feeling late-cycle tremors – narrower market leadership, investors' unwillingness to pay up for fast earnings growth, a flattening yield curve, stingier credit markets.

I've suggested the market might be telling us companies are "over-earning" through front-loaded capex recycling. It's probable that the Iran war and its macro disturbances prevented the AI theme from going full bubble mode, restricting the craziness to semis and related groups. But that doesn't mean we're sure to rebuild toward a broad bubble this cycle.

And I've argued that even if stocks do fine, bonds now offer a useful yield cushion against concentrated equity risk.

Last year around this time, cyclical-sector outperformance, approaching fiscal tailwinds and benign credit conditions were telling us not to worry about economic growth into 2026. So then what are the recent defensive-stock leadership, fading fiscal impulse and unsettled corporate credit whispering in investors' ears now?

I also believe in the laws of mean-reversion, even though they are enforced only sporadically. A post by Ben Carlson of Ritholtz Wealth Management on his "A Wealth of Common Sense" blog details how great trailing 15-year S&P 500 returns have been, and what this could mean looking ahead.

-This writeup by Dario Perkins of TS Lombard entered heavy rotation in the past couple of days, for good reason. It's a nicely articulated and sobering thought experiment on how the AI boom might now be incubating its own nasty bust.

The migration of money toward pure, traditional defensive stocks has been a bit too mechanical to infer that it's entirely a macro "tell," given the clockwork factor rotations that look almost too scripted to be trusted.

Still, the results are a convergence of valuations between consumer staples and technology. This might seem perverse for current-generation investors but there was a time when staples commanded a premium for their stability and enduring brands, while tech was viewed as cyclical and fickle.

Procter & Gamble has long been the class of the consumer-products industry, standing in for quality management in the way Pampers are synonymous with diapers. And somewhat the way Google is interchangeable with looking something up on the Internet.

Whether this crossover in P/E strikes you as the world's proper order being restored or as a screaming buy signal for Alphabet shares is the measure of what sort of investor you are.

#1220. Big, noisy and coming to a town near you - why the data centre backlash is growing

Big, noisy and coming to a town near you - why the data centre backlash is growing

Until a few years ago many of us may have been blissfully unaware of what a data centre was.

These giant, warehouse-like buildings power virtually all our internet activity, from our web searches and emails to movie downloads and online banking.

They are at the heart of the AI boom, housing the advanced computer chips and servers needed to run services like ChatGPT and Claude.

But the speed at which they're growing, the enormous amount of electricity they consume and concerns about their environmental impact are fuelling a public backlash around the world.

In the US, they've become a huge issue ahead of the midterm elections on 3 November, with both Republicans and opposition Democrats coming out against their development.

It's putting opponents of data centre expansion on a collision course with US President Donald Trump, who has dismissed the pushback as a "sick conspiracy", even as public anger grows.

Here's what you need to know about the data centre boom, and why opposition is growing.

There are about 12,250 data centres around the world, according to Data Center Map, external, a company that tracks both operational and pre-operational sites.

That's up sharply from 2021, when there were around 8,000, external operational sites.

As the chart below shows, data centres are most densely clustered in the US which has 4,767 sites. It is followed by Europe, where the UK and Germany lead.

Data centres have typically been located near to cities where it's easier to access high voltage power lines or water resources for cooling. But as they get bigger, more are being built in rural areas.

But when it comes to actual capacity, the US is ahead by a much larger margin, with China in second place and Europe lagging far behind.

This gap is set to widen in the coming years, leading some to warn Europe risks missing out on the potential economic benefits of the AI boom, external.

Data centres vary wildly in size, ranging from ones that fit inside a garden shed to others covering vast expanses of land.

The world's largest operational data centre is widely reported to be one run by China Telecom in Hohhot, Inner Mongolia, covering an area of approximately one million square metres (10.7 million sq ft). That is equivalent to about 140 Fifa football pitches.

However, much larger sites are under construction as the graphic below shows.

All these sites are being built exclusively to provide the immense computing power needed to run AI services.

For instance, Colossus 2, which is part of the wider Colossus campus, will house hundreds of thousands of advanced AI chips made by tech giant Nvidia.

It will also be used to train xAI's chatbot Grok. Elon Musk's company will use 41 methane gas turbines to help power the site, which activists say could "significantly increase" local air pollution, external. Local regulators say the turbines will meet air quality standards.

The pressure data centres put on local resources has sparked increasing concern. These facilities can use significant amounts of water to cool their systems, which could lead to water shortages, some experts say.

Data centres worldwide are also thought to consume more electricity than the whole of France, as the chart below shows.

This growing hunger for power is driving up carbon emissions, analysis shows, while putting pressure on local grids, which some fear could push up energy prices.

With others worried about the noise data centres make and the space they take up, a public backlash is gathering steam.

Some 16 US states have proposed laws to ban or temporarily block new facilities, and it could be a key issue in November's midterm elections.

Outside the US, opposition to data centres has emerged in countries like Mexico, France, Indonesia and the UK.

But supporters say data centres are critical to national security, and the development of AI.

They also say they are good for the economy, external, attracting investment, generating tax revenue and creating jobs in areas like construction.

A recent report by the Brookings Center, external suggests data centres do create local jobs, although fewer than industry advocates claim.

The type of data centre matters too. So-called hyperscale facilities - massive sites owned and run by tech giants like Amazon and Microsoft - have a bigger positive effect on jobs, it found.

But "colocation" facilities, which lease space to remote tenants without a local presence, brought fewer benefits.

As the debate over their merits intensifies, the data centre rollout continues.

This year, the tech industry is expected to spend a combined $765bn, external ($544bn) on AI infrastructure in 2026, with this topping $1tn next year.

But as concerns about the environmental impact grow, the tech industry is exploring alternatives.

One idea is to put data centres in space, external or on the Moon, where they could harness abundant solar energy.

Others predict that more AI processing could eventually be carried out by the hardware already inside our computers and smartphones, reducing the need for vast data centres altogether.

#1225. Gambero Rosso 2027, Guida ristoranti: Tre Forchette, premi, novità

Il Reale di Niko Romito a Castel di Sangro in Abruzzo è il migliore ristorante della Guida Ristoranti d’Italia 2027 del Gambero Rosso con 99/100. Tre Forchette, dunque, con il punteggio in centesimi che resiste all’introduzione delle novità (ma niente punteggi scorporati e non ci sono più i Mappamondi).

Al 2° posto, l’Osteria Francescana di Massimo Bottura a Modena con 98/100.

Segue al 3° posto il ristorante Piazza Duomo di Enrico Crippa ad Alba (CN) a 97/100.

La Top Five è completata da Atelier Moessmer di Norbert Niederkofler a Brunico (BZ) e Uliassi a Senigallia (AN) con Tre Forchette e il punteggio di 96/100.

Al 5° posto ci sono Le Calandre dei fratelli Alajmo a Rubano (PD) con 95/100.

Nella classifica dettata dalle Tre Forchette sono 56 i ristoranti che ricevono il massimo riconoscimento. In aumento di un ristorante rispetto all’edizione dell’anno scorso. Che vedeva in testa il trio Osteria Francescana, Piazza Duomo e Reale di Niko Romito a 97/100.

Ed è ancora l’Abruzzo a vincere il premio Ristorante dell’anno 2027 della Guida del Gambero Rosso: il riconoscimento va all’Osteria dei Maltagliati di Torano Nuovo (TE). Cioè il ristorante di Maicol Capriotti e Federica Brandimarte che, dopo le esperienze nell’alta ristorazione, hanno scelto un piccolo borgo per costruire un’offerta fondata sulla brace, sui grandi tagli e sul vino, affiancando alla tavola anche l’ospitalità.

Invece, le migliori trattorie con Tre Gamberi sono 61, mentre 21 locali ricevono le Tre Bottiglie per la selezione del vino è parte centrale dell’esperienza.

Il riconoscimento Chef emergente del Gambero Rosso 2027 va a Genya Malafronte di Legàmi, a Morro d’Oro (TE)

Sextantio – Cucina, a Santo Stefano di Sessanio (AQ), è la Novità dell’anno.

Cascina Lago Scuro, a Stagno Lombardo (CR), riceve il premio Cucina e territorio.

Il ristorante daGorini, a San Piero in Bagno (FC), riceve il premio per il Menu degustazione dell’anno

Somnium di Pasquale Trotta, a Eboli (SA), riceve il premio Ricerca e innovazione.

Il premio per la migliore pasta fresca va Al Cambio a Bologna.

Ristorante che valorizza al meglio l’olio Evo per la Guida 2027 del Gambero Rosso è il Ristorante degli Angeli a Magliano Sabina.

Sono tre le professioniste premiate come Pastry chef dell’anno 2027 dal Gambero Rosso: Ambra Campodonico del Ristorante Sentiero all’Elba, Rosita Mammone di Uliassi a Senigallia e Martina Tramis di Lilith a San Cesario di Lecce (LE).

Il premio Miglior ospitalità va a Michela Scarello di Agli Amici dal 1887, a Udine.

Non ci sono più i Mappamondi ma Le migliori cucine del mondo in Italia: sono 11.

Luca Belleggia del Pagliaccio di Roma è il Miglior sommelier.

Al Ristorante Del Lago di Bagno di Romagna (FC) il riconoscimento per la Miglior carta dei vini.

Hebbo di Dobbiaco riceve il premio per la Migliore mescita.

La novità più evidente riguarda il sistema di valutazione. I simboli di riferimento diventano tre: Forchette per i ristoranti, Gamberi per le trattorie e Bottiglie per i luoghi del vino. Bistrot e cucine internazionali vengono riclassificati in base all’offerta, mentre per i ristoranti scompare il punteggio scorporato: resta il voto complessivo in centesimi, che prende in esame cucina, cantina e servizio. Una scelta che valorizza l’identità di ogni locale e restituisce al lettore un giudizio sull’esperienza nel suo insieme.

La guida rende inoltre omaggio a Dal Pescatore Santini, Enoteca Pinchiorri e Don Alfonso 1890, Tre Forchette fin dalla prima edizione del 1990. Accanto ai riconoscimenti per il rapporto qualità prezzo, le avanguardie e le migliori cucine del mondo, compare la selezione “Ci tornerei domani”, che riprende il filo conduttore dell’edizione. Il percorso prosegue anche sul digitale: i contenuti della guida diventano interrogabili, geolocalizzati e indicizzati sui motori di ricerca, raccogliendo la sfida dell’intelligenza artificiale.

Nell’anno in cui il Gambero Rosso festeggia i quarant’anni, la guida riparte da una domanda concreta: dove si vorrebbe tornare già domani? Un criterio che attraversa il lavoro di oltre cento professionisti, coordinati dalle curatrici Valentina Marino e Annalisa Zordan, e mette al centro il gusto, l’accoglienza e la piacevolezza complessiva dell’esperienza. Ne emerge il racconto di una ristorazione sotto pressione per l’aumento dei costi e la difficoltà di trovare personale, ma capace di cercare nuove formule e opportunità anche lontano dai percorsi più battuti.

«La domanda da cui siamo partiti è semplice: in quali ristoranti vorremmo tornare domani? Cerchiamo luoghi che abbiano qualcosa da dire attraverso la verità del piatto, l’accoglienza e le persone. La ristorazione italiana cambia più velocemente delle categorie con cui siamo abituati a raccontarla: il nostro compito è riconoscerne la qualità, da una grande tavola d’autore a un’osteria di provincia. A quarant’anni dalla nascita del Gambero Rosso, continuiamo a farlo con curiosità e scelte nette» dichiara Lorenzo Ruggeri, direttore responsabile del Gambero Rosso.

«Abbiamo voluto una guida più immediata da leggere, capace di seguire l’evoluzione dei locali senza costringerli in categorie troppo rigide. I simboli cambiano, ma l’attenzione rimane sulle materie prime, sull’ospitalità, sulla cucina e sul vino. Ci interessa aiutare il lettore a scegliere il posto giusto per il tipo di esperienza che cerca: un Tre Gamberi e un Tre Forchette esprimono la stessa eccellenza, ciascuno nel proprio linguaggio» commentano le curatrici Valentina Marino e Annalisa Zordan.

Dall’economia ai campi di ulivo, il mio percorso è una ricerca continua di qualità e sostenibilità. Ho trasformato la passione in professione diventando una figura poliedrica nel settore: dalla critica enogastronomica a "naso" professionista, provo a sintonizzarmi con vini, oli extravergine, pizze, cucina e molto altro. Il mio approccio? Un insolito mash-up tra rigore strategico ed esperienza sensoriale pura. Sempre in viaggio tra l'Italia e l'estero, esploro le filiere con il mantra imprescindibile della sostenibilità, in vigna così come nei bilanci. Quando non sono impegnata in un panel di assaggio o in un'azienda agricola, mi trovate immersa tra i numeri o tra le pagine dei classici della letteratura.

#1227. Anthropic's IPO is risky business

Anthropic's much-anticipated initial public offering is giving potential investors some perspective on the risky business of artificial intelligence.

More than 90 pages of Anthropic's IPO prospectus, revealed Monday, center on the AI lab's multitude of corporate risk factors, many of which go beyond the kinds of boilerplate scenarios typically found in corporate filings.

From the end of humanity to the company's current clash with the Trump administration, Anthropic's IPO document underscores how one of the most well-capitalized startups in history foresees the future of its operations.

The Claude maker's risks include a laundry list of ways its models can cause harm, including potentially "catastrophic or existential risks to humanity."

It's imperative for Anthropic to emphasize AI safety because failure to do so could adversely affect its "brand, business, financial condition, and results of operations," the filing said. But fierce competition, market pressure and stakeholder expectations make the task of safely developing and implementing bleeding-edge foundation models particularly challenging.

Anthropic can't guarantee that its AI safety efforts will be adequate, as the technology's inherent complexity makes it difficult for the company to plan for and predict every potential scenario.

The public's souring position on data centers poses a major risk for Anthropic, which relies on an ever-expanding portfolio of state-of-the-art computing facilities to train and maintain its prized foundation models.

And with the midterm elections approaching, the tech industry's massive data center buildout has turned political, with lawmakers in 16 states considering moratoriums, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures.

"Opposition to data center development  has also become more organized and coordinated across jurisdictions and our public profile may draw particular attention to projects associated with us," the filing said.

Anthropic's future success depends not only on building giant data centers, but also on the electrical and related power infrastructure needed to juice those computing facilities.

The lack of "sufficient electrical power" across the nation and world poses big risks to Anthropic and its rivals, the filing notes. Even if energy becomes more readily available through "on-site natural gas-fired generation," that power could become more expensive with so much demand, the filing said.

Rivals like OpenAI and Meta have come under fire from lawmakers and plaintiffs' attorneys over allegations that the design and implementation of their AI models and apps have fostered certain child-safety-related harms. Meta recently agreed to pay roughly $17 billion in a settlement with multiple state AGs in litigation involving child mental health and technology addiction.

Thus far, Anthropic has largely avoided scrutiny, but the filing noted that the company could potentially face its own legal headaches. Based on its terms of service, minors aren't allowed to access Claude and related products.

Anthropic knows it has work to do protecting children "as adoption of our models grows, including by minors and other vulnerable users, notwithstanding our efforts to restrict such access."

The company calling to pace the frontier also says it's a risk to move too slowly.

Anthropic needs to keep racing and needs the rest of the business world to keep up. If companies curb their AI spending, Anthropic could feel the burn.

"If the market for our models, platform, and applications develops more slowly than we expect or declines, our growth may slow or stall, and our business, financial condition, and results of operations could be adversely affected," the filing says.

The prospectus also cites reduced demand for frontier models as a risk. Customers might find that lower-cost models work fine for them and that "incremental performance gains at the frontier do not justify the additional cost," instead choosing cheaper, or open-source alternatives.

#1232. Will a new code end 'rip-off parking charges'?

Rosey Greenwood was asked to pay Â£1,906 because she took more than five minutes to pay for parking

"I was completely on edge, every single day," said Rosey Greenwood. "I had letters coming through - I had debt collectors after me."

Two years ago, Rosey was being told to pay Â£1,906 because she had taken too long to pay for parking.

Rosey had paid every single time she parked at the Copeland Street car park in Derby, and had bank records to prove it. But Rosey had unknowingly broken the car park's terms and conditions, which stipulated that drivers must pay within five minutes of entering.

Rosey could not afford to pay Â£1,906 - she was due to get married and also saving up to buy her first home.

As she prepared to fight the case in court, her fiance emailed the BBC and asked us to "shed some light" on what was happening.

The case was then raised in Parliament, external by Derby North MP Catherine Atkinson, who described the charges - which had caught out countless other motorists - as a "five-minute rip-off charge".

The parking sector subsequently banned the five-minute payment rule by updating its code of practice, external, but the government is going further by bringing in a statutory Private Parking Code of Practice.

"These charges leave people feeling ripped off and out of pocket, so I'm putting a stop to them," Prime Minister Andy Burnham said, external on Monday.

But will the new code actually put the brakes on "rip-off" parking charges?

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said parking charges left people "feeling ripped off"

The government's new Private Parking Code of Practice was laid out in Parliament on Tuesday.

It sets out standards that parking operators must follow.

Housing and communities minister Florence Eshalomi said, external the new code "will give drivers a range of rights and protections to make these unfair practices a thing of the past".

The code is now subject to a 40-day period of parliamentary scrutiny, during which MPs and peers can object before it is formally issued.

The code will then come into force 21 calendar days from the point of issue.

The five-minute payment rule - as stipulated on this sign - had already been banned by the parking sector itself

In places, the code appears to be very similar to the private parking sector's existing code of practice, external.

For example, Eshalomi said drivers would "now have a guaranteed minimum five minutes to decide whether to park", known as the consideration period.

However, the sector's code already gives drivers a minimum consideration period of five minutes, so this does not appear to be new.

The government's code also gives drivers a 10-minute grace period, external in which to leave a car park following the end of their permitted stay.

However, the sector's code already gives drivers a 10-minute grace period, so this does not appear to be new either.

The government's code sets the maximum parking charge at Â£100, or Â£60 if paid within a fortnight. This is also the same as in the sector's code.

The government's code states charges should be reduced to Â£20 on appeal, external under four circumstances: not displaying a parking permit despite having a valid one, entering the wrong vehicle registration into a parking machine, not entering a registration at all, and not displaying a Blue Badge despite having one.

The sector's code already said charges should be reduced to Â£20 under those circumstances.

Parking operators will also still be allowed to add a Â£70 debt recovery fee, external to each parking charge if drivers do not pay, as well as court fees and legal costs.

Car park operators who break the rules should, in theory, lose access to DVLA data

The government code states parking charges should be cancelled on appeal where the driver or a passenger in the vehicle suffers the onset of illness, where the driver or a passenger is delayed by an overrunning medical appointment, where the driver suffers delays due to childcare arrangements, and where a vehicle is broken down.

In contrast, the sector's code said these charges should be reduced to Â£20.

The government's code says parking operators who do not comply will lose access to DVLA vehicle keeper data, meaning they will no longer be able to issue parking charges.

This is meant to happen already, because parking operators need to be members of one of two trade associations in order to access DVLA data, and they can theoretically lose their membership if they break the rules.

Campaigners claim this has not happened in practice, but the government insists it will happen in future.

There will also be what the government describes as a "fully independent Scrutiny and Oversight Board".

Jack Cousens, head of roads policy at the AA, said the benefit of the new code was that it was backed by the government, rather than the parking sector itself.

"That means, if there are any changes to be made, it will come via the government and indeed via the independent scrutiny panel," he added.

"Up until now, the private industry have held the pen on changing the code of practice. Now the pen is firmly in the hand of the government."

Lynda Eagan does not believe the new code will lead to fewer parking charge notices being issued

Both the AA and RAC have welcomed the statutory code of practice - which they campaigned for - but believe it does not go far enough.

For example, the AA believes there needs to be a single and independent appeals process.

"Drivers need to have confidence that when they are making their representations, it's being heard by an independent body, as opposed to the private parking operators and their trade bodies marking their own homework," Cousens said.

The AA also believes the government needs to find an alternative to debt recovery fees and charges, which often "spiral" into the threat of court action and County Court Judgments.

This was how Rosey was asked to pay a total of Â£1,906 for 10 parking charges, and also how Hannah Robinson was asked to pay Â£11,390.

"We've long called for the banning of debt recovery fees being added on top of parking charge notices, and a single independent appeals body to replace the two industry-run ones, but neither have been included [in the code] which is disappointing," head of policy Simon Williams said.

The government said it was "consulting as soon as possible next year on private parking debt recovery fees, including on whether to cut an existing Â£70 cap or scrap the fees altogether".

Parking campaigner Lynda Eagan, who helped Rosey, is sceptical about how much has changed.

"I've been screaming at the TV every time I see someone saying 'we've got these new things'," she said.

"They've tweaked a few things here and there, but it's not actually going to make an awful lot of difference to people.

"How, when not much has really changed, is that going to reduce the number of PCNs [parking charge notices]?"

In response, a Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government spokesperson said: "We don't accept these claims. We've introduced a new Private Parking Code of Practice that will have statutory force and independent oversight.

"We've introduced significant changes to make life fairer for drivers, including cancelling the Â£20 charge for circumstances outside a someone's control like an overrunning medical appointment, and helping motorists get a fairer outcome with strengthened requirements for appeals."

One thing Eagan is looking forward to is the new oversight board, external, although she is concerned it will not be truly independent.

"We are hopeful that it could make some difference to some drivers, and we hope that it stops some of the more spurious claims being stopped at source, but we will be watching," Cousens said.

The International Parking Community said "any changes must remain fair to motorists while staying workable"

The two trade associations for parking operators, which wrote the sector's existing code, are reading and reviewing the government's changes.

Alison Tooze, chief policy officer at the British Parking Association, said: "Overall, the code strikes the right balance between stronger protections for motorists and effective parking management, helping keep communities, businesses and local economies moving."

She said retaining a Â£100 parking charge was important.

"Evidence shows that meaningful deterrents support compliance and good behaviours, helping ensure parking remains available for those who need it and enabling parking to be managed effectively," she added.

A spokesperson for the International Parking Community (IPC) said: "The IPC has long supported a code that raises standards, and we are now reviewing it in detail to understand what it means for motorists, landowners and operators alike.

"Any changes must remain fair to motorists while staying workable, so that compliant motorists are not disadvantaged by those who choose to ignore the rules."

Rosey married her fiance Simon, and they have bought a house together

The Â£1,906 court claim against Rosey was dropped following publicity about the case. She has since married her fiance and they have bought a house together.

She is hopeful the new code will prevent other people going through what she did.

"I feel like our voices have been heard; fellow motorists like myself have been listened to," she said.

"I hope that in the future people won't be so worried or fearful of going into car parks like the one I went to."

#1233. Il ristorante in Sardegna con piatti strepitosi e menù a 44 euro

Nel cuore della Marmilla, dove il paesaggio della Sardegna si fa rurale e collinare, il ristorante Arieddas si impone come modello d’avanguardia della cucina territoriale. In tavola, infatti, arriva tutta l’essenzialità di un menù che traduce la biodiversità locale in un linguaggio gastronomico contemporaneo. Attraverso una rete di micro-fornitori locali, lo chef Francesco Vitale dimostra manico e mente nel rendere concreta la visione di Pier Giorgio Parini, già chef dello stellato Povero Diavolo e consulente della struttura. Quindi, piatti raffinati ma capaci di conservare aspetti rustici.

Il menu è un condensato di sapori della Marmilla, in cui il “tempo dei ricordi” non è rievocato in chiave nostalgica, ma declinato da Francesco Vitale in una visione contemporanea. Che rende onore alla sfida di portare in tavola una tradizione che non tradisce la memoria, ma resta collegata al futuro per affermare la propria identità. Via dunque inutili esercizi di stile per dar voce ad ingredienti di indiscussa qualità e ad un pensiero di cucina “netta”, fatta di estrema pulizia, di equilibrio tra rigore filologico e precisione tecnica.

Arieddas sa creare una elegante liaison tra cibo e cultura, memoria e futuro, antichi saperi ed evoluzione. E lo fa in un ambiente avvolgente e coinvolgente con una cucina che rifugge dall’iper-inflazionato binomio tradizione /evoluzione. Preferisce trasformare le peculiarità agroalimentari dell’entroterra sardo in un’esperienza d’alta cucina rigorosa e alla portata di molti.

La conferma arriva dal menù degustazione “Viaggio in Marmilla” (44 euro), un percorso di 7 assaggi (5 antipasti, un primo e un secondo) che permette di gustare la Sardegna autentica ed il pensiero dello chef ad un prezzo super accessibile.

Ma anche i piatti alla carta offrono un ottimo rapporto qualità – prezzo. Oltre a quelli assaggiati e di cui vi racconto ecco qualche esempio.

— Pane lentu e gallina, 13 €— Pan brioche, fegatini, agrumi e alloro, 12 €— Lorighittas e ragù di cortile, 16 €— Coniglio al Vermentino, 16 €— Sanluri-Brest, 9 €

Con questi prezzi, un pasto completo con 3 piatti salati vi costa in media 45 euro. Difficile fare meglio.

L’entré, pane di semola e farine macinate a pietra con testa in cassetta, è un goloso biglietto da visita che ben predispone all’inizio della degustazione.

Gli antipasti, pensati per essere condivisi, vengono serviti in contemporanea per favorire l’interazione a tavola e quel tanto rimpianto dialogo tra i commensali.

La tartare di pomodoro arrosto con olio all’origano, fichi, mandorla e agrumi (12 euro) è un atlante di colori, profumi e paesaggi di macchia mediterranea. È l’esempio concreto di come una cucina ragionata d’entroterra possa declinare l’ingrediente vegetale con rigore e originalità. Un vero e proprio manifesto di sostenibilità e intelligenza gastronomica che denota l’abilità dello chef nel nobilitare materie prime povere attraverso un’esecuzione tecnica d’autore. Nulla da aggiungere ad un boccone inclusivo e rassicurante al tempo stesso.

Medesimo costrutto per l’anguria al bbq con pesto di basilico ed erbe aromatiche (12 euro), che stravolge la percezione comune attraverso una cottura ancestrale, ma di grandissimo impatto emozionale e di “gola”. Lo chef sa impreziosire la dolcezza del frutto con una piacevole e inattesa tridimensionalità, giocando sui rimandi aromatici del pesto che allunga oltremodo la persistenza. Un bite che rende omaggio alla filosofia agricola, cui conferisce spessore culturale, senza risultare banale. Qui la mano di Parini è evidente anche per ricordo storico.

La Kofta – lo spiedo di pecora e maiale con semi misti, spezie e salsa allo yogurt (13 euro) – è un compendio di eleganza, tecnica e conoscenza della materia. Un piatto che, pur conservando un’anima sarda, strizza l’occhio alla cultura mediorientale, senza mai perdere di vista l’obiettivo. Francesco conferma dunque di saper giocare con dosate contaminazioni e dimostra maturità professionale nel rendere omaggio al genius loci, ampliandone l’orizzonte in maniera ponderata.

L’uovo della festa all’occhio di bue con pomodoro arrosto, pecorino e basilico (12 euro), tra i signature del ristorante, è un inno alla cucina golosa ingentilita dal know-how dello chef. Un boccone rotondo, capace di regalare la purezza strutturale dei sapori “di casa” attraverso consistenze millimetriche e una studiata freschezza.

La zucchina brasata con fondo di carne, riduzione di vino, erbe aromatiche e pecorino (12 euro) è la combinazione tra grandi classici e nuove vibes. Qui da Arieddas i colori vivi e intensi raccontano le colline, la Marmilla, i frutti della terra. Un antipasto che dà continuità alla alla filosofia no-waste in modo leggibile e diretto.

I lorighittas fatti a mano con ragù di cortile e uovo di gallina marinato (15 euro) sono omaggio alla tradizione e esaltazione di un pensiero di cucina in cui la tecnica è a servizio dell’ingrediente. Un primo piatto che compie il miracolo di dar spessore a pochissimi ingredienti, divertendosi a stuzzicare il palato in un crescendo di sensazioni. La texture da manuale di una pasta dai ricami complessi, il ragù perfetto nella cottura e il tocco dell’uovo marinato, rendono questo piatto una felice, golosa versione POP di un classico senza tempo. Una forchettata che nasconde dietro un apparente “così com’è” il lavoro di ricerca dell’armonia.

I filindeu in brodo di pecora (15 euro) sono l’essenza di una cucina testarda, di quella resilenza sincera tra campi e fornelli a tutela della salvaguardia della biodiversità territoriale. Un gusto che va in crescendo, arricchendosi di un pot-pourri di sfumature gustolfattive, ad ogni cucchiaiata. Eclatante per maestria e studio maniacale di dosi e ingredienti. Un piatto che sa asciugare la tradizione portandola a livelli di finezza inattesa e che arriva dritto al cuore di molti nostalgici.

La pecora di Sanluri (12 euro) è in tre diverse cotture, ognuna riservata ad uno specifico taglio. Contemporaneità della mano e della tecnica per questa felice espressione di una cucina riduttivamente etichettata come “di casa”. Ma che è un profondo e atavico insieme di gesti innati della cultura gastronomica locale. Impossibile resistere a questo grande classico sardo che stupisce per cotture e lavorazione.

Il gelato di Arieddas alla crema, accompagnato da ciò che la stagione e il territorio offrono (9 euro) è un piacevole gioco di gusto che incuriosisce l’ospite, invitandolo a comporre il proprio abbinamento ideale, attingendo dal territorio. Un’idea fresca per ritoccare un tipico “fine pasto”.

La winelist dà giustamente spazio ai vini della Cantina Su’Entu, che ospita il locale, cui si affianca una corretta selezione di bottiglie sarde, nazionali ed internazionali. Una carta che sa parlare tanto all’appassionato quanto al tradizionalista, senza far sentire in difetto nessuno.

A rendere più piacevole l’esperienza è un servizio di sala, professionalmente informale, che sa accogliere l’avventore e il cliente con sorriso e savoir-faire.

Arieddas – La Cucina della Marmilla. S.P, 48/Km 1,8, 09025 Sanluri VS. Telefono: 070 705 0418. Instagram

Dall’economia ai campi di ulivo, il mio percorso è una ricerca continua di qualità e sostenibilità. Ho trasformato la passione in professione diventando una figura poliedrica nel settore: dalla critica enogastronomica a "naso" professionista, provo a sintonizzarmi con vini, oli extravergine, pizze, cucina e molto altro. Il mio approccio? Un insolito mash-up tra rigore strategico ed esperienza sensoriale pura. Sempre in viaggio tra l'Italia e l'estero, esploro le filiere con il mantra imprescindibile della sostenibilità, in vigna così come nei bilanci. Quando non sono impegnata in un panel di assaggio o in un'azienda agricola, mi trovate immersa tra i numeri o tra le pagine dei classici della letteratura.

#1235. Melania Trump-brokered local ceasefire begins as Russia continues attacks on Ukraine

As a ceasefire brokered by First Lady Melania Trump took effect in a city in southern Ukraine, Russia continued pounding Ukraine's cities overnight.

The local ceasefire, due to last until Saturday in Russia-occupied Oleshky near the Crimean Peninsula, began at 3:00 a.m. local time to permit humanitarian aid to reach the city's inhabitants who are stranded amid shortages of food, water, and medicines.

Oleshky, in Ukraine's partially occupied Kherson region, lies across the Dnipro River from the city of Kherson, about 340 miles southeast of Kyiv. Russian forces captured the town at the start of their 2022 invasion

The temporary Oleshky ceasefire came as Kyiv reported Russian ballistic missile and drone attacks targeting some of Ukraine's biggest cities overnight.

As many as 16 ballistic missiles and 280 drones were launched by Russia, resulting in casualties, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said early Tuesday.

"Almost everywhere, Russia's targets were the energy sector, logistics, and ordinary urban infrastructure," Zelenskyy said.

"Strikes are taking place every day. Russia is constantly taking new steps toward escalation."

The developments come ahead of a new round of trilateral peace talks between Ukraine, Russia and the U.S.

Following a visit to Europe by U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff for separate talks with Zelenskyy and Putin, the leaders emphasized that they were open to negotiations, but security guarantees were essential.

On Tuesday, Putin held talks with leaders of bordering countries, Finland's President Alexander Stubb and Norway's Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre, to discuss diplomatic efforts to end the conflict.

In a phone call, Stubb and Støre emphasized to Putin that their countries would continue to support Ukraine and that negotiations to end the war must resume, according to the Norwegian government.

The so-called "energy ceasefire" announced by President Donald Trump on Oct. 11 appears to have failed to yield any meaningful outcome.

A deal with the U.S. that will see Russia supply global markets with diesel, as well as recently reported restrictions on military applications of SpaceX's Starlink internet service, led Ukrainian officials to warn that Russia was emboldened to intensify attacks on civilian and energy targets.

#1247. GM will switch to Nasdaq from the NYSE on Nov. 17

DETROIT — General Motors plans to transfer shares of its common stock from the New York Stock Exchange to the Nasdaq as the automaker attempts to position itself more as a technology-focused company.

The Detroit automaker said Tuesday that it expects to begin trading as a Nasdaq-listed company on Nov. 17. Its ticker symbol is expected to remain "GM," the company said.

"GM's customer-focused, technology-driven strategy is creating value for our stockholders, making Nasdaq a natural home for our listing as we grow," GM CFO Paul Jacobson said in a release. "We're grateful for our long-standing partnership with the New York Stock Exchange and its remarkable legacy."

GM noted the move will provide eligibility for potential inclusion in the Nasdaq-100 Index.

Current shareholders do not need to take any action with respect to the transfer, the company said.

The switch marks a notable loss for the NYSE, as GM first listed on the exchange in 1911. The Detroit automaker also relisted on the stock exchange in 2010 following a government-backed bankruptcy.

GM follows other companies such as Walmart, DoorDash and Palantir Technologies that have transferred from the more traditional NYSE to the historically technology focused Nasdaq in recent years. Hilton Worldwide Holdings last week also announced plans to move trading from the NYSE to Nasdaq.

The key drivers for a listing transfer differ from company to company, but the Nasdaq in 2024 said common reasons include "index inclusion opportunities, cost effective fee structure, brand visibility partnership, access to Nasdaq's event space, and Nasdaq's suite of investor relations and ESG products."

GM's decision comes a week after the automaker held a technology-focused event where executives laid out the company's roadmap for artificial intelligence and self-driving vehicle technologies.

Shares of GM, which has been aggressively buying back stock, have more than doubled since 2024. GM's stock closed Monday at $76.31 per share. The company's market cap is roughly $64.4 billion.

#1248. Spaghetti aglio, olio e peperoncino: ricetta cremosa alla romana

Quando ho letto in questo modo si scioglierà creando una crema perfetta senza stracciare ho avuto un sussulto. Da quando in qua gli spaghetti aglio, olio e peperoncino, quelli che chiudevano un qualsiasi party giovanile, sono diventati cremosi? L’era internet pare li voglia cremosi almeno a giudicare dai follower che Marco Meschini, chef social, esibisce su Instagram.

Quindi correggete il titolo della ricetta in Spaghetti aglio, olio e peperoncino con mentuccia e pecorino. E non sono una boutade perché la ricetta che leggete di seguito è pubblicata nel libro Pasta per tutti i gusti edito da Mondadori Electa. Una ricetta, ci avvertono, che reinterpreta la semplicità della tradizione. Arricchendola con il tocco erbaceo e fresco della mentuccia e la sapida cremosità del pecorino romano.

Modestamente Marco Meschini propone questi spaghetti che sono – copio incollo – la sua versione iconica, migliore e definitiva (sic) di uno dei classici più amati di sempre.

Però poi questa idea del pecorino è nelle corde del giovane food creator che ha i suoi natali nel quartiere tiburtino. Nel libro raccoglie 80 ricette che rappresentano la sua idea di cucina immediata e profondamente legata alla tradizione romanesca. Quindi, se avete intenzione di regalarvi o regalare il libro, sappiate che dentro ci trovate il sacro quartetto: carbonara, amatriciana, gricia, cacio e pepe. Ma anche variazioni come l’amatrigialla e la gricia alle pere, quella da non dire al contadino.

E quindi che formaggio sia in questa versione degli spaghetti aglio, olio e peperoncino visto che Marco Meschini usa la salsa cacio e pepe anche nella ricetta con la porchetta. La cacio e pepe è proposta anche con scampi e lime (qui la crema deve essere più fluida per un piatto leggero), con le cozze e il lime e pure con il gambero rosso. Il pecorino, insomma, lo ama senza dubbi.

Pasta per tutti i gusti. Mondadori Electa. 224 pp. 22,90 €

Nuestros logros hablan de aquello que hacemos; nuestras decisiones, nuestra integridad y nuestra manera de tratar a los demÃ¡s revelan quiÃ©nes somos.

Van Gogh muriÃ³ en 1890 sin conocer la admiraciÃ³n universal que despertarÃ­an sus pinturas. Hoy su obra continÃºa iluminando la sensibilidad de generaciones enteras, recordÃ¡ndonos que las consecuencias de una existencia pueden extenderse mucho mÃ¡s allÃ¡ del tiempo que nos corresponde vivir. Su reconocimiento posterior no borra el dolor que experimentÃ³, pero permite reconocer la fecundidad de una obra que trascendiÃ³ a su creador.

QuizÃ¡ por eso la vida exige una forma de esperanza: trabajar con responsabilidad sin exigir garantÃ­as de reconocimiento, perseverar sin convertir cada dificultad en una derrota y comprender que algunas de nuestras mejores contribuciones quizÃ¡ florezcan cuando ya no estemos presentes para contemplarlas.

MartÃ­n Descalzo nos recuerda, en una reflexiÃ³n sobre la grandeza, que el desaliento no tiene por quÃ© escribir la Ãºltima palabra de nuestra historia.

Y acaso la enseÃ±anza mÃ¡s profunda de Van Gogh sea que no necesitamos conocer el destino de todo cuanto sembramos para encontrar sentido en el acto de sembrar. Porque al final de la existencia quizÃ¡ descubramos que lo importante no fue cuÃ¡ntas personas admiraron nuestra obra, sino cuÃ¡ntas vidas recibieron algo de nuestra luz.

Que una vida concluya antes de contemplar su cosecha no disminuye el milagro de su siembra. Hay existencias que, aun en silencio, dejan una huella profunda, valiosa y luminosa en el alma de los demÃ¡s.
