#1258. A 'canary in the coal mine': Measles resurgence exposes weaknesses in U.S. public health, experts say

For nearly two years, the U.S. has had to swallow an uncomfortable reality: A highly infectious disease it once eliminated is spreading again.

More than 4,400 measles cases and at least three deaths have been reported nationwide this year, marking the country's worst outbreak in more than three decades. The spike followed nearly 2,300 cases in 2025. But many public health experts argue that the return of measles isn't the only concerning development — it's also what the resurgence signals about America that's causing alarm.

Measles is often described as one of the most contagious viruses, and it is uniquely unforgiving of weaknesses in public health defenses. A safe and highly effective vaccine has existed for decades.

But the virus's spread exposes declining vaccination rates, eroding trust in health institutions and growing challenges in persuading people to protect themselves, their children and their communities, experts said.

Together, those vulnerabilities have made measles a revealing test of the country's public health defenses. For some experts, the resurgence of a disease the U.S. eliminated more than two decades ago is a warning sign of its ability to contain future threats, from other vaccine-preventable diseases to emerging pathogens.

"Measles is the canary in the coal mine for so many different reasons," said Jennifer Nuzzo, an epidemiology professor and director of the Pandemic Center at Brown University School of Public Health. "It's the canary in the coal mine for other vaccine-preventable illnesses, where we could see a return of things that used to harm kids, but also for very acute, no-notice dangerous infectious disease emergencies."

The U.S. is on track to lose its official measles elimination status during an upcoming review by the Pan American Health Organization, which will meet in Washington, D.C., in mid-November.

"It says a lot about a country if it is unable to control measles," said Nuzzo, who is one of 10 experts CNBC spoke with about the ongoing outbreak and its implications.

The U.S. has the tools to prevent measles from spreading. But pockets of low vaccination coverage are leaving the country vulnerable.

The measles, mumps and rubella, or MMR, vaccine is about 97% effective against measles after two doses, while a single dose is 93% effective, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Yet data aggregated by the CDC shows that vaccination coverage for that shot among U.S. kindergarteners fell to 92.4% in the 2025-2026 school year, which is below the 95% threshold public health officials generally recommend to prevent sustained transmission.

That translates to 280,000 kindergarteners who did not complete their MMR vaccination series, according to the CDC. Childhood vaccination exemptions in the U.S. also reached a record high 4.2% for incoming kindergartners during the 2025-2026 school year, up from 3.6% the previous year, the agency says.

"The bottom line is that not enough people are vaccinating their kids," said Brown's Nuzzo.

While some cases stem from international travel, much of the recent spread has been driven by local transmission in "too many" communities where vaccination coverage falls below 95%, she added.

Among states across the U.S. collecting MMR vaccine data, 67% of counties and jurisdictions now have immunization rates below 95%, according to a September investigation by NBC News.

Recent U.S. outbreaks have often occurred in "closely knit communities" where people have frequent contact and low vaccination coverage, said Dr. William Moss, an epidemiology professor at Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health.

But declining vaccination rates do not mean most Americans have turned against immunization. Polling suggests broad support for childhood vaccines. A July KFF survey found that many Americans sit in a more uncertain middle ground about the shots, leaving room for conflicting information to influence their decisions.

"This is not an edge-case issue," Nuzzo said, adding that the vast majority of parents still vaccinate their children.

Even if outbreaks are concentrated in a minority of communities, it can create a "dangerous situation" far from those areas, she said. Infants too young to be vaccinated and people who cannot receive immunizations for medical reasons can be particularly vulnerable when the virus spreads into communities with high vaccination rates.

Those risks come as the Trump administration reshapes federal vaccine policy.

President Donald Trump signed an executive order in August suggesting that the combined MMR vaccine be split into separate shots, while repeating false claims about its safety. Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has also overhauled a key federal advisory committee responsible for recommending childhood immunizations, though the changes are frozen amid ongoing litigation.

Several experts told CNBC that such moves risk further eroding confidence in vaccines and weakening efforts to protect children.

Public health infrastructure was also "really decimated by Covid," and the CDC in particular lost many experienced scientists and physicians "who had spent their lives working on vaccine-preventable diseases," said Scott Weaver, a virologist who is the research director of Galveston National Laboratory.

He added that the CDC, as of September, is also no longer immediately incorporating state-reported "measles-associated" deaths into its national published tally, making it harder to track outbreaks in real time. The agency lists three measles-related deaths in 2026, but Pennsylvania has reported at least five deaths.

"We have folks in federal health leadership right now that are throwing gasoline on the fire, and that is not helping the situation," said Jess Steier, a public health scientist and founder and CEO of Unbiased Science, an organization that aims to make complex scientific concepts understandable.

If the U.S. fails to materially improve vaccination rates, the measles resurgence could extend beyond ongoing outbreaks.

At "current" state-level vaccination rates, measles could become endemic again in the U.S., resulting in an estimated 851,300 cases over 25 years, according to a large-scale epidemiological model published in JAMA in April 2025 by researchers at Stanford and other institutions. Under that scenario, the model predicts the measles cases could lead to 170,200 hospitalizations and 2,550 deaths over that period.

The model, which simulated infectious disease spread in the U.S. at various childhood vaccination levels, relies on immunization data from 2004 to 2023 for that baseline scenario.

Michael Osterholm, an epidemiologist and the director of the Center for Infectious Disease Research and Policy at the University of Minnesota, said he views the measles situation in Canada as a direct warning for the U.S.

Canada lost its official measles elimination status in November after a multi-province outbreak that generated more than 5,400 cases across 10 jurisdictions in 2025. Canada has a population of more than 40 million people.

"We have a population of 350 million. If you extrapolate, if we had the very same experience that Canada had over the next year or two, that would be up to 50,000 cases of measles in the U.S.," Osterholm said. "I think that's a potential future we have to be mindful of."

An even larger measles outbreak isn't the only potential problem.

Vaccination coverage for other childhood diseases has similarly declined. The share of U.S. kindergartners vaccinated against polio fell to 92.4% in the 2025-2026 school year, while coverage for diphtheria, tetanus and acellular pertussis, or DTaP, dropped to 92%, according to CDC data.

The U.S. has already seen a sharp rise in pertussis, or whooping cough. U.S. reported cases reached roughly 43,300 in 2024 and nearly 28,000 in 2025, up substantially from pandemic-era levels, according to the CDC. Brown's Nuzzo said the resurgence reflects, in part, fewer people getting vaccinated and the fact that protection from the pertussis vaccine wanes over time.

The simulation model published in JAMA also examined how falling childhood immunization rates could affect the future spread of several diseases previously eliminated from the U.S. through vaccines. Under current vaccination levels, the researchers found that diseases including rubella and polio were unlikely to become endemic in the U.S.

But in a hypothetical scenario in which childhood vaccination rates fell by 50%, the model projected 9.9 million cases of rubella, 4.3 million cases of polio and 197 cases of diphtheria over 25 years.

Rubella can cause devastating complications when an infection during pregnancy passes to a developing fetus, while polio can cause paralysis and death, said Dr. Nathan Lo, assistant professor of infectious diseases at Stanford Medicine.

The projections are not predictions that these outbreaks will occur, but they illustrate how much risks could grow if vaccination coverage deteriorates.

"What vaccines often buy you is not just the protection, but also less uncertainty," said Mathew Kiang, an assistant professor of epidemiology and population health at Stanford Medicine who also worked on the simulation model. "I think even more frightening is just the really wide uncertainty that we just wouldn't be sure of what could happen."

The measles resurgence is also raising questions about how effective the U.S. can be at detecting and responding to emerging public health threats before they spread.

"Public health is all about prevention," said Dr. Manisha Juthani, president of the Association of State and Territorial Health Officials and commissioner of the Connecticut Department of Public Health. She said the country must maintain its ability to detect threats, invest in surveillance, and recognize that infectious diseases do not respect national borders.

Those capabilities are crucial for curbing emerging pathogens, especially when scientists initially know little about how a new disease spreads, how severe it is or how to treat it. A pathogen could spread before vaccines or treatments are available, making early detection, clear public communication and coordination especially important.

Other experts argue that weaknesses in those capabilities could also have implications for the country's defenses against deliberate biological attacks.

In an April 2025 op-ed, Steph Batalis, a research fellow at Georgetown University's Center for Security and Emerging Technology, argued that the measles outbreak exposed a broader vulnerability in the U.S.' biodefense strategy and, specifically, a weakened ability to deter potential biological attacks.

She argued that the country's struggle to contain a known, vaccine-preventable disease "might only embolden those who see our public health vulnerabilities as an opportunity."

But Osterholm, who works extensively on bioterrorism, said low MMR immunization rates and rising measles cases do not necessarily indicate that Americans would refuse a vaccine or antibiotic during a biological emergency. The shots and drugs used to counter biological threats can differ from those routinely administered to the public, he said, and the prospect of a severe outbreak could prompt urgency among the public to seek protection.

That point highlights an important limitation: The measles resurgence by itself does not establish whether the U.S. could withstand entirely different or novel public health threats.

But as a disease the U.S. knows how to prevent spreads, experts say the stakes of addressing those vulnerabilities extend to whatever might come next.

#1260. Pizzoccheri originali della Valtellina: ricetta per farli cremosi

Grano Saraceno e formaggio Valtellina Casera Dop sono le caratteristiche dei pizzoccheri originali, quelli veri, della Valtellina. Diffidate dalle imitazioni e ricordate che una quota del 20% o poco più è riservata alla farina di grano tenero 00. Eliminarla significa fare una pasta gluten free e dunque adatta ai celiaci.

Non possono mancare altri ingredienti nella composizione del piatto tipico valtellinese. Sono patate, verze, burro d’alpe. Non ve ne priverete in alcuna stagione: al posto della verza sono ammessi coste o fagiolini.

Dove sono nati i pizzoccheri? L’ingrediente principale, cioè la farina di grano saraceno, arriva da lontano. Nel tardo Medioevo il grano saraceno arriva attraverso l’Europa Centrale e il Mar Nero dalla Manciuria e dalla Siberia. E trova residenza stabile nei campi terrazzati della Valtellina. La sua farina scura è il protagonista dei pizzoccheri. La nascita si vuole nel piccolo borgo di Teglio – nel cuore della Valtellina – dove nel 2002 è nata l’Accademia del Pizzocchero. A lei è affidata conservazione e diffusione della ricetta originale dei pizzoccheri.

Che prevede anche l’impiego del Valtellina Casera Dop, formaggio da latte vaccino parzialmente scremato. Perché questo formaggio nella ricetta dei pizzoccheri originali? Perché ha una naturale capacità di fondere e amalgamarsi con la pasta e gli altri ingredienti. Con il Casera, la cremosità è assicurata.

E poi c’è il burro da panna del latte delle vacche al pascolo di alta quota. Ancora morbidezza, ancora sapore inconfondibile per i pizzoccheri originali.

E qui ci affidiamo alla leggenda perché di sicuro c’è poco. Se non che Dante e Boccaccio usassero “pinzochera” per indicare povertà e semplicità. Caratteristiche proprie dei pizzoccheri della Valtellina.

Derivazione da questo significato o, come sostengono alcuni studiosi, parola legata alle beghine. Cioè alle suore talmente povere che vivevano al di fuori dei chiostri da nullatenenti. Tranne il loro abito che era un mantello grezzo che ricorda appunto i pizzoccheri. E il nome di pizzocchere era dato a queste suore povere nell’Italia centrale dove erano considerate eretiche.

Leggerete comunque di una ricetta semplice. Ma attenzione: l’Accademia di Teglio non è lì per spargere ciclostili nel mondo. Perché dovreste frequentarla per imparare la scarellatura che non è una fregatura della ricetta. Ma l’arte di lavorare e stendere la sfoglia con il matterello nello spessore ideale delle listarelle da cui ricavare i veri pizzoccheri.

Tocca quindi imparare partendo dalla ricetta dei pizzoccheri.

Sappiate solo che esistono anche i pizzoccheri “bianchi” ma sono della Valchiavenna e che a Milano trovate da Crotto Quartino. Mentre a Teglio avete più di un ristorante che propone i pizzoccheri originali della Valtellina: Ai Tigli, La Galeda, Al Castello (che è anche pizzeria). E li trovate anche negli hotel dove potete soggiornare: Combolo, Bellavista e La Rosa

#1261. PAN names 6 state coordinators ahead of 2027 gubernatorial elections

The National Action Party (PAN) has now announced its presumptive gubernatorial candidates in six states after unveiling its pick in Querétaro on Sunday.

Gubernatorial elections will be held in 17 of Mexico’s 31 states on June 6, 2027. Voters will also elect 500 federal deputies and thousands of other officials at the state and municipal level on the same day.

As is the case with Morena, Mexico’s ruling party, the PAN is calling its presumptive gubernatorial candidates “state coordinators.”

In the PAN’s case, the presumptive candidates’ full title is “state coordinators for the defense of the homeland, the family and freedom.” They are almost certain to be officially designated as the party’s candidates at a later date.

The six presumptive gubernatorial candidates selected so far by the PAN are listed below in alphabetical order by the states they are seeking to govern. The PAN — currently Mexico’s main opposition party — governs four of Mexico’s 32 federal entities, including three states that will hold gubernatorial elections next year (Aguascalientes, Chihuahua and Querétaro).

The PAN has not yet named its presumptive gubernatorial candidates in Aguascalientes, Baja California, Campeche, Colima, Guerrero, Nayarit, Nuevo León, Quintana Roo, San Luis Potosí, Sinaloa or Sonora. It is possible that the PAN and the Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI) will nominate common gubernatorial candidates in some states. The PRI has not yet named any presumptive gubernatorial candidates.

Morena completed the selection of its 17 “state coordinators for the transformation and national sovereignty” last month. The party founded by former President Andrés Manuel López Obrador is currently in office in 23 of Mexico’s 32 federal entities.

#1265. Government turning to AI to solve the acknowledged problem of medication shortages

President Claudia Sheinbaum has introduced an Advisory Council for the Digital Transformation of the Health Sector, aimed at improving control, storage and distribution of medications.

The move was in response to supply shortages publicized during recent mobilizations by Mexican Social Security Institute (IMSS) workers. The president has acknowledged the legitimacy of the complaints.

According to an announcement made during Sheinbaum’s morning press conference on Friday, the council will be divided into two groups of experts.

The first group will be the Advisory Board composed of four researchers specializing in logistics, engineering, information systems, and resource distribution, while the second group — dubbed the Youth AI Team — will be made up of five individuals specialized in Artificial Intelligence.

The project will use digital tools and AI to detect medication shortages, track warehouse inventory and expedite delivery to public hospitals and health centers.

“What we want is to modernize the system to ensure that the entire process — from procurement, warehousing and arrival at the hospital pharmacy, to distribution across various hospital departments and delivery to patients — is automated, so that we know the exact traceability of every medication,” Sheinbaum said on Friday.

Members of the council are expected to present their initial projects in November. The federal government plans to begin implementing the new system in January 2027.

Deputy Health Minister Eduardo Clark said the program aims to identify medication needs in real time, improve inventory management, and optimize distribution routes to reduce both time and costs. If a medication is unavailable at one pharmacy, healthcare staff would be able to determine whether it is in stock at another health facility or warehouse and arrange for its delivery.

Public healthcare workers plan more protests this week to demand better pay and working conditions

The scale of the program’s challenge, however, is considerable.

According to figures presented by Clark, the health sector uses approximately 3 billion units of medicines and medical supplies each year. The products must be distributed among more than 1,000 hospitals and nearly 15,000 health centers and primary care units.

Sheinbaum explained that the lack of medication does not always stem from non-procurement. She noted that there are instances when medications have been purchased but fail to reach medical facilities on time, due to difficulties in the processes of storage, distribution and delivery.

Also, Sheinbaum’s administration recently said it has identified practices in which medications from the public sector end up being sold privately and, in some cases, outside of hospitals.

With reports from Latinus, Eje Central, La Silla Rota and Infobae

#1266. Il ristorante in Penisola Sorrentina che cerca la stella Michelin

Di nuovo al Maxi ristorante del Capo La Gala a Vico Equense. Per confermare, lo anticipo, quanto di buono visto (e assaggiato) due anni fa. Luogo magico, oserei dire stellare, con Mario Acampora che dirige con precisione.

In cucina c’è Emanuel Scotti in costante progressione da tre anni a questa parte. E in sala c’è Giulia Tavolaro che giusto l’anno scorso ha conquistato il premio il premio come Miglior Servizio di Sala del 2026.

Un buon auspicio per la cerimonia del 12 novembre sulle orme di quanto già accaduto al ristorante Cetaria di Baronissi.

Corsi e ricorsi di Totostella che non mi fanno dimenticare di sottolineare che all’hotel Capo La Gala (1 Chiave Michelin) ci sono splendide camere da full immersion di mare e buon cibo. E il Nerea, trattoria di mare veramente sul mare.

Prima di raccontarvi il percorso ora solo stellare, un’occhiata ai prezzi verificati in questo ottobre 2026 che alterna giornate autunnali a quelle di una fine estate lunghissima.

— Sulla cresta dell’onda di 7 portate a 140 €— Radici in viaggio: 6 portate di terra a 130 €— Materia Verde con 3 portate a 80 €— A modo mio, 5 portate salate e un dessert al buio, 120 €

Dalla carta del Maxi del Capo La Gala è possibile scegliere almeno 2 portate salate a persona. Ecco qualche piatto oltre quelli assaggiati.

— Cavolfiore, limone, mandorle, capperi (20 €)— Agnello Laticauda in prima corsa che è una calamarata (30 €)— Crocchettine di cicerchie dei Campi Flegrei cioè tahina, salsa verde, cipolla ramata di Montoro in agrodolce (25 €).

Va da sé che con 2 portate siete a livello di osteria. E comunque in media un pasto completo vi costa 90 euro.

Inizio schioppettante con i benvenuti divertenti e saporiti. Ottimi e anche belli esteticamente. I lievitati di Carlo Gabbiano e Carlo Carandente Coscia lasciano sempre un segno positivo. Il problema diventa fermarsi. Pane grissini e un Danubio al top. In abbinamento l’olio dell’azienda agricola Russo di Vico Equense e il burro.

La Merenda di Ciccio – Katsu-sando di coniglio all’ischitana, gambero rosso e rafano (25 €) – è un omaggio all’amicizia tra lo chef e il vecchio amico pescatore che portava i gamberi. Qui creano un connubio incredibile con il coniglio che farcisce il lievitato. Bella idea e ottimo sapore

Il Baccalà con fagioli butirri, alghe, zuppa forte (25 €) è piatto molto ben realizzato e gradevole. Baccalà in versione elegante senza rinunciare al sapore.

La Linguina con zuppetta di murena, emulsione ai ricci, lattuga di mare (30 €) è un piatto molto saporito. La murena è ottima protagonista unitamente ai ricci e la cottura della linguina è impeccabile.

Anche il Raviolo con verza, riso e parmigiano (25 €) è gustoso. Una versione originale del classico verza e riso racchiusa in un raviolo molto ben realizzato.

La Ricciola con friarielli, mandarino ed escabeche (35 €) è visivamente bello da vedere, ma soprattutto buono da mangiare. Il sapore per lo chef ischitano, cresciuto alla corte di Gaetano Trovato in Toscana, resta giustamente un caposaldo imprenscindibile.

Il Pollo bianco di Laura Peri con funghi autunnali, patate e spinaci (40 €) è una delizia. Petto cotto alla perfezione e farcito benissimo. Poi la chips di pelle farcita ad accompagnare con gusto una grande materia prima. Il pollo di Laura Perì non tradisce.

Dopo un fresco predessert arriva una buonissima Tarte au citron: lemon curd al limone sfusato amalfitano, meringa, vaniglia di Tahiti (20 €). Siamo felici per l’esecuzione del pastry chef.

Chiusura affidata al Cioccolato al latte con lamponi, noci e miso (20 €).

Maxi del Capo la Gala. Via Luigi Serio, 8, 80069 Vico Equense NA. Telefono: 081 801 5757. Instagram

Il Capo La Gala a Vico Equense è sempre un felicissimo approdo in Costiera Sorrentina con i due ristoranti Maxi e Nerea. La bellezza e l’eccellenza sono di casa grazie alle cure ed alla capacità imprenditoriale di Enzo Acampora e famiglia che hanno fatto di questo luogo una delizia per occhi, palato ed ospitalità.

Le redini sono ora in mano a Mario Acampora, figlio di Enzo.

20 tra camere e suite iper panoramiche, Nerea, la trattoria di mare praticamente quasi nell’acqua, il Maxi che è il ristorante gastronomico. In breve questo è il mondo del Capo La Gala.

Il ristorante Maxi, segnalato in guida Michelin, è guidato dall’anno scorso da Emmanuel Scotti che è allievo di Gaetano Trovato, 2 stelle Michelin storiche in Toscana. Può contare sul sous chef Carlo Carandente, sul pastrychef e panificatore Carlo Gabbiano che ci ha deliziato con lievitati e dessert. Completano la squadra, Marianna Ciufo, Michele Langella, Valerio Montuori e Yesenia Montes Guzman.

La sala è il regno di Giulia Tavolaro, figura storica e riferimento assoluto, vicana doc coadiuvata dal giovane e bravo Mariano Fiorentino.

Inizio scoppiettante con il Ponte con alici, caffè Guatemala di Gianni Frasi e limone bio di Sorrento. La presentazione è molto bella e il sapore non è da meno. Bei contrasti tra i vari elementi con un risultato molto gradevole. Ottimo inizio per collegarsi con quello che arriverà dopo.

È tutta una bufala è un antipasto in grande equilibrio con grandi prodotti. Oltre alla carne di bufalo magistralmente cotta, completano il piatto la ricotta in salvietta di Costanzo e un cremoso di carciofi con brunoise di carciofi arrostiti. Realizzazione da wow.

Scalo di Procida sono le linguine alla brace con insalata di limoni in conserva, ricci di mare, polvere di limoni e le sue foglie. Un primo piatto interessante con sentori di brace che si abbinano benissimo con il resto degli elementi dai sapori decisi per un risultato veramente molto saporito.

Intramontabile è il bottone alla genovese di coda stufata, ostriche perle noir e zuppa di prosciutto e basilico. Gran bel piatto del Maxi Capo La Gala, complesso e gustoso. Volutamente sapido ma buono nel complesso. Il livello resta comunque alto .

Quando arrivi manda un messaggio cioè il risotto alla pizzaiola al nero di seppia che provo in versione ufficiale al Maxi. Bello a vedersi e ottimo da mangiare. Wow.

Benedetta primavera è un rombo cucinato ottimamente e che, come gli altri piatti, si presenta anche molto bene. Si presenta come una rollatina di rombo con verdure primaverili, fiori eduli e salsa Beurre blanc. Direi che qui al Maxi Capo La Gala se esiste una difficoltà in più per lo chef è riuscire a colpire i commensali spesso distratti da uno scenario fantastico che li circonda. Emmanuel Scotti fino ad ora ci riesce.

Con Cambio d’identità arriva in tavola l’agnello Laticauda alla brace, carciofo violetto di Castellammare, salsa aiolì e bernese montata con estrazione di grasso d’agnello. Continua la giostra di sapori molto intensi e identitari. Il bravo chef ischitano si fa forza delle sue esperienze segnanti e soprattutto quella con Gaetano Trovato. Cotture giuste di carne e carciofo e anche quest’ultimo recita la sua parte da protagonista.

Dulcis in fundo assaggiamo le Fragole buone buone, una mousse al lime con inserto al cetriolo, sorbetto al finocchietto, burro d’arachidi e salsa di fragole.

Ottima realizzazione come anche Tu vuo’ fa l’americano. La mousse è alla banana accompagnata da cremoso fondente 55%, biscuit alle mandorle, caramello passion fruit, cioccolato bollato fermentato in bucce di banana, gelato arachidi. Entrambi dolci di spessore che dimostrano le ottime doti di Carlo Gabbiano già a me note per aver assaggiato un eccellente panettone ad un evento. Il pastry chef del Maxi Capo La Gala è da tenere d’occhio.

La cena è una prova superata dallo chef Emmanuel Scotti e dal suo team e spero che il Maxi torni nell’empireo delle stelle dove ha già meritato di stare.

Ci sono solo menu degustazioni con formule interessanti e soprattutto c’è un degustazione open “A 4 mani “ dove due portate le sceglie lo chef e le altre due i commensali. Il costo è di 90 € .

Il degustazione Contemporaneo da 6 portate costa 110 €.

Ancora il degustazione Ci pensa Emmanuel, 6 portare a sorpresa al costo di 110 €

Infine, il degustazione “Artigianato gastronomico “ di 8 portate a 130 €.

#1269. Frozen housing market sends remodelers mixed messages

A version of this article first appeared in the CNBC Property Play newsletter with Diana Olick. Property Play covers new and evolving opportunities for the real estate investor, from individuals to venture capitalists, private equity funds, family offices, institutional investors and large public companies. Sign up to receive future editions, straight to your inbox.

Home remodelers have always served two different markets, but the current state of housing is now pulling them opposite directions. First, people tend to remodel when they move, but high interest rates, high home prices and weak consumer sentiment have put the housing market in a deep freeze. Homeowners also tend to renovate when they are unable or don't want to sell. So which way will the remodeling market shift?

Annual spending on home improvements and repairs is expected to remain relatively flat through late 2027, according to the latest Leading Indicator of Remodeling Activity (LIRA) from the Remodeling Futures Program at the Joint Center for Housing Studies of Harvard University. It puts spending growth on renovation and repairs at just 1.5% year-over-year by the third quarter."Retail spending on building products has been flat to negative, and remodeling permits have stagnated, which points to continued sluggish renovation activity," said Rachel Bogardus Drew, director of the remodeling futures program at the Center, in a release. "We expect annual spending to hover around $525 billion through the third quarter of next year."

The U.S. Census Bureau's monthly read on single-family housing starts for September came in well below expectations, as did building permits, an indicator of future construction. Pending home sales, measured by signed contracts, also plunged beyond expectations, according to the National Association of Realtors.

"These ongoing headwinds could slow growth in remodeling spending even further in the quarters ahead," said Chris Herbert, managing director of the center in the release.

A separate October report from the National Association of Home Builders on sentiment among home remodelers was slightly more positive, but also did not forecast big growth in 2027.

"Remodeler sentiment remained stable in the third quarter, although remodelers in certain parts of the country continue to report issues with high material costs and finding enough labor to finish projects on time," said Elliott Pike, national chair of the NAHB remodelers council and a remodeler from Homewood, Alabama. "Remodelers also report that economic uncertainty is making some potential customers hesitant to move forward with projects."

Finally, another October report from Houzz, an AI platform for construction and design professionals and homeowners, showed an improved outlook, with some caveats.

"Construction pros are closing out 2026 with optimism, as expectations reach their highest level since early 2022 following a rebound from a long stretch of slow activity. Design firms are more measured, though cautiously optimistic," said Marine Sargsyan, head of economic research at Houzz. "Fuel costs remain a pressure point for most businesses, with some pros passing them on to clients through higher prices and surcharges and others absorbing them in their margins."

#1270. How a Johnson Mentor Shapes the Next Generation of NASA Talent

When Rice University student Malvika Bhardwaj asked her mentor Daniel Cohen, a Guidance, Navigation & Control (GN&C) engineer at NASA’s Johnson Space Center, whether he had time to keep teaching interns with his busy workload, he answered, “You decide what’s important.”

In honor of National Mentoring Day on Oct. 27, Bhardwaj reflects on how Cohen’s advice and support has shaped her internship experience at Johnson.

Through NASA’s Office of STEM Engagement, interns like Bhardwaj contribute to agency projects while learning from NASA mentors and gaining technical skills and hand-on experience to build a future career in space exploration.

Bhardwaj studies computational and applied mathematics at Rice University and interns with the GN&C team, which focuses on how spacecraft determine their position and maneuver in orbit. She is developing tools to analyze thruster firings on the U.S. Deorbit Vehicle that will help NASA safely deorbit the International Space Station at the end of its operational life. Bhardwaj also uses computer simulations to test the vehicle’s control system and identify conditions under which it could fail.

“I’ve learned about the culture of community and support at Johnson and NASA as a whole. Daniel made an effort to introduce me to the team and include me in conversations and meetings. I saw how team members step up to help one another and keep the whole unit moving forward,” Bhardwaj said.

Cohen, a Rice University alumnus with a master’s in mechanical engineering, began his NASA career as a flight operations intern in 2020. He later held internships in docking dynamics, propulsion systems, and GN&C analysis before joining Johnson as a full-time engineer in August 2024.

His current work includes developing simulations and models for studies of the U.S. Deorbit Vehicle, analyzing its control algorithms and GN&C performance, and evaluating SpaceX’s design at multiple life-cycle reviews.

He also analyzes settings for the Orion spacecraft’s docking camera, which provides positioning measurements that can help inform navigation during future Artemis rendezvous activities.

Cohen supports Bhardwaj beyond her internship, giving her a closer look at how colleagues collaborate on projects and share ideas. He sets aside a couple of hours each week to teach interns topics such as orbital mechanics and control systems.

Bhardwaj took Cohen’s advice to heart: How she spends her time and energy reflects what she values. She believes that her internship has shown her that problem-solving is rarely an individual effort. Team members bring different perspectives and need to understand how their work connects to a larger project.

Working alongside interns in outreach, social media, and digital design has also broadened Bhardwaj’s view of STEM careers. “No matter what interests you, there’s likely a role for you here,” she said.

She was proud to complete her first project, a set of analysis tools she built from scratch. Working through the debugging process and seeing a finished, functioning product was especially rewarding.

Bhardwaj’s advice to students interested in NASA internships is to apply even if they do not feel fully prepared.

“You’re probably never going to feel 100% ready, but so much of the learning happens on the job,” she said. “Trust in your ability to navigate new environments.”

NASA explores the unknown in air and space, innovates for the benefit of humanity, and inspires the world through discovery.

#1275. Mining giant Grupo México plans to expand its US copper operations to the tune of US $4-6B

The mining and transportation conglomerate Grupo México announced on Thursday plans to double down on its investments in its U.S. copper mining unit, Asarco.

Grupo México plans to spend between US $4 billion and $6 billion over the next three years on Asarco projects, to expand the Ray and Silver Bell mines in Arizona and restart the Hayden smelter and refinery, the head of the mining division, Leonardo Contreras, told analysts on a call.

The investment is far higher than recent spending on the unit, which totaled just $101 million in 2024, and marks a significant expansion in the U.S. market.

It follows news of a 2% fall in copper output during the third quarter due to lower production in the U.S. and Peru. Even so, the firm’s profits grew by 56% during this period to a net profit of US $2 billion, owing to robust base metal prices. Overall revenue increased by 38% to $6.33 billion, surpassing consensus estimates from analysts polled by LSEG.

Corporate leadership has revised the company’s copper production target downward to 1.026 million metric tonnes in 2026, from the previously targeted 1.034 million tonnes.

Contreras emphasized that work is continuing on expanding the Ray facility as feasibility studies are conducted. In addition, the company is “increasingly optimistic” about the restarting of Hayden, which has an annual processing capacity of 1.4 million metric tonnes of copper concentrate.

“That would represent almost 350,000 metric ⁠tonnes of contained copper,” Contreras said. “If that feeds into our refinery, we could be looking at 500,000 metric tonnes of copper.”

The Silver Bell project is also in the feasibility stage, according to Contreras.

Grupo México plans to assess the potential to integrate Mexican concentrates and U.S. copper scrap into U.S. operations, according to Itaú analysts.

Grupo México will also continue expanding operations in Peru.

Its long-term growth focuses closely on its Peru operations through its Southern Copper subsidiary, with the delayed flagship Tia Maria project expected to finally come online in the first half of 2028.

Southern Copper is developing two other projects in Peru — Los Chancas and Michiquillay, both of which are expected to commence operations in 2032 and are expected to produce 130,000 and 225,000 metric tonnes of copper a year, respectively.

#1278. A rising wealth tide lifts all yachts

A version of this article appeared in CNBC's Inside Wealth newsletter, a weekly guide to the high-net-worth investor and consumer. Sign up to receive future editions, straight to your inbox.

As the yachting industry prepares for the Fort Lauderdale International Boat Show this week, executives are betting that the American wealth machine can continue to power the industry.

Americans now account for about 40% of all global yacht sales, according to industry executives. At the higher end, with yachts over 250 feet, Americans are the majority of the market. Executives say that as demand from Europe and the Middle East has slowed, Americans are increasingly critical for growth.

"Recently, it's the Americans that have increased their purchasing," said Kevin Merrigan, chairman of Northrop & Johnson, the yacht brokerage. "We've had several big closings heading into the end of the year. It's quite remarkable and it's American buyers."

Overall, the yacht industry has slowed since the post-COVID peak of 2022 and 2023. For the year through September, global sales of pre-owned yachts over 78 feet are down about 1% from the same period last year, while sales value fell about 5%, according to Northrop & Johnson.

Orders of new yachts over 78 feet were down slightly, from 266 last year to 216 year-to-date in 2026, according to Northrop & Johnson. Yet the yachting market increasingly mirrors the new top-heavy structure of global wealth, with centimillionaires and billionaires gaining wealth the fastest.

Orders for yachts between 40 meters and 50 meters (131 feet and 164 feet) increased from 49 sales to 63 sales this year, according to Northrop & Johnson. Brokers say demand is strongest for newly built or good condition large yachts over 200 feet. A buyer ordering a new mega-yacht today might have to wait until 2031 or later for delivery, since the top shipyards are booked solid. So an almost-new mega-yacht can fetch a large premium.

"In the last four or five years, we've definitely been in a situation where we're inventory constrained at the very top end," said Anders Kurtén, CEO of Fraser Yachts. "Demand is greater than supply."

The yacht charter business has also fallen off its post-pandemic peak. While the summer started out weak, due mainly to the war in the Middle East, charter bookers say business picked up in August and the pipeline looks strong into 2026.

They said many of the charter customers today are young Americans in their 30s and early 40s, and many made their money in tech. Many yachters start with charters before deciding whether to buy their own yacht.

"Charter is the entry level drug," Merrigan said. "We're seeing more and more younger families and couples come into charter."

The Fort Lauderdale International Boat Show, which begins Wednesday, Oct. 28 and features more than 150 yachts, is a big test for the market. Brokers say the Monaco Yacht Show, which was in September, had strong attendance and sales. Kurtén said Fraser had four yachts on display at Monaco and one went into contract during the show.

He said Fraser will have eight or nine yachts on display at Fort Lauderdale. He had planned on more, but in recent weeks the company sold four of the yachts that were scheduled to appear.

"I think that tells you something about the state of the market in general," he said.

#1281. Morelia festival wraps 24th edition; ‘Six Months in a Pink and Blue Building’ takes top honors

A childhood memory reshaped into fiction won big at the recently concluded Morelia International Film Festival, with “6 meses en el edificio rosa con azul” (“Six Months in a Pink and Blue Building”) taking both the judges’ top prize and the audience award.

The double win — the Ojo for best Mexican feature and the audience award in the same category — marked a meeting of jury and moviegoer tastes that the newspaper El Universal described as rare on the festival circuit.

The 104-minute Spanish-language drama is the first fiction feature by Bruno Santamaría Razo, a documentary filmmaker born in Mexico City in 1986.

Planned for a 2027 theatrical release in Mexico — with no streaming dates yet announced — the film follows an 11-year-old boy discovering his feelings for his best friend as his family confronts his father’s HIV diagnosis in 1990s Mexico City.

Reconstructing family memories through imagination rather than strictly retelling events, the film premiered at Cannes Critics’ Week, becoming the first Mexican feature to compete in the section in 20 years.

The 24th edition of the Morelia International Film Festival (FICM) was held in the Michoacán capital from Oct. 16 through Sunday.

For its 25th anniversary next year, FICM officials are promising a landmark edition with major guests, bold retrospectives and a stellar lineup — and it will move the dates to the week immediately before the Day of the Dead.

This year’s festival included 96 Mexican films in competition, alongside international screenings, retrospectives and tributes.

The guest list was strong, as usual, with appearances by directors Guillermo del Toro (“Pan’s Labyrinth”) and Alfonso Cuarón (“Roma”), along with “Y Tu Mamá También” stars Diego Luna and Gael García Bernal — underscoring Morelia’s standing as a gathering place for Mexican cinema.

International guests included U.S. director James Gray, who presented “Paper Tiger,” which competed for the Palme d’Or at Cannes this year. The winner at Cannes, “Fjord,” also played in the FICM.

Festival president and Cinépolis CEO Alejandro Ramírez described this year’s event as a particularly Mexican celebration.

Mexican Nicolás Pereda won best director for “Lo demás es ruido” (“Everything Else Is Noise”), an absurdist comedy about a musician preparing for her first television interview. Its star, Teresa Sánchez, also a Mexican, won best actress.

Sam Louwyck of Belgium took best actor for playing a gay hairdresser in Mexican Nathalia Acevedo’s “Salón de belleza” (“Beauty Salon”).

Mexican Joaquín del Paso’s “El jardín que soñamos” (“The Garden We Dreamed”), about a Haitian family traveling north, earned a special mention and the cinematography award.

Mexican Fernanda Tovar received the first-time director award for “Chicas tristes” (stylized as “Sad Girlz” in translation), about two teenage girls supporting each other after one is sexually abused. Pablo Vaca’s “Forensita” won best Mexican documentary feature.

With reports from El Universal, Variety, Animal MX and Proceso

#1284. Israel election puts Netanyahu’s wartime leadership on the line as Trump urges voters to return him to power

Israeli voters will head to the polls Tuesday in an election with implications beyond the country’s borders.

It is Israel’s first election since Hamas’ Oct. 7, 2023, attacks, which killed around 1,200 people and saw more than 250 abducted. The Palestinian Ministry of Health says Israel’s subsequent military campaign in Gaza has killed more than 74,500 people. It is also the first vote since the U.S. and Israel began their joint war against Iran in February.

With defense at the forefront of the debate for all the main contenders, tens of thousands of Israeli citizens are believed to have flown home to cast their votes in what is expected to be a tight-knit race.

Israelis vote for parties rather than directly electing a prime minister, with the Knesset’s 120 seats allocated through proportional representation. Parties must win at least 3.25% of the national vote to enter parliament.

Because outright majorities are rare, parties typically form coalitions. The president asks a Knesset member — usually the leader best placed to assemble a 61-seat majority — to form a government. If repeated attempts fail, another election can be called.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who leads the right-wing Likud party, returned to power in late 2022 with a coalition including far-right and ultra-Orthodox parties. The alliance has since been strained by disputes over a Gaza ceasefire and the conscription of ultra-Orthodox men.

Recent polls put both Netanyahu's bloc and the main opposition bloc, led by centrist former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, short of the 61 seats needed to govern, making smaller parties potentially decisive.

Arab parties are also in the running, but most of the main Jewish parties have ruled out alliances with them. More than 20% of Israel's population is Arab, but Arab parties have rarely joined governing coalitions.

The impending vote is effectively a referendum on Netanyahu, with the Hamas attacks having "transformed Israeli society," according to László Csicsmann, a Middle East expert at Corvinus University of Budapest in Hungary.

"Israel has been at war since October 7, 2023, and the so-called 'seven-front war' launched by Netanyahu has undoubtedly worn down Israeli society," he told CNBC. "The side that can better convince voters that it can protect the population is likely to win. Other campaign issues include mandatory military service, which is particularly sensitive for religious Jewish parties and Haredi communities."

Military service is compulsory for most Jewish, Druze and Circassian Israelis over 18, while most other Arab Israelis are exempt. The conscription of ultra-Orthodox men remains a major legal and political dispute.

The economic toll of the war is also a major issue, Csicsmann said.

"Due to the war and high military spending, economic issues are also dominating the political campaign," he told CNBC, noting that Israel currently spends around 8% of its gross domestic product on military expenditure. "In addition, nearly every family has a soldier or reservist who has been called up and has left their job for months."

Defense and security are also at the forefront of the election, said Daniel Schatz, a political scientist and former visiting scholar at Harvard, Stanford and Georgetown.

"For Israel, the stakes include restoring confidence in government and deciding how military power translates into lasting security," he told CNBC in an email. "For its neighbors and international partners, the question is whether the next government can turn battlefield achievements into workable political arrangements."

Schatz said that while Netanyahu's supporters see the incumbent prime minister as "an experienced leader confronting formidable threats," his critics see failures of preparedness, accountability and strategic direction.

In September, book extracts published by Israeli newspaper Haaretz alleged that Netanyahu had been warned that Hamas was planning a major offensive around a week before the Oct. 7 attacks. Netanyahu called those claims an "absolute lie," and has reportedly filed a defamation lawsuit against the newspaper.

But Schatz told CNBC that any lingering dissatisfaction with Netanyahu should not be confused with support for the left.

"Some voters want different leadership precisely because they believe it would deliver security more effectively," he said.

He added that a change in prime minister and the governing coalition would also be unlikely to produce a dramatic shift in Israel's stance on Palestinian statehood, Iran and other foreign policy issues.

Netanyahu's right-wing Likud party is running on a manifesto promising "security without compromise," along with pledges to maintain a free economy and financial markets and a bid to strengthen "Israel as a regional and technological power."

Eisenkot's Yashar party says it wants to make Israel a "democratic, powerful, progressive and secure" country, and it also has a focus on national security – including a proposed policy of integrating ultra-Orthodox and Arab communities into compulsory military service.

Farzan Sabet, senior analyst at the Eurasia Group think tank, told CNBC the main blocs competing for power are "quite hawkish on security" and would have comparable policies across key areas like confronting Iran and Hezbollah in Lebanon.

But he added that a new coalition government composed mainly of anti-Netanyahu bloc parties would "probably prefer to review the Israeli strategy towards Tehran" before pursuing any major escalation.

The U.S. and Israel have reportedly drawn up plans for possible renewed strikes on Iran after the midterm elections on Nov. 3, while Iran's army chief has said it is ready for "asymmetric warfare."

The outcome could be consequential for U.S.-Israel relations.

Trump reiterated his endorsement of Netanyahu in a Truth Social post on Sunday, urging Israeli supporters to reinstate him as prime minister so the pair could "finish the job" in Iran.

"As everyone is aware, including the enemy, Bibi and I have had a great relationship in winning together," he said, referring to Netanyahu by a common nickname. In his post, Trump pointed to the U.S. and Israel's joint military operations in Iran, which he said had destroyed the country's military and economy.

"When you go to the Polls please remember that Bibi has been an outstanding Warrior Prime Minister!" he said, in comments directed at voters in Israel. "Vote for Bibi Netanyahu for Prime Minister, we have to finish the job that we started!"

Eurasia's Sabet told CNBC that the anti-Netanyahu bloc might be "more conciliatory on some issues," such as military action in Gaza, especially if doing so would improve U.S. ties and Israel's international standing while still meeting the country's basic security needs.

He said a government composed mostly of the anti-Netanyahu bloc would likely take fewer actions in the West Bank, crack down on settler violence against Palestinians there, and avoid annexation of Palestinian land.

The West Bank is a Palestinian territory west of the Jordan River where Israeli settlements have been expanding for decades. In recent years, violence and forced displacement of Palestinians by settlers have drawn condemnation from lawmakers in the U.S. and beyond.

But Sabet told CNBC: "While the opposition to Netanyahu has the edge in the latest Israeli election polls, this will be a tight race, with several possible outcomes."

#1293. NASA’s Perseverance Offers Clues to Protect Crews From Mars Dust

Over 1,645 Martian days, NASA’s Perseverance Mars rover measured the fine and ultrafine Martian dust particles found clinging to samples of spacesuit materials that are carried aboard the rover, including some that are small enough to penetrate the lungs and enter the bloodstream. The findings will be published Tuesday, Oct. 27, in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences and could inform spacesuit and habitat design, dust-removal procedures, and crew health standards for future NASA missions to Mars.

“NASA has a long history of turning challenges into workable solutions and of finding creative ways to use the data that we have to answer questions beyond what it was originally collected for,” said Lindsay Hays, acting director, Planetary Science Division, NASA Headquarters in Washington. “Dust has been a surface-exploration challenge since the Apollo program. Perseverance is giving our engineers and flight surgeons measurements they can use to improve our existing designs well before the first American astronauts arrive on Mars.”

Lunar dust scratched visors, degraded outer spacesuit layers, and damaged their seals during NASA’s Apollo missions, and some crew members reported symptoms similar to hay fever.

Rounded by wind-driven collisions with other particles, dust grains on Mars are less abrasive than those on the Moon. They also are enriched in sulfur, chlorine, and iron and contain more silica than lunar dust. Regional and global dust storms on Mars can keep the grains recirculating throughout the atmosphere as well.

The rover carries a set of five samples of spacesuit material. The swatches, each three-quarters of an inch (20 millimeters) square, are part of a calibration target used to test the settings of SHERLOC (Scanning Habitable Environments with Raman and Luminescence for Organics and Chemicals), an instrument on Perseverance’s robotic arm. The calibration target for another instrument that provided the dust measurements, called PIXL (Planetary Instrument for X-ray Lithochemistry), carries a sample of Teflon and of basaltic glass.

Because Teflon contains no elements that PIXL can directly detect, whatever elemental signals the X-ray spectrometer picks up from that sample comes from dust resting on it.

The team also analyzed swatches of Teflon and Vectran, two materials used in spacesuits, on SHERLOC’s calibration target. NASA sent the swatches to Mars to study how spacesuit materials hold up on the planet’s surface.

“Perseverance’s main job is to search for signs of ancient microbial life, but the mission was also designed to help prepare for human explorers. That effort includes technology demonstrations like MOXIE (Mars Oxygen In-Situ Resource Utilization Experiment) and Ingenuity, as well as the spacesuit samples,” said Katie Stack Morgan, Perseverance’s project scientist at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California.

While earlier measurements on Mars resolved dust particles down to about 3 micrometers across, PIXL detected two categories of even smaller particles: fine particles measuring less than 2.5 micrometers (a human hair is about 70 micrometers wide) and ultrafine particles around 100 nanometers (about 700 times thinner than a human hair). Particles on PIXL’s Teflon target and SHERLOC’s Vectran swatch averaged about 2 micrometers. On PIXL’s basaltic glass and SHERLOC’s Teflon swatch, dust particle sizes ranged down to about 100 to 300 nanometers.

Static electricity appears to determine which size dust particles stick to which surface. Dust grains become charged as they collide in the air, and different materials on the calibration target attract grains of different sizes. The finest particles stayed attached through years of driving and drilling. Organic polymers like SHERLOC’s Teflon spacesuit sample are common in the outer layers of spacesuits, and the results show they readily collect fine dust.

The study also found that some materials hold less dust than others, which could guide future choices of materials and protective coatings for spacesuits and habitats. Designs such as suitports, which let astronauts enter a suit attached to the outside of a habitat, and dual-chamber airlocks could reduce how much dust gets inside astronauts’ living quarters.

“The existence of Mars dust at these ultrafine sizes has been predicted for a long time, and PIXL gave us the chance to measure it directly on Mars,” said Scott VanBommel, a Perseverance scientist at Washington University in St. Louis and the paper’s lead author. “The larger clumps, the Martian dust bunnies, get shaken off over time. But the smallest particles stay behind, and those are the ones that pose the greatest challenge for human support systems.”

Chemically, the dust matches the iron- and sulfur-rich composition that earlier missions measured. The PIXL instrument also found the dust to be enriched in phosphorus and detected signs of calcium sulfate.

On Earth, airborne particles, or particulate matter, below 2.5 micrometers (that is, fine particles) are tied to a range of negative health effects because they can penetrate deep into the lungs and enter the bloodstream. Studies have shown that ultrafine particles (those no larger than 100 nanometers) can travel from the nasal cavity to the brain along the olfactory nerve.

Martian dust is composed predominantly of silicate minerals and carries chemically reactive compounds, including perchlorates that can disrupt thyroid function and reactive iron that induces cellular damage. Scientists believe that the health risks of Mars dust depend on the quantity of dust and length of exposure.

The PIXL results are the first on-site measurements of fine and ultrafine particles on Mars, and this research can inform broader efforts to refine indoor dust-exposure limits for astronauts, develop safe habits, and establish ways to remove dust while exploring Mars.

NASA is already working on solutions to extraterrestrial dust hazards, using ground test facilities and lunar missions as proving grounds for future Mars explorers. In March 2025, the agency tested an Electrodynamic Dust Shield, which used electric fields to clear lunar regolith from glass and thermal radiator surfaces on the Moon. Developed at NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida, it landed on the Moon aboard Firefly Aerospace’s Blue Ghost Mission 1. At NASA’s Johnson Space Center in Houston, engineers at the Lunar Development and Test Facility use vacuum chambers and lunar regolith simulant to test spacesuit components, mechanisms, and a Handheld Lunar Electrostatic Dust Mitigation tool ahead of Artemis missions to the lunar surface.

Managed for NASA by Caltech, JPL built and manages operations of the Perseverance rover on behalf of the agency’s Science Mission Directorate as part of NASA’s Mars Exploration Program portfolio. NASA JPL also built PIXL and SHERLOC.

#1294. Why are more roofs not made of solar tiles?

From installer to instructor Kate Collardson (left) has a long history in solar systems

Some people in the US "still hate the look of solar", Kate Collardson acknowledges.

She would know. Collardson handles operations for the Solar Service of Colorado, a solar maintenance and inspection company. She's also held just about every other job in the industry, from installer to instructor.

For those that hate the look of solar panels, an alternative is a solar roof, where the tiles (or shingles) house solar cells, but look much the same as regular tiles.

This is especially important for historic buildings, where heritage rules limit changes to their appearance.

For many people, the first time they'd heard of this product category was in August, when Tesla's website stopped offering solar roofs, external. This followed disappointing sales and a lawsuit over sudden price hikes, external.

Other companies have also pulled out, but Tesla's decision in particular sent shockwaves through the solar roof industry.

Some see it as a death knell for solar tiles; others, as an opportunity.

Tesla abruptly stopped marketing its solar tiles in August

For instance, the small Swiss company Freesuns is considering expanding to the US.

Deborah Learoyd, Freesuns' CEO and managing director, estimates that the company's sales have grown 20â30% since it was established in 2019.

In general, solar roof components continue to be manufactured in smaller batches. This limits the economies of scale and standardisation, though flexible manufacturing could help somewhat.

Learoyd says that while the unit costs for Freesuns' products are slowly decreasing, "a lot of the cost is actually the fact that every roof is a little bit different. And so it has to be engineered a little bit differently, installed a little bit differently".

Solar roofs typically require collaboration among roofers, solar installers and electricians. And building regulations tend to be more complex than for solar panels.

The additional time and paperwork can take a toll on a roofing business, Collardson explains. "You try to put a roofer into the equation and they're going, 'This is taking forever. I'm losing money. I could have sold 10 roofing jobs in the time that it takes me to sell this one'."

Collardson has to charge more for repair of solar shingles, compared to a standard photovoltaic (PV) setup.

She explains, "With traditional solar, we generally have electronics on the panel and a map that shows us exactly how much each panel is producing." So when something goes wrong, it's easy to spot where.

"With solar shingles, we don't really have the benefit of that mapping; there's no room underneath the shingle for the electronics." Thermal cameras can identify the trouble spots, however.

But then there's the matter of accessing them. "You can remove the one in the middle of the array, but you have to walk on the others, and you really shouldn't walk on them because you're going to create micro-fractures and that's going to cause issues down the road."

Before repair costs are factored in, a solar roof might cost twice as much as a system of solar panels mounted on a roof.

Freesuns solar tiles on the LycÃ©e Jean-Piaget in NeuchÃ¢tel, Switzerland

Solar roofs are also less efficient - one reason is that the tiles are just smaller.

Another factor is the energy lost as heat. Since the tiles sit close to the roof, there's less airflow than with standard solar panels mounted on a roof. Heat impairs solar performance.

Coloured tiles are even less efficient, comments Ben Graves, co-founder of UK solar company Sunsave. "The reason why all solar cells are black, and increasingly the whole panel is now black, is because black is the best absorbing colour."

Overall, much more space would need to be devoted to solar roof tiles to produce the same amount of energy.

Sunsave does not offer solar roofs. "Most people in the UK just don't have enough money to pay for it," Graves believes.

While appearance was a bigger factor five years ago, now "the vast majority of consumers are most interested in how much they can save".

But supporters of solar roofs argue that they should not be pitted against standard solar modules on roofs.

"Let's not compare PV roof tiles to a standard PV system, but look at PV roof tiles as generating additional electricity from our roofs instead of just having the roof sit there," urges Martin Heinrich who leads a research group at the Fraunhofer Institute for Solar Energy Systems in Germany.

A solar roof can cost twice as much as installing solar panels

While standard solar panels have gone from strength to strength, solar roofs have not advanced to the same extent.

One advancement that could especially help solar roofs is matrix shingling technology.

This is a different way of connecting solar cells. The solar cells are cut into narrow strips, layered like overlapping shingles, and connected to each other using electrically conductive adhesive, rather than metal wires.

This means that the electrical current can flow around shaded areas, unlike with standard modules. "If you get like a bird pooping on a part of the cell, the current can go around it," Learoyd explains.

In addition to increasing energy output, this improves the appearance as the silver wires aren't visible.

Another advantage, Heinrich says, is that "since we cut the cells into smaller areas, we can fill out special sizes more easily. You don't have to adhere to the regular pattern size."

Freesuns is an early adopter of matrix shingling technology in building-integrated PV. "We see it as a big opportunity for the future in terms of how we would make our tiles," Learoyd says.

What would also help the company is better software for automated design. This would speed up the design process, since each roofing job is unique.

Learoyd believes this would lower costs and give "the whole construction industry much more confidence in using the product".

Ten years after her own solar roof was installed, and despite the sector's setbacks, Learoyd remains optimistic.

She believes that for people with the means, it will eventually become standard to install a new roof with some sort of embedded solar. "It's just a no-brainer."

Luis Carlos Ugalde, a former chief of the electoral authority, told Bloomberg Línea that both allegations of corruption against an electoral chief and Taddei’s resignation as INE president are “unprecedented.”

Taddei’s announcement came after Mexican media outlets, including Reforma, El Universal and Latinus, reported last week on alleged irregularities in INE contracts and her ties to businessman José Alfredo Hernández Casillas. The outgoing INE president reportedly has a close personal relationship with Hernández, whose family’s companies have received lucrative INE contracts.

In an article published on Monday under the headline “Taddei is leaving,” the newspaper Reforma noted that it documented how Hernández — who is linked to various electoral materials suppliers — “obtained [electoral authority] contracts since Taddei presided over the electoral organization of Sonora” between 2014 and 2021.

Taddei’s “closeness” to Hernández allowed the latter to obtain contracts awarded by high-ranking INE officials, Reforma reported. The newspaper also reported that Jonathan Navarrete Torres, an employee of Hernández, was on the INE’s payroll as Taddei’s chauffeur without actually working in that role.

In addition, Reforma reported on Monday that it had “revealed” that seven INE suppliers remained under investigation by the federal government’s Financial Intelligence Unit for money laundering and “simulation” in bidding processes. The allegation is that seven companies linked to Hernández and his brother feigned competition for contracts awarded by the INE and the State Electoral Institute in Sonora under Taddei’s leadership.

Reforma also noted that video footage had emerged showing Taddei and two of her children socializing with Hernández.

“One video filmed by the businessman shows a son of Taddei [Jorge Francisco Piñeda Taddei] enjoying a stay at the most expensive hotel in Paris,” Reforma reported. “‘Paris at your feet, young man,’ the businessman says in the video, boasting about the gift.”

In light of the various media reports about alleged corruption at the INE, the Federal Auditor’s Office (ASF) announced on Friday that it had begun an investigation into allegations regarding the “improper use of public resources.”

In a statement, the ASF said the investigation “covers” the INE, state-based electoral authorities, companies, public servants and suppliers “that are related to each other.”

The ASF said there is “already evidence … related to irregularities in several contracts” as well as conflicts of interest, collusion and triangulation of resources.”

It said it would investigate allegations involving the INE with “complete independence, objectivity and technical rigor.”

“A Mexico without corruption is possible,” concluded the ASF statement.

In her statement on Sunday, Taddei acknowledged the accusations that have been leveled against her.

“I am aware of the allegations that have circulated in the media and on social media in recent days, including rumors, fabrications, leaks and accounts whose authenticity, context and purpose — as in all cases — must be verified and corroborated,” she said.

“… Each allegation must be examined with evidence and through institutional channels,” Taddei said.

In a separate statement on Saturday, she said that “no hiring process, public servant or supplier is above the law.”

Taddei also said that some high-ranking INE officials had been stood down, but she didn’t name them.

The outgoing INE president said on Sunday she was resigning “with calmness and dignity” after dedicating 33 years of her life “to electoral service in Mexico.”

Taddei said her decision “does not relieve anyone of the duty to clarify, with transparency, rigor and due process, the events that must be investigated.”

The 63-year-old Sonora native began what was supposed to be a nine-year term at the INE in early 2023. Mexico News Daily reported at the time that Taddei had family links to both the federal government and the ruling Morena party.

The opposition National Action Party (PAN) said at the time that it was “completely unacceptable that the person who seeks to preside over our electoral umpire is clearly linked to Morena.”

The PAN had called for Taddei’s resignation in light of the corruption allegations outlined in various media reports.

“If contracts were rigged, we are very concerned that elections will be rigged as well,” said PAN national president Jorge Romero.

At her Monday morning press conference, President Claudia Sheinbaum described Taddei’s decision to step down as INE president as “good.”

“… Obviously, an investigation has to be carried out. … There has to be an audit in order to review the suspicions or the allegations there have been regarding abuses or privileges within the INE,” she said.

Sheinbaum stressed that there will be no interruption to the INE’s work despite Taddei’s decision to resign. One of the INE’s electoral councilors will head up the electoral authority until the Chamber of Deputies appoints a new president.

The INE’s main focus is currently the federal, state and municipal elections that will be held on June 6, 2027.

With reports from EFE, Reforma and Bloomberg Línea

#1296. Nvidia to invest $3 billion in Meta as tech giants deepen AI partnership

Nvidia has said it will invest $3 billion in Meta after the social media and AI giant announced plans to raise $95 billion to support its investments in artificial intelligence infrastructure.

Meta on Monday said it would initially raise $35 billion in underwritten public equity offerings, before raising an additional $60 billion with an at-the-market program.

The announcement said Nvidia, Advanced Micro Devices, and Broadcom were interested in purchasing up to $5 billion in shares.

Nvidia announced its investment on Tuesday, adding that Meta would expand Vera Rubin and Vera CPU deployment, and that the two companies would deepen their partnership on Muse, the social media giant's AI agent that launched last month.

"AI agents represent a new computing paradigm — software that understands our goals, reasons, uses tools and gets work done on our behalf," said Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang in a statement.

"This changes how we use computers, from operating applications to working with intelligent agents."

"We're excited to keep working with NVIDIA to deliver the best personal agents and frontier models for billions of people," said Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg.

Both companies' shares were flat in premarket trading on Tuesday.

Nvidia has been rapidly building up stakes in companies powering the AI boom, investing in OpenAI, Anthropic, Intel and XAI.

The chip giant has participated in 121 investment rounds so far this year, according to Dealroom, up from just 13 in 2022.

#1301. NEO Surveyor’s Sunshade Gets Inspected

The large sunshade of NASA’s Near-Earth Object (NEO) Surveyor is mounted on an assembly ring during inspections in a clean room at BAE Systems Space & Mission Systems in Boulder, Colorado, in July 2026.

The sunshade structure stands 20 feet (6 meters) tall and measures 8 feet (2.4 meters) wide at its base. Its two flat panels, joined at a 23.5-degree angle, were covered with 864 interconnected solar cells and then tested before arriving in Colorado. This specialized solar array can produce up to 2 kilowatts of power and will generate all the required electricity to charge the onboard batteries that power the spacecraft’s systems.

Built by Applied Aerospace in Stockton, California, the sunshade structure was outfitted with its solar cells by SolAero Technologies in Albuquerque, New Mexico, in January. Environmental testing of the sunshade and solar array was completed at a commercial thermal vacuum testing facility in El Segundo, California, in March and it was delivered to BAE Systems Space & Mission Systems ahead of schedule in May.

When in space, NEO Surveyor will seek out some of the hardest-to-find asteroids and comets, some of which may be located in the direction of the Sun — a region of sky where ground-based optical telescopes have a harder time searching.

More information about NEO Surveyor is available at:

https://science.nasa.gov/mission/neo-surveyor/

NASA explores the unknown in air and space, innovates for the benefit of humanity, and inspires the world through discovery.

Over the weekend, national trucking associations said the indefinite national strike could involve as many as 1 million trucks, while warning the public of potential disruptions to the supply of goods and fuel.

Industry representatives have sought to explain the reasons for their strike action, telling the media they “are not seeking to harm families, but rather want answers to their legitimate demands.”

Truckers face what they describe as a “double imposition” — paying steep taxes and high private toll fees, only to receive low-quality, dangerous highway infrastructure in return.

The truckers also object to proposed changes to the toll tax incentive, urging President Claudia Sheinbaum to review the proposal in the 2027 federal budget.

The budget submitted by the Finance Ministry last month would slash fiscal incentives for the freight transportation sector by lowering the annual corporate revenue limit required to qualify for the highway toll tax credit from 300 million pesos down to 250 million pesos.

The lower threshold would impact mid-to-large freight and transport companies making between 250 million and 300 million pesos annually by locking them out of the incentive program.

The National Chamber of Freight Transportation, the largest trucking association in Mexico, claims that the sector is already suffering due to soaring diesel costs and high toll fees. They warn that removing the toll tax safety net will dramatically increase operational costs for dozens of companies, potentially forcing some into bankruptcy.

They also argue it is unfair for the government to strip away tax credits while treating organized crime’s grip on transport routes as “an acceptable condition of doing business.”

Through September, the sector has recorded 1,105 cargo truck robberies and 15 driver fatalities this year.

Truckers previously blockaded highways in April to highlight the need for stronger road security, teaming up with farmers demanding fairer conditions for agricultural producers. They also staged similar actions in November 2025, again teaming up with farmers citing rural sector grievances.

With reports from La Silla Rota, El Financiero, Eje Central and The Latin Times

#1305. Inherited IRAs can boost wealth — and trigger a tax bill. Here's how to reduce it

An inherited individual retirement account can be a sizable windfall for some investors — but taxes can take a chunk without proper planning, experts say.

On average, heirs receive inherited IRAs at age 59, and the mean balance of those accounts is $128,000, according to a recent Vanguard report that analyzed nearly 83,000 accounts in 2024.

"Most people inherit an IRA in their 50s, right at the peak of their earning years, and then have to empty it within 10 years," said certified financial planner Michael Walstedt, founding advisor of Reliant Wealth Advisory in Hoboken, New Jersey.

Since 2020, a "10-year rule" applies to some inherited accounts, requiring certain heirs, including adult children, to generally empty the balance by the 10th year after the original account owner's death.

If it's a pretax inherited IRA, the 10-year withdrawal timeline can boost adjusted gross income, potentially triggering higher taxes and reducing eligibility for other tax breaks, experts say.

Inherited IRA planning will continue to be important amid the so-called "great wealth transfer," with baby boomers expected to pass trillions of dollars to Gen Xers and millennials in the coming decades.

Over the next 20 to 25 years, total transfers between generations could be an estimated $74 trillion, according to a 2025 report from financial services firm UBS.

Whether you're preparing to leave a future gift or to inherit an IRA, there are some key tax moves to consider, financial experts say.

Since 2025, some adult children who receive an inherited IRA generally must start taking required minimum distributions, or RMDs, over the 10-year period or face an IRS penalty. The yearly RMD requirement applies if the original IRA owner reached RMD age, usually 73, before their death.

But even without yearly RMDs over the 10-year period, experts say, heirs should have a plan for pretax inherited accounts. Otherwise, they may have to take a large distribution in the 10th year, which could trigger a bigger-than-expected tax bill.

"I recommend projecting income over those 10 years and planning withdrawals around it," said CFP James Mayo, founder of IronFjord Wealth Management in Lakewood, Colorado.

For example, if you're expecting lower-income years due to retirement or a sabbatical, you could be in a lower tax bracket during those periods. Those years could be an opportunity to take bigger IRA distributions, he said.

Original account owners should also consider each heir's income tax bracket when choosing IRA beneficiaries, said certified public accountant Tim Steffen, director of advanced planning at financial services firm Baird.

For example, if one child is a law firm partner and the other is a teacher, "their incomes are wildly different," he said.

In that scenario, you might leave more of your IRA to the teacher because they'll pay less income tax, and you might leave a tax-free life insurance policy to the higher-earning attorney, Steffen said.

"Be more thoughtful about who actually inherits what, instead of just saying everybody gets an equal share of everything," he said.

If you're the original account owner, Roth IRA conversions during life "can make a big difference" for heirs, according to CFP Dinon Hughes, a partner with Nvest Financial in Portsmouth, New Hampshire.

Roth conversions transfer pretax or nondeductible IRA funds into a Roth IRA, which begins tax-free growth. The move triggers higher income in the year of the conversion, but could provide future heirs with more tax-free funds, experts say.

While certain inherited Roth IRAs are still subject to the 10-year rule, beneficiaries can generally withdraw the proceeds tax-free.

"The sweet spot for Roth conversions" is typically early retirement years, because income is lower before Social Security payments start and required minimum distributions kick in, Hughes said.

However, you'll need tax projections to see how extra income could affect other tax breaks, such as the $6,000 senior "bonus" deduction.

Plus, boosting adjusted gross income can affect income-related monthly adjustment amounts, or IRMAAs, which increase Medicare Part B and Part D premiums once income exceeds a certain level.
