#1340. 4 fratelli e 2 pizzerie per assaggiare la pizza di Napoli che cambia

4 fratelli, 2 pizzerie e 2 modi di intendere la pizza allo stesso tavolo o, meglio, allo stesso banco per una serata evento. Bro di Antonio e Ciro Tutino, I Vesuviani di Federico e Francesco De Maria.

I fratelli Tutino a Napoli rappresentano la quinta generazione della famiglia di pizzaioli.

I fratelli De Maria a Castello di Cisterna e a Casoria si definiscono «pizzaioli da zero generazioni».

Il featuring nasce come momento di condivisione e divertimento, ma noi vediamo l’occasione di verificare come cambia il mondo della pizza napoletana.

Entrambi i progetti, infatti, dimostrano che la pizzeria contemporanea può sviluppare un’identità riconoscibile senza limitarsi a ripetere modelli consolidati. Ne avete già letto su queste pagine quando Francesca Brunzo (al tavolo con me e co-autrice di questo report) ha definito I Vesuviani la «Repubblica democratica della pizza», grazie a una proposta capace di dare spazio a interpretazioni diverse senza eleggere un unico formato a protagonista assoluto. Dei Bro aveva sottolineato i «talenti indiscutibili di una nuova Napoli». Raccontando una realtà che conserva un legame con la tradizione ma non rinuncia a intervenire sul prodotto. La loro pizza, per stile e personalità, l’aveva definita «brobordante»: un gioco di parole che restituisce bene un’identità gastronomica tutt’altro che timida.

La serata a Castello di Cisterna ha permesso di mettere queste due visioni alla prova nello stesso menu, senza trasformare la collaborazione in una sfida a chi abbia ragione.

Assaggiamo subito queste due visioni, allora.

Il menu della serata è rimasto alla carta, senza un percorso obbligato. Ogni cliente ha potuto scegliere cosa assaggiare. Una soluzione coerente con la libertà dei due progetti.

Ad aprire la degustazione, due proposte fuori carta che entrano nel nuovo menu stagionale de I Vesuviani.

— Pandoro alle papacelle, papacelle in agrodolce, crema di baccalà e polvere di pelle di baccalà

— Panettone artigianale lievitato 72 ore, alici del Cantabrico, pomodorini confit, burro francese ed alghe essiccate.

— Teglia Napoli per il mondo (I Vesuviani). Mozzarella di bufala, alici di Cetara, origano di montagna, concentrato di pomodoro, polvere di olive nere caiazzane, olio all’aglio (12 €).

— Domenica alle 15 (Bro). Frittatina di manfredi con ragù napoletano 8 ore, ricotta di bufala e basilico (4 €).

— Padellino Da Vittorio (I Vesuviani). Mix di datterino caramella, cuore di bue, piennolo e san Marzano, burro acido, parmigiano reggiano e polvere di basilico (20 €).

— Roastbeef e Patate (Bro featuring I Vesuviani). Impasto pizza in teglia con crosta di patate, fiordilatte, girello di manzo, fondo bruno, purea di carota ossidata, basilico e olio EVO (10 €). Questa pizza riprende uno dei grandi classici de I Vesuviani, la porchetta in crosta di patate. La mattonella romana, in questo caso, prevede un ripieno di roastbeef invece che porchetta e una purea di carote ossidate al posto della mayo.

— Margherita a Ruota di Carro dei Bro (7 €). Il classico ineludibile

— Non è una pizza per napoletani (Bro featuring I Vesuviani). Impasto I Vesuviani con ingredienti firmati Bro. Salame piccante, fiordilatte, composta di ananas piccante, fonduta di provolone del Monaco DOP, basilico, olio EVO (14 €). La celeberrima Non è una pizza per napoletani di Bro viene proposta con l’impasto della tonda dei Vesuviani. Una pizza dalla personalità decisa, dove l’ananas non compromettere la fedeltà a quella componente «brobordante» dei Tutino.

— Natale in casa (Bro featuring I Vesuviani). Pizza in pala, salsa al pecorino, scarole saltate in padella. Dopo la cottura, scarola riccia marinata, mela annurca ossidata e caramello dell’acqua di fermentazione (26 €). Una rivisitazione della tradizionale pizza di scarole napoletane. Il topping di Bro sulla pala de I Vesuviani che esprime perfettamente le personalità dei protagonisti: l’appartenenza alla propria terra non dovrebbe mia diventare una gabbia.

— Pain au Chocolat Genovese (I Vesuviani). Genovese napoletana di vitellone bianco, pecorino romano e cioccolato fondente (9 €).

— Il Panettone Artigianale (I Vesuviani) al cioccolato fondente dei Bro con crema chantilly (9 €).

— Caffè Sansone Guatemala (2 €). Disponibile il Blend (70% arabica e 30% robusta) oppure nella variante Guatemala, dal profilo aromatico e dalla persistenza differenti. Gusti decisamente memorabili raccontati da Vincenzo Sansone.

Nel Campionato della Pizza 2026, i fratelli Tutino hanno conquistato il quarto posto, fermandosi a un soffio dal podio (qui la classifica). Un risultato che conferma la loro crescita.

Ciro e Antonio, prima di aprire Bro, nel 2019, hanno maturato esperienza nella pizzeria di famiglia a San Giorgio a Cremano. Ciro ha inoltre trascorso due anni a Firenze, un’esperienza che ha contribuito alla sua formazione prima del ritorno in Campania e dell’avventura imprenditoriale condivisa con il fratello.

La divisione dei compiti è precisa. Antonio si occupa della sala e dell’accoglienza, mentre Ciro segue la preparazione delle pizze, dalla gestione dell’impasto alla cottura. Due ruoli distinti che concorrono a costruire un progetto nel quale la componente gastronomica e quella organizzativa procedono insieme.

A prima vista, la pizza di Bro richiama la classica ruota di carro napoletana: diametro generoso, profilo riconoscibile, un riferimento immediato alla tradizione partenopea. Ma fermarsi all’aspetto sarebbe riduttivo.

I Tutino utilizzano un impasto indiretto ad alta idratazione. La lavorazione prevede tempi prolungati, mentre la cottura avviene a temperature inferiori rispetto a quelle comunemente associate alla pizza napoletana tradizionale.

Il risultato è una pizza che conserva la riconoscibilità visiva della ruota di carro, ma interviene su alcuni dei suoi parametri tecnici.

Bro, con il locale a Piazza Mercato a Napoli, genera un flusso importante in una zona dove regna la tradizione più radicata. In una città in cui la pizza è anche memoria collettiva, distinguersi senza perdere il legame con la tradizione non è esercizio banale. Bro ha scelto di lavorare su questo equilibrio: partire da un riferimento familiare al pubblico napoletano e modificarlo dall’interno.

L’augurio è che possano ampliare la loro sala: seppur cambiando location, siamo certi abbiano già saputo dimostrare che i posti più belli sono fatti di persone.

La storia dei fratelli Federico e Francesco De Maria comincia da un punto diverso. Il loro claim è I Vesuviani «pizzaioli da zero generazioni». Nessuna dinastia da rivendicare, nessuna tradizione familiare da proseguire. Il loro percorso nasce dalla panificazione e dalla preparazione di pizze al taglio (scuola Bonci) per poi trasformarsi in un progetto di pizzeria.

La prima sede apre nel 2018 a Castello di Cisterna. Nel 2023 arriva quella di Casoria: Federico guida stabilmente il secondo locale, mentre Francesco segue la sede originaria.

La differenza rispetto a Bro è evidente soprattutto nella struttura del menu.

Per i Tutino la pizza è a ruota di carro, senza sottoinsiemi. Per I Vesuviani la pizza tonda napoletana non è il centro attorno al quale ruota ogni scelta. Condivide la scena con pizze in pala, in teglia, padellini e mattonelle.

È qui che si riconosce l’eredità della panificazione. La familiarità con le farine, le fermentazioni e le differenti strutture degli impasti permette di costruire una proposta che  considera la pizza (non solo la tonda) parte di una vetrina più ampia. La pizzeria diventa così uno spazio in cui convivono tecniche e interpretazioni.

È il senso della «Repubblica democratica della pizza»: non un menu senza identità, ma una pizzeria che non attribuisce a un solo formato il diritto di rappresentare tutto il mondo della pizza. La varietà non è un’aggiunta decorativa, bensì una componente strutturale della proposta.

Anche la crescita delle due sedi racconta la capacità di intercettare un pubblico ampio. I due locali dispongono di molti posti a sedere che consentono un significativo ricambio di clienti anche nelle serate infrasettimanali.

Bro e I Vesuviani si sono affacciati alle classifiche di settore. Ma questo dato, da solo, non è mai stato utile a definire il valore di una pizzeria, né a misurarne la capacità di conquistare il pubblico. Ancora una volta vi proponiamo una ri-lettura della Brunzo sul tema.

Le classifiche sono strumenti utili per orientarsi, ma non esauriscono la complessità di una pizzeria. Riconoscimento e successo possono incontrarsi, ma non coincidono necessariamente.

I Tutino scelgono di mantenere il riferimento visivo. La loro identità si costruisce proprio nello spazio tra ciò che il pubblico riconosce e ciò che il prodotto propone di diverso.

I Vesuviani percorrono una strada differente. La loro identità nasce dalla pluralità dei formati e degli stili, come se il Vesuvio non fosse semplicemente la vista ma l’affaccio sul mondo.

Ecco perché abbiamo definito Bro e I Vesuviani talenti indiscutibili di una nuova Napoli: non perché rappresentino una rottura assoluta con il passato, ma perché dimostrano che il panorama della pizza partenopea non è immobile. La tradizione resta un riferimento fondamentale, ma non può diventare un recinto entro il quale ogni nuova idea debba chiedere il permesso di esistere.

I due progetti, pur diversi, condividono questa consapevolezza. Non cercano di essere uguali agli altri e non hanno bisogno di dichiarare guerra alla tradizione per costruire una propria identità. La conoscono, la utilizzano come punto di partenza e scelgono dove intervenire.

Pizzeria I Vesuviani. Via Madonnelle, 65, 80030 Castello di Cisterna NA. Telefono: 081 329 6996. Instagram

Bro. di Ciro e Antonio Tutino. Piazza Mercato, 222b, 80142 Napoli NA. Telefono: 081 379 7908. Instagram

La mia missione è semplice: trovare posti che meritino davvero di essere visitati. Sono sempre alla ricerca di locali che sappiano sorprendermi e mi piace raccontare il cibo senza troppi giri di parole, con curiosità e spirito critico, perché sono convinto che siano i piccoli dettagli a fare la differenza. Ho un debole per i dolci: il dessert è sempre gradito... soprattutto se è più di uno.

#1347. How Voting Is Like a Klein Bottle

Get the latest news delivered to your inbox.

An editorially independent publication supported by the Simons Foundation.

Create a reading list by clicking the Read Later icon next to the articles you wish to save.

Popular Searches

Click to tell Google to prioritize Quanta and see more of the best coverage of science and math in your search and AI results.

Mathematically speaking, democracy is next to impossible.

That may sound like the premise of a Silicon Valley billionaire’s six-hour podcast, but it’s actually a statement about a remarkably stubborn problem: How do you translate a group of individual preferences into a single choice?

In 1785, the French mathematician and philosopher Nicolas de Condorcet discovered that a majority can sometimes vote itself into a logical loop. In elections with three or more candidates, each voter might rank the candidates in a perfectly clear and consistent way — yet when all the votes are tallied, every candidate loses in a head-to-head contest against one of their rivals. Changing the rules only gets us so far: As the economist Kenneth Arrow later proved, any method for combining individual rankings into a collective order must sacrifice at least one seemingly reasonable democratic requirement.

Now three researchers have shown that Condorcet’s 240-year-old paradox has a shape, and it’s suitably peculiar: a Klein bottle, a surface with no distinct inside or outside. The result gives mathematicians a geometric way to explore why seemingly reasonable rules for collective decision-making can become impossible to reconcile.

When there are only two choices, the will of the people is easy to divine: Barring a tie, the candidate preferred by a majority wins. Add a third contender, however, and things get weird. Suddenly, even agreeing on what it means to win becomes a problem.

You might simply elect whoever receives the most votes, as in a typical American election. But suppose Alice receives 35% of the vote, Bob 34%, and Carol 31%. Alice wins. Yet if Carol’s supporters all prefer Bob to Alice, then 65% of the electorate would rather have Bob. By one perfectly reasonable definition of majority rule, the wrong candidate has won.

Before anyone reaches for a tinfoil hat, let’s be clear: Every ballot is counted correctly. The question is what should count as winning.

One solution is to ask voters to rank the candidates, then choose whoever would defeat every rival in a head-to-head contest. But consider the following scenario:

Every voter has a perfectly coherent ranking, yet together they have produced a result that runs in circles.

Nicolas de Condorcet, a French mathematician, philosopher, and politician, championed women’s rights and helped spark the abolitionist movement in France in the late 18th century. He died in prison during the French Revolution.

Lithograph by Joseph-Bordes – Musée Carnavalet, Paris

This is the paradox that Condorcet, a passionate believer in democracy, encountered in the late 18th century. As the secretary of the French Academy of Sciences, he’d been looking for ways to make sure the group was choosing new members fairly. (More enlightened than most, Condorcet would also question the democratic arithmetic of excluding half the population, explicitly defending women’s political rights in a 1790 essay. A few years later, during the Reign of Terror, the revolution he had supported put him in a prison cell; he was found dead two days after his arrest.)

Over the centuries, mathematicians, political scientists, and reformers have devised an astonishing variety of voting systems in hopes of breaking Condorcet’s impasse. Yet every method brings its own vulnerabilities. Change the system and you may well change the winner, even when the voters and their preferences remain exactly the same.

In 1951, the economist Kenneth Arrow showed how deep the problem ran. He sought a voting system that stayed consistent while meeting just a few simple democratic requirements. Voters should be free to rank the candidates in any order. No single voter should unilaterally dictate the outcome of an election. (Read: no kings.) If everyone prefers one option to another, the group’s ranking should reflect that preference. And the ranking of two candidates should depend only on how voters compare those two: Where voters place Carol on their ballots shouldn’t affect whether the group ranks Alice above Bob.

Each requirement sounds reasonable enough on its own. But, Arrow showed, no method can satisfy them all. “Quite often the will of the people doesn’t exist,” said Iain McLean of the University of Oxford.

Arrow’s impossibility theorem, as this result is now known, extended Condorcet’s paradox beyond majority rule, establishing a fundamental limit on how individual votes can be combined into a group decision. Different voting systems can change which of Arrow’s requirements fail, but no single system can ever preserve them all. “You have to make a choice as a system designer as to which of the conditions it’s most harmless to fail,” McLean said.

In 1980, to better understand this phenomenon, the mathematician and economist Graciela Chichilnisky turned to topology, an area of math in which shapes are considered equivalent if one can be stretched into another without tearing. In a footnote, she mused that Condorcet’s paradox in particular could be thought about as a topological problem.

Now mathematicians have proved her intuition true.

What, then, does a voting paradox look like?

To answer this question, the new work builds on a model that Yuliy Baryshnikov, now a professor at the University of Illinois, Urbana-Champaign, proposed in 1993. First, consider a single voter’s ballot in an election with three candidates. There are six possible ways to rank the options. Each one can be represented by a triangle:

Get Quanta Magazine delivered to your inbox

Each corner of this triangle represents one of the comparisons the ballot implies: Alice over Bob, Bob over Carol, and Alice over Carol.

A different ballot listing Alice first, Carol second, and Bob third agrees on two of those comparisons, since both ballots put Alice above her rivals. Their triangles therefore share two corners and can be joined along the edge connecting them.

Now join all six triangles (representing all possible ballots) along their matching edges. You get a strip:

The edges at its two ends also match. So bend the strip around and glue those edges together, matching the labels. You get a tube with an opening at each end:

Baryshnikov used this model to give a new topological proof of Arrow’s impossibility theorem.

But look at what happens at either end of the tube. Around one rim, the comparisons read Alice over Bob, Bob over Carol, and Carol over Alice. Around the other, the cycle runs in reverse.

We’re left with Condorcet’s paradoxical cycles — voting results that run in circles. Baryshnikov had ignored these rims. But 30 years later, in April 2025, Ori Livson, a doctoral student at the University of Sydney, reconsidered them. After all, sometimes such circular relationships are allowed, as in the rules of rock-paper-scissors. The trouble arises in situations like elections, when those relationships are expected to form a consistent ranking. Livson wanted a topological model that could distinguish cases where the cycles are allowed from cases where they aren’t.

Together with his adviser, Mikhail Prokopenko, and Prokopenko’s longtime colleague Siddharth Pritam of the Chennai Mathematical Institute, he set out to model the troublesome case.

Each cycle around the tube’s rims leads to the same impossible conclusion: Every candidate ranks above every other. In that sense, both rims are saying the same thing. And in topology, “once you realize two things are the same, you can glue them together,” Livson said.

Graduate student Ori Livson (center), his adviser Mikhail Prokopenko (right), and Siddharth Pritam showed that a famous centuries-old voting paradox has a geometric shape: a Klein bottle, a strange surface with no inside or outside.

Srishti Saloni; Georgia Callinan; Natalia Kishigami

If you bend the tube until its two openings meet, you get a doughnut-shaped surface called a torus. But this gluing also connects individual edges from each rim in pairings that represent incompatible relationships. An edge representing “Bob over Alice over Carol,” for instance, gets glued to an edge representing “Bob over Carol over Alice.” The researchers needed a way to join the rims without creating such contradictions.

The solution? A twist. Instead of matching one rim to the other point by point, in the same order, the twist allowed the researchers to reverse the order of preferences around one of the rims — making the cycles equivalent. “Gluing with the twist is the only valid option,” Livson said.

If you twist a strip of paper and join its edges, you get a surface with only one side, called a Möbius strip. But what happens when you twist a tube? You end up with something remarkable and strange: a Klein bottle.

Like a Möbius strip, a Klein bottle has only one side, with no distinct inside or outside. Unlike a Möbius strip, it has no edge. (If it looks as if this surface crosses itself, it does — in three dimensions. Mathematicians avoid this by constructing the Klein bottle in four dimensions, where it can close up without self-intersecting.)

The trio had their model. Just as each voter can supply a coherent ranking, and yet the electorate’s preferences refuse to fit into a single order, each small patch of a Klein bottle appears to have two sides, yet those sides cannot be distinguished consistently across the whole surface. In both cases, something that makes sense piece by piece breaks down when we try to put the pieces together.

For Livson, Pritam, and Prokopenko, that resemblance raises a larger question: Can topology help explain other fundamental limits on what mathematics can accomplish? Perhaps these different impossibilities, when given a shape, will turn out to share a deeper geometric explanation.

Topology makes the paradox tangible, but choosing a voting system still means picking your poison. Mathematics can tell us what the trade-offs entail. Our priorities determine which ones are worth making. And that’s something no theorem can settle for us. “It’s not really a mathematical debate,” McLean said. “It’s a debate about values.”

#1350. Gambero Rosso Guida pizzerie 2027, spoiler: Bonci perde 3 spicchi

La risata è pronta. Gabriele Bonci e il Pizzarium a Roma non possono perdere i 3 Spicchi del Gambero Rosso nella nuova Guida 2027 alle Pizzerie e lo spoiler non è valido. Perché 3 sono le Rotelle che indicano la migliore pizza al taglio. Ma il Direttore Lorenzo Ruggeri ha spiegato anche durante Pizza Maxima a Roma che Spicchi e Rotelle saranno unificati. Nella Guida 2027 ci saranno solo gli Spicchi. E – nota ben più forte – che il numero dei 3 Spicchi (ed ex Rotelle) sarà minore rispetto ai 100 + 18 dell’ultima Guida.

Lo spoiler nasce da una ricerca sul sito del Gambero Rosso che sembrerebbe auto spoilerarsi. Stanno aggiornando il sito in vista della presentazione delle Guide alle Pizzerie e ai Ristoranti lunedì 26 ottobre negli spazi della Nuvola a Roma?

[AGGIORNAMENTO: qui la presentazione della Guida con i Tre Spicchi. Spoiler confermato]

Se sono prove di “stampa” lo sapremo tra qualche giorno. Intanto la scheda relativa al Pizzarium di Gabriele Bonci l’anno scorso aveva il massimo punteggio con 96/100 e Tre Rotelle. Qui la grafica sembra confermare il downgrade a 2 Spicchi. Cioè sotto il 90, anche se a partire da quest’anno – altra novità – ci saranno solo i pittogrammi. Ma non i punteggi.

Ecco la scheda della Pizzeria in quello che sembra uno spoiler della Guida Gambero Rosso 2027.

Locale rinnovato, più spazi a disposizione, il nuovo corso di Pizzarium, il locale fondato 23 anni fa da Gabriele Bonci – vedi scheda Panificio Bonci – continua a smuovere romani e tantissimi turisti curiosi di provare almeno una volta la pizza in teglia più famosa d’Italia. Pizza che con le idee e la creatività di Bonci è diventata negli anni un vero e proprio marchio di fabbrica. Oggi Pizzarium è capofila di una serie di insegne che in Italia (con la nuova sede milanese di Bonci Pizza in Teglia) e all’estero (altra recentissima apertura quella di Dubai) portano avanti quest’impostazione creativa.

E ora la parte critica. “Qui in via della Meloria nelle nostre ultime visite non abbiamo ritrovato l’inconfondibile morso e la magia nei condimenti cui l’insegna ci aveva abituati, fritti compresi; sempre efficiente il personale che illustra con disinvoltura le numerose proposte che ogni giorno arricchiscono il bancone vetrina. Nelle ore di punta la nutrita fila fa allungare i tempi di fruizione; ci si gode qualche tavolino all’interno oltre ai piccoli appoggi all’esterno”.

Due Spicchi alla pizzeria, dunque, mentre il Panificio di Via Trionfale rinnovato e con la filosofia a tutto vegetale di Spicchi ne ha 3 nella Guida Gambero spoiler. E ha anche 3 Pani nella Guida ai migliori panifici del 2027.

Per restare a Roma, Pier Daniele Seu conserva 3 Spicchi sia a Seu Pizza che a TAC. 3 Spicchi anche per Francesco Arnesano, Ruver e Sancho (che avevano 3 Rotelle). Sembrerebbero confermati i 2 Spicchi ad Avenida Calò (che macina premi altrove) e non si ha notizia di Santini nemmeno per 1 Spicchio.

Non sono ex Rotelle ma proprio 3 Spicchi quelli che aveva Ciro Oliva con la sua Concettina ai Tre Santi nel quartiere Sanità a Napoli. Per il 2027, gli Spicchi del Gambero Rosso 2027 alla pizzeria sono solo 2 almeno in spoiler.

La bocciatura è nel testo della scheda pubblicata. “Si tratta indubbiamente di una delle insegne storiche della città, in una location bellissima e autentica, con il dehors ospitato nella corte di un palazzo del Rione Sanità, quartiere antico ora sotto l’occhio del turismo. L’ambiente è piacevole e tranquillo, il fascino dell’atmosfera napoletana non manca. Oggi però facciamo fatica a ritrovare la forza gastronomica del progetto portato alla ribalta da Ciro Oliva, guadagnandosi poi un palcoscenico internazionale con l’acquisizione da parte della famiglia Ruffini di Moncler”. Chiusura dedicata al servizio (migliorabile) e ai prezzi elevati.

Raf Bonetta ha una scheda incompleta della pizzeria di Pozzuoli che aveva 3 spicchi (e 93/100) ma ora è chiusa. I 3 Spicchi risultano trasferiti nella pizzeria del Vomero in via Cimarosa. Il testo della scheda specifica anche la chiusura della sede di Pozzuoli e la prossima apertura di Fuorigrotta “quartiere da cui tutto, professionalmente, è cominciato.”

Ma ci sono anche pizzerie che non erano in guida nel 2026. E hanno guadagnato Spicchi nella Guida alle Pizzerie del Gambero Rosso 2027 che fa auto spoiler.

Come Borgotto a Paestum (1 Spicchio) e Mirko Patrizio a Baronissi (2 Spicchi) che – se la memoria non ci tradisce – sono new entry. Almeno nella Guida del Gambero Rosso 2027 Pizzerie auto-spoiler.

Ma forse è tutto un incubo (o un sogno) per le pizzerie. Che potranno cercare la propria scheda nella guida on line.

#1356. Backward motion is easier to judge at walking speed

When we walk forward, the scene ahead spreads outward from a central point. Moving backward produces the opposite pattern, with the scene appearing to contract inward. These patterns, known as optic flow, help us judge our movement through the world. Previous studies have disagreed about which pattern people are more sensitive to, prompting the team to examine whether movement speed makes a difference.

#1357. Why we’ll never have another Black Death

The death of a worker at a Russian plague lab was alarming, but the disease is extremely unlikely to become a worldwide problem as it has in the past

Scientists disagree over how scared we should be by the mysterious death of a worker at a Russian plague lab. A young laboratory technician died earlier this month of an undisclosed illness after working on research at the Irkutsk Antiplague Research Institute of Siberia and Far East. Although officials have not released details about the cause of death, scientists agree that if it was caused by ordinary plague, the wider world has little to worry about. This bacterial illness is infamous for the explosive killing spree known as the Black Death, which wiped out between a third and half of the population of Europe between 1347 and 1353. Today, however, plague is curable and extremely unlikely to blow up into a new pandemic, experts say. That’s thanks to a combination of antibiotic development, scientific understanding and luck.

Experts who study plague are reluctant to say it’s been completely conquered. The World Health Organization (WHO) recently reported approximately 3,800 infections and 423 deaths from plague between 2019 and 2025. And scientists haven’t cracked all the mysteries behind the plague bacterium, known as Yersinia pestis—one of the biggest being how it hides for years in cryptic reservoirs only to spring out in unpredictable new waves of infection in humans or other animals.

The disease is endemic in rodents living in the Americas, Central Asia and Africa, says David Wagner, a plague expert who directs the Pathogen and Microbiome Institute at Northern Arizona University. “It’s constantly cycling between rodents via fleas, and it just does that in perpetuity in a manner we poorly understand, despite 100 years of research.”

If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.

Studies of ancient DNA show plague-infected prehistoric hunter-gatherers in Siberia 5,500 years ago. Plague is known for causing three major pandemics: in addition to the one that started with the Black Death, which peaked between 1347 and 1351 and was followed by outbreaks into the 18th century, there was the plague of Justinian from C.E. 541 to 549 and a third pandemic that started in the 1800s and spread to every inhabited continent by 1900. That last pandemic was accelerated by a boom in rail and steamship travel but was eventually quashed by advances in science.

In 1894 French-Swiss bacteriologist Alexandre Yersin isolated the plague bacterium and connected rat infestations to the disease. Rat eradication campaigns followed around the world, drastically slowing the spread of plague, Wagner says. Though it was really the fleas that spread the disease to people, rat control worked because fleas are very specific about hosts. Different animal species have their own flea species, so rats and plague-carrying fleas traveled together.

Quarantines also helped, Wagner adds, because doctors started to recognize that the bacteria could sometimes spread from person to person through respiratory droplets. In the 1940s, when antibiotics had become widely available, doctors started curing plague cases with the drugs. Several vaccines have been developed over the years and deployed in severe outbreaks, in which they offered partial protection. No vaccine has been deemed effective enough to gain approval from the WHO or the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, but labs in Russia and the U.S. continue to work on them.

Today most plague cases occur in Madagascar. Because food can be scarce there and people fear theft, individuals will store rice in their dirt-floor homes, Wagner says, allowing close contact with the rats that infest the island.

Though fleas are picky about their hosts, plague-carrying fleas in the U.S. are commonly found on prairie dogs, thanks to the animals having some functional similarities to rats. The plague bacterium now infects all five known species of prairie dogs and is one of the factors that contributed to a population decline in these social, burrowing rodents of about 98 percent from their historical levels. Because prairie dogs are a food source for other animals, including the critically endangered black-footed ferret, plague has been wreaking ecological havoc.

Even now it’s not clear where Y. pestis hides out between detectable outbreaks, Wagner says, and it’s surprising that it can be transmitted both by respiratory droplets and through fleas. But important clues about how the sickness operates are emerging from the latest studies of bacterial DNA in ancient bones and teeth.

The plague bacterium appears to have emerged as a human pathogen more than 5,700 years ago, evolving from a soil bacterium called Yersinia pseudotuberculosis, says Hendrick Poinar, a biologist at McMaster University, who works with ancient DNA. For the next 3,000 years, it infected Late Stone Age hunter-gathers and Bronze Age herders. Scientists suspect it was transmitted from human to human via respiratory droplets or via contaminated food because it hadn’t yet acquired the genes needed to travel through fleas.

Despite the versatility of Y. pestis, we’re lucky it can’t spread between humans unless an infected person is very sick and the contact is very close. Because of this limitation, even the emergence of an antibiotic-resistant strain won’t necessarily spark a new pandemic, Wagner says, noting that such strains have already shown up in Madagascar.

Though most scientists aren’t too alarmed about the situation in Russia, some are speculating that the death was caused by some highly genetically modified version of the plague bacterium or a different germ entirely. There’s no evidence for this, though the lack of transparency from Russia is unnerving. Regardless of the cause, the death of the worker is tragic. But if it was caused by the plague we know, the rest of us need not worry.

Faye Flam is a science journalist and podcaster who has written for Science, Sky & Telescope, the Philadelphia Inquirer, the New York Times, Psychology Today, Bloomberg Opinion and The Free Press.

#1358. 50 Best 2026: un solo ristorante italiano nella classifica da 51 a 100

La classifica delle posizioni 51-100 di The 50 Best Restaurants 2026, svelata oggi, vede la presenza di un solo ristorante italiano. Si tratta del ristorante Uliassi di Senigallia, che troviamo alla 51a posizione, in discesa rispetto al 2025, dove era al 43° posto.

Mentre esce di classifica Al Gatto Verde, che era al 92° posto – anche se esiste la possibilità di una rimonta fra i primi 50 (che segnerebbe anche un incredibile balzo).

Il ristorante di Mauro e Catia Uliassi sulla spiaggia di Senigallia può vantare 3 stelle Michelin dal 2019. L’apertura risale al 1990 – per la precisione, era il 27 maggio. La filosofia di Uliassi? «Cucinare è avere la straordinaria possibilità di dare piacere agli altri».

Il nostro Fulvio Zendrini ci ha mangiato a luglio scorso: potete leggere il suo articolo qui, con la descrizione del menu Lab 26. Un piatto lo vedete qui sopra. Cannolicchio, fiori di pesco, sedano, sugo di cannolicchio e olio di pepe di Siltimur. Mentre in copertina potete vedere un altro piatto di questo menù. Per illustrare il suo piazzamento al #51 della classifica 51-100, The 50 Best 2026 ha scelto infatti il suo iconico colombaccio ai fichi e albicocche.

«Quello che un tempo era un modesto chiosco sulla “Spiaggia di Velluto” è oggi uno dei ristoranti di pesce più apprezzati d’Italia, capace di conservare intatto il calore di una gestione familiare.» Così The 50 Best 2026 descrive il ristorante di Mauro Uliassi e la sua posizione nella classifica 51-100. «Il menu affonda le radici nel gioco tra olfatto, memoria e gusto: la sua pasta affumicata alle vongole, ad esempio, nasce dal ricordo di una passeggiata accanto ai chioschi che preparavano pesce alla griglia sulle spiagge di Rimini.»

Rispetto alla classifica di The 50 Best del 2025, non troviamo più Al Gatto Verde, che nel 2026 esce dai primi 100 al mondo. Entrato in classifica proprio l’anno scorso, Al Gatto Verde si trova all’interno di Casa Maria Luigia, l’elegante residenza di campagna a San Damaso (Modena).

La struttura, creata da Massimo Bottura e di Lara Gilmore, fa capo alla loro Osteria Francescana. La stessa chef di Casa Maria Luigia, la canadese Jessica Rosval, viene dalle cucine della Francescana.

La classifica pubblicata oggi riguarda i posti dal 51 al 100: quella dei 50 Best 2026, sponsorizzata da S.Pellegrino & Acqua Panna, verrà rivelata durante la cerimonia del prossimo 4 novembre a Lima, in Perù. Che è la città dove si trova Maido, il ristorante di Mitsuharu ‘Micha’ Tsumura primo nella classifica dei 50 Best 2025.

Ristorante Uliassi. Banchina di Levante, 6, 60019 Senigallia AN. Telefono: 071 65463. Instagram

#1359. Malaria Parasite Caught in the Act of Breaking and Entering

Get the latest news delivered to your inbox.

An editorially independent publication supported by the Simons Foundation.

Create a reading list by clicking the Read Later icon next to the articles you wish to save.

Popular Searches

Click to tell Google to prioritize Quanta and see more of the best coverage of science and math in your search and AI results.

Plasmodium, the parasite that causes malaria, invades and proliferates inside red blood cells. Researchers imaged the proteins (dark purple ovals) it places on the cell membrane that let it slip through unnoticed.

In medieval Italy, it was accepted wisdom that anyone walking near a swamp risked falling ill from “bad air” — mala aria. Victims were struck with fever, headache, nausea, and chills, and occasionally the illness escalated to vomiting, jaundice, and death. Today, we still call this affliction malaria. For much of human history, it has ravaged populations in humid tropical and subtropical regions, killing untold numbers. In the 20th century, it was responsible for up to 5% of deaths worldwide; it still kills approximately 600,000 people each year.

What malaria was and how it infected humans was deeply mysterious until barely 150 years ago. In 1880, the French physician Charles Louis Alphonse Laveran peered at a sample of a soldier’s blood through a crude microscope and discovered the true cause of the disease: not miasma, but a genus of shape-shifting single-celled protists called Plasmodium. Since then, scientists and doctors have described in precise detail the parasites’ life cycle, hosts, and disease progression, and even the nuances of various Plasmodium species, which present slightly different forms of the disease. But some crucial aspects have remained a mystery.

Chi-Min Ho is a microbiologist and structural biologist mapping the proteins that malaria parasites use to invade our red blood cells.

For example, Plasmodium invades human red blood cells as part of its life cycle. To get in, the microbe creates a ring-shaped structure called the moving junction, which briefly creates a gap in the cell membrane it can slip through. The gap then disappears without a trace. It opens and closes so rapidly, at such a small scale, that imaging technologies couldn’t capture it. Researchers had no clue what the portal structure actually looked like. “Because of that,” said Chi-Min Ho, a microbiologist and structural biologist at Columbia University, “we didn’t really know anything about how it works.”

Now, Ho’s lab has imaged the moving junction right at the moment of invasion, in unprecedented detail. Her team found that when the Plasmodium parasite installs molecular gaskets in the host cell, it radically remodels the cell membrane to slip through without a trace. This knowledge could help inform the next generation of malaria treatments and influence the drug-discovery process for other parasitic diseases, such as cyclosporiasis and toxoplasmosis.

“It’s a totally mind-blowing paper,” said Jake Baum, a parasitologist at the University of New South Wales, who was not involved in the research. “At the end of the day, this is not molecular biology. This is biophysics.”

The history of malaria research has paralleled advances in microscopy, from the development of simple light microscopes like the one Laveran used to the cutting-edge cryo-electron techniques of Ho’s lab. This is because the cells the microbes invade are extremely tiny — and the parasites are even smaller. At about 8 micrometers across, red blood cells are among the smallest cells in the human body, and all species of Plasmodium are a fraction of that size during the invasion stage.

Attempts to image the parasites in the act of breaking and entering got off the ground in the 1970s, when pioneering microbiologists first applied electron microscopy. These scientists observed a distinct thickening of the cellular membrane near the parasite’s access point. Then the tiny, round Plasmodium seemed to simply merge with the cell, like a water droplet coalescing into a larger pool. It would be decades before techniques developed enough to isolate the proteins that make this possible, much less image them.

Get Quanta Magazine delivered to your inbox

James Dvorak’s lab at the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases took the first microscopic videos of Plasmodium parasites entering a red blood cell. This one was filmed in 1978. Arrows point to parasite entry points.

Another hurdle is that malaria parasites have a very complicated life cycle. They are most at home in the gut of a mosquito where they can reproduce sexually. Humans are what’s known as a reservoir host — a place for the parasite to live while it waits to be taken up by an insect.

“The food supply happens to be our red blood cells,” said Kirk Deitsch, a microbiologist and immunologist at Weill Cornell Medicine in New York. “That’s why they’re invading us.”

To this end, the Plasmodium parasite assumes a variety of shapes and sizes as it moves through its life stages: Sometimes it’s shaped like an egg, sometimes a spindly thread, sometimes a gangly starfish. It can move through this cycle in rapid succession or hang out in one stage (the hypnozoite phase in the human liver) for years. When it enters its tiny, round merozoite stage, the parasite is ready to invade a red blood cell.

If you’re trying to push an orange into a balloon, the balloon mustn’t pop, right?

Plasmodium pulls up to the scene of the crime with all the proteins and other biological equipment it needs. The entry procedure is more delicate than simply punching a hole in the host cell. “If you’re trying to push an orange into a balloon, the balloon mustn’t pop, right?” Baum said.

Based on previous research, scientists knew the broad strokes of this process. The parasite approaches a host red blood cell and inserts a ring of protein anchors into the cell’s membrane. Collectively these anchors are known as the moving junction. Plasmodium locks into them with proteins expressed on its surface — and then pushes forward. The moving junction forms a continuous portal in the host cell membrane for the parasite to travel through. Once the parasite is fully inside, the cell membrane seals up behind it. The whole process takes less than a minute.

Ho and the other authors of the new paper used cryo-electron microscopy to probe the four individual protein units in each anchor. What they learned allowed them to propose a more detailed model for how the moving junction actively remodels the host cell’s membrane. The parasite injects into the red blood cell three proteins, which form a dense wedge beneath the membrane surface; a fourth protein connects this structure to the invader. Plasmodium places many of these anchors on the red blood cell surface. The proteins produce electrostatic forces and pressure in the cell membrane, which crowd and displace its lipid molecules. This deforms the membrane and reverses its curvature. It bows slightly inward around the parasite — in fact, some lipids slough off and reassemble into a protective membrane for the invader — before re-forming and sealing behind it.

“It’s a really nice example of how a field has built step by step by step toward a really powerful observation,” Baum said.

A visualization of four proteins in the moving junction anchor complex. The electrostatic properties of these proteins destabilize the membrane’s lipid bilayer and deform it, letting the parasite slip through.

Once inside, Plasmodium approaches its remodeling work more comprehensively. Red blood cells are essentially bags of hemoglobin; they have no nucleus or organelles to speak of. So Plasmodium builds from the ground up. It secretes proteins that allow it to feed on hemoglobin, remove waste, and stretch the cell’s cytoplasm. Ho compared it to the conversion of an empty warehouse floor into a stylish lofted apartment.

“It’s putting in plumbing,” she said. “It’s putting in the floors. It’s literally building everything for itself.”

In this process, the parasite also redecorates the cell’s exterior. It is equipped with genes that allow it to make a series of distinct but closely related adhesive proteins that it can express on the red blood cell’s surface. These proteins cause the cells to stick to the walls of the blood vessels around them — one of the main causes of malaria’s painful symptoms. In 2025, research from Deitsch’s lab found that by periodically switching between proteins, the parasite can avoid tipping off the immune system to its presence for days or weeks at a time. Such extensive exterior cellular remodeling serves a purpose: It helps Plasmodium avoid a trip to the spleen, an organ that filters out dead, defective, or broken red blood cells as well as any undercover parasites.

Protrusions called knobs cover the surface of an infected red blood cell. Plasmodium, the parasite that causes malaria, expresses these proteins after it invades the cell. They make cells clump to the walls of blood vessels, causing the disease’s most dangerous symptoms including organ distress, seizures, and coma.

Rick Fairhurst and Jordan Zuspann, National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases, National Institutes of Health

The parasite itself undergoes a radical change inside the cell. It transforms from a roundish merozoite into an amoebalike trophozoite. It grows several cytoplasm “arms” and flattens out, said Christiaan van Ooij, a molecular parasitologist at Keele University in the United Kingdom. This also helps it evade the immune system. The trophozoite shape is more flexible than that of the spherical merozoite, and the immune system clocks supple cells as healthy and stiff cells as dead.

The parasite then replicates asexually for about 48 hours, dividing inside the red blood cell until it’s so full of Plasmodium that it bursts. Like house flippers, the parasites move on to other blood cells. Within days, millions could be lurking in the bloodstream.

In this way, malaria can quickly overwhelm a human host. It is all enabled by the moving junction that allows the parasites to set up shop without tipping off the authorities. The structure of the moving junction could help researchers intervene, with drugs to block the parasite from invading a host blood cell in the first place.

Malaria treatment has long been something of a hit-or-miss proposition. Without a granular view of how Plasmodium interacts with host cells, researchers had to test various compounds by trial and error. If a given drug seemed to fight the illness, they had little idea what part of the infection process it had disrupted. “All that work was done essentially blind,” Deitsch said.

This has made developing new malaria treatments notoriously difficult. The former workhorse antimalarial drugs, such as chloroquine, sulfadoxine, and pyrimethamine, are now known to target the parasites in the bloodstream. But the Plasmodium species that infect humans are rapidly evolving resistance to these compounds.

Invasion offers a tantalizing choke point for new medicines. “If you block invasion, then you stop the parasite in its tracks,” Ho said. To make her point, her team used an AI-powered protein-design platform to craft an inhibitory protein that could block the moving junction. In test tubes, it prevented Plasmodium from entering red blood cells. But its safety and efficacy haven’t been tested in animal models.

It’s possible that the moving junction could be something of a skeleton key that could be used to treat other parasitic diseases. Plasmodium is a member of the apicomplexans, a large phylum of parasitic protists that also includes Toxoplasma gondii, a cat parasite, and Cyclospora, which causes explosive diarrhea. These single-celled organisms appear to enter using the same biochemical equipment as Plasmodium. “All of these are parasites that have this invasion machinery,” Deitsch said. The study of those conditions could in turn inform malaria treatment. A 2026 paper described the mechanism by which Toxoplasma senses the right moment to deploy its moving junction, and malaria may operate the same way.

But the moving junction may prove to be too much of a moving target. “Some people have always argued that invasion is a really bad drug target because it’s a very short process,” van Ooij said. Any drug with the ability to stop invasion would have a roughly 60-second window in which to do so, which means it would need to remain stable in the body for a long time or act extremely quickly, or both.

Ho’s team already has their sights set on another target. They plan to use similar cryo-electron microscopy techniques to solve the structure of other protein complexes involved in malaria infection, such as those adhesive proteins that keep infected blood cells from journeying to the spleen.

“We’ve caught one white whale,” Ho said. “So we want to go after the other remaining white whales.”

#1363. SpaceX, Tesla and Anthropic may reshape the S&P 500—but not right away

Financial experts from Warren Buffett on down often urge retail investors to own a portfolio spread across the broad U.S. stock market. And if you own a fund that tracks the S&P 500, you more or less have just that — a who's who of the largest stocks available on U.S. exchanges.

But what happens when a new bombshell enters the proverbial villa?

Index fund investors may be pondering that exact question, given the news that SpaceX CEO Elon Musk said he's considering a tie-up with Tesla. When SpaceX reported its third-quarter financial results last week, Musk said on the earnings call that he'd consider a combination with the Austin, Texas-based electric car maker, in what would be the largest merger in history.

Adding fuel to this quandary, on Monday, AI firm Anthropic filed an S-1 with the Securities and Exchange Commission, signaling the company's intention to go public.

Both could be huge companies. Doing a little back-of-the-napkin math, SpaceX and Tesla sport market capitalizations, calculated by multiplying share price by shares outstanding, of $2 trillion and $1.55 trillion, respectively. Smash those together, and a theoretical $3.55 trillion company would be the fifth-largest company on the market. Experts say Anthropic could seek a valuation between $1.5 trillion and $2 trillion at its offering, which at current prices could make it between the world's eighth- and twelfth-largest firm.

But if you hold an S&P 500 fund, that doesn't necessarily mean you're about to have new top-10 holdings. Here's why, and why index mechanics matter for your portfolio.

It's easy to think of the S&P 500 as a very straightforward, math-based index. If you assumed the index merely held the 500 largest stocks on the market, weighted by market size, you'd be mostly right.

But if you're already invested in an S&P 500 fund — and many people are; S&P Dow Jones Indices estimated about $16 trillion was invested in products designed to track the S&P 500 as of year-end 2025 — you may have noticed that SpaceX isn't included in the portfolio. That's because S&P generally has a 12-month waiting period for newly public stocks to join the index, meaning that Musk's rocket firm will have to wait until June 2027 to be considered for inclusion.

Anthropic could face a similar waiting period before S&P's index committee considers the stock for admission.

As for a potential Musk-led supercompany, experts say its inclusion and weighting in the index would come down to several factors, including the mechanics of the merger and the percentage of shares of the combined company made available to the public.

A representative from S&P Dow Jones Indices told CNBC Make It that the firm does not comment on hypothetical scenarios or any company's eligibility for index inclusion. The firm's methodology states that each merger and acquisition is reviewed on a case-by-base basis. If an acquiring company is in the S&P 500 and acquires a firm not in the index, that firm generally stays in the index, though S&P could remove it if the transaction affects its eligibility. Non-members that acquire members can be added, too, provided they meet other eligibility criteria, at the index committee's discretion.

It remains to be seen if and when Anthropic or a Tesla/SpaceX combo would be added to the S&P 500. But if they eventually make it into an index fund you own, experts say there are a couple of key things to consider.

One would be a bump in exposure to Musk-led firms, meaning that more of your portfolio could be tied to the tech CEO's vision of the future, says Seth Goldstein, a senior equity analyst at investment research firm Morningstar.

"For direct holders of Tesla or SpaceX, you're holding the stock because you believe in Elon Musk's vision and believe that he can turn seemingly conceptual products into a reality," Goldstein says. "Whether that is cars that can drive themselves [or] humanoid robots that can be useful, he has these sort of grand visions for future technologies, and he has the ability to bring them into real products."

Another consideration is concentration risk — the idea that much of the fate of a particular portfolio is tied to a small number of investments. Nearly 40% of assets in any given S&P 500 fund are currently invested in the index's top-10 holdings, many of which are directly or tangentially tied to the proliferation of artificial intelligence. From December 1965 through March 2026, the S&P 500's top-10 constituents accounted for 23% of the index, on average, according to research from T. Rowe Price.

Additions of a SpaceX/Tesla firm or of Anthropic could further tilt the S&P 500 toward tech and AI, and, more broadly, toward companies whose stocks have already seen major run-ups, says Brent Leadbetter, head of RAFI distribution at investment research firm TMX VettaFi.

"We are wary of concentration. By definition, the shares of firms that reach the top of cap-weighted indices have appreciated at a faster rate than the firms they have surpassed," Leadbetter says. "These recent winners are often expensive as a result. Investing in expensive companies is too often a way for investors to chase strong past returns only to realize modest future returns."

#1368. See Inside Cells Like Never Before in These Vivid Microscopic Images

Get the latest news delivered to your inbox.

An editorially independent publication supported by the Simons Foundation.

Create a reading list by clicking the Read Later icon next to the articles you wish to save.

Popular Searches

Click to tell Google to prioritize Quanta and see more of the best coverage of science and math in your search and AI results.

For this image of neurons in mouse brain tissue, Kaelin Wulf and Rachel Flannery of the Allen Institute used a home-built light-sheet microscope. In light-sheet fluorescence microscopy, a thin sheet of light illuminates a sample, which can then be scanned plane by plane. “I hope people can take away a sense of awe at how intricate, beautiful, and unimaginably vast the brain is,” Wulf said.

Kaelin Wulf, Rachel Flannery/Allen Institute; all photos courtesy of Nikon Small World

On a frigid February morning in Edinburgh, Scotland, Patrick Hickey had run out of living things to put under his microscope. The plants and fungi in his garden had dried up, and summer puddles, with their flamboyant biological complexity, had long frozen over.

Hickey, a mycologist at Hypha Research Ltd., was using plant leaves to study mitochondria, cellular organelles that generate energy. He was planning to sprout mustard seeds for fresh samples, but he was impatient. While making coffee in his kitchen, he noticed a cold-hardy turtle vine hanging from the windowsill. “I snipped off an inch or so, put it in my pocket, took it into the lab, and was just amazed at what I saw,” Hickey said.

Under the microscope, mitochondria darted around the cells. They nimbly maneuvered around slower chloroplasts, like motorcyclists dodging traffic. “It was absolutely alive with activity,” Hickey said.

His time-lapse video of this microscopic dance, which leads our gallery below and was recently honored in Nikon’s 2026 Small World in Motion Competition, reveals the close partnership between the organelles: chloroplasts (red) spin sunlight into sugar, and mitochondria (green) convert sugar into energy.

The Nikon Small World competition, established in 1974, honors excellence in microscopy. The annual contests have charted not only the evolution of creative photomicrography but also the progress of imaging technology.

Hickey — and many of the other honorees featured here — relied on a technique called confocal laser scanning microscopy.

Unlike a standard microscope, which illuminates an entire sample at once and can produce blurry images, a confocal microscope focuses on one depth level at a time. Researchers first “label” a sample with fluorescent dyes that attach to specific structures within the cell. A laser then illuminates a thin layer of the sample, and the microscope detects the resulting fluorescence. Scanning line by line, the system builds a detailed image.

As imaging technology advances, so too does our understanding of cellular processes. Hickey’s video shows that mitochondria are more dynamic than previously thought, which suggests that they are “more than just a ‘powerhouse of the cell,’” he said. “They are likely involved in cytoplasmic streaming, signaling, and interactions with other organelles.”

The full list of awardees can be found here for the photo contest and here for the video contest. We’ve chosen to feature a several winners and honorable mentions that reveal the intricacies of the cellular world.

Get Quanta Magazine delivered to your inbox

Mitochondria (green) navigate around chloroplasts (red) in the leaf cells of a turtle vine. “Their movement looked like rivers of electricity flowing within the cells,” Hickey said.

To study diseases, Gauri Kulkarni of Wake Forest Institute for Regenerative Medicine grows miniature organs in her lab, including the 1.3-millimeter human gut tissue shown in this image. The glowing network reveals the connections between epithelial cells that make up a healthy gut barrier. This barrier acts like a microscopic security guard, keeping harmful microbes and food toxins from leaking into the bloodstream. “In science, we often rely on cold data and numbers to understand disease, but photomicrography bridges the gap between logic and emotion,” Kulkarni said.

Gauri Kulkarni/Wake Forest Institute for Regenerative Medicine

This video shows how heart muscle cells contract and how calcium regulates their beating. The green chains are sarcomeres, the smallest contractile units of heart muscle. The red flashes show calcium inside the cell. At the start of a beat, an electrical impulse sends calcium into the cell, which triggers the release of more calcium. All this calcium tells the sarcomeres to contract. The calcium then leaves the cytoplasm, which allows the cell to relax in preparation for the next beat. “The same video can reveal the beauty of living heart cells while providing quantitative information about their structure and function,” said Yasaman Maaref of Simon Fraser University, who created the video.

This video of a mouse’s brain cells shows actin (blue), a protein that helps the cell change shape, and lysosomes (orange), organelles that break down cellular waste. While both structures move, the lysosomes are much faster, making the actin network appear almost stationary in comparison.

Bruno Cisterna, Halli Lindamood, Eric Vitriol/Medical College of Georgia at Augusta University

The top layer of this image of a mouse trachea shows the epithelium, the outer layer of skin cells. Each green dot is the nucleus of a single cell. Beneath, a layer of black basement membrane, mostly made of collagen, provides structure and acts as a filter. Next, a thick layer of yellow reveals the actin packed inside smooth muscle cells that control the movement of air through the trachea. And that faint layer of dark blue at upper right? That’s “the kind of mucus you cough and spit out,” said Julien Resseguier, who created the image to study the interplay between neural and immune systems.

This image of a rat liver endothelial cell shows actin filaments (brownish orange) and microtubules (white). Both of these protein structures work together to give the cell its shape. Intracellular gaps are visible in the image; these holes can disrupt the liver’s protective blood barrier and might indicate injury, inflammation, or cancer.

Francisco Lázaro-Diéguez/Albert Einstein College of Medicine

Embryonic cells from the skin of Xenopus, a clawed frog, have cilia, seen here in green, that beat in unison to generate a wave of fluid movement past the cell surface. Confocal laser scanning microscopy allowed the researchers to distinguish individual cilia, the centrioles that anchor them (red), and cell boundaries (white) that help the cells stick together.

Pierre Nouaux, Laurent Kodjabachianan, Camille Boutin/IBDM Marseille

Trypanosoma cruzi, the parasite that causes Chagas disease, is an intracellular pathogen that can infect almost all mammal cell types. Richard Atherton of the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine captured this image of a T. cruzi nest inside a host cell. “If my image can raise even a little more awareness about Chagas disease, then I will be happy,” Atherton said. “I also hope my image can get people excited about science, nature, and the infinite microscopic worlds hidden all around us.”

Richard Atherton/London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine

This video, by Andrew Moore of the Howard Hughes Medical Institute, illuminates how actin (white) and mitochondria (blue) interact during cell division. Moore found that the actin seemed to be involved in positioning and organizing the mitochondria; the actin cycles through the mitochondrial network in a wave and forms “comet tails” that drive bursts of motion. Over the course of mitosis, these comet tails “mix up the mitochondrial network, shuffling their spatial position, almost like a card dealer shuffling a deck of cards,” Moore said.

Andrew Moore/Howard Hughes Medical Institute

#1371. Low testosterone may make sugar far more harmful to your liver

Low testosterone can contribute to several health problems, and an unhealthy diet may make some of those risks even worse. One major concern is metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD), a condition that affects approximately 40% of adult men worldwide and has become a significant global health issue.

Fatty liver, the earliest stage of MASLD, occurs when excess fat builds up in the liver. Several factors are associated with the condition, including obesity, type 2 diabetes, low testosterone levels, and excessive fructose consumption from sugary drinks and processed foods. However, scientists have not fully understood how these factors interact or whether their combined effects are more harmful than each one individually.

How Low Testosterone and Fructose Affect the Liver

To investigate this connection, a research team from the Graduate School of Agriculture, led by graduate student Hiroki Takahashi and Associate Professor Naoki Harada, examined how reduced testosterone and high fructose intake influence liver health.

The researchers used eight-week-old male mice and divided them into six experimental groups. Some underwent castration to lower testosterone levels, while others received a sham operation. The groups included Sham/Control, Sham/Fructose, Sham/Fructose + Antibiotics, Castration/Control, Castration/Fructose, and Castration/Fructose + Antibiotics.

To determine how these conditions affected the animals, the team analyzed liver cells and tissues, blood plasma, organic acids from the cecum, and samples of gut bacteria.

The results revealed that mice with reduced testosterone levels developed heavier livers when they consumed fructose. However, this increase in liver weight was smaller in mice that also received antibiotics.

When examined separately, low testosterone and fructose intake produced only modest changes in liver triglyceride levels. When combined, however, the two factors had a much stronger effect, significantly increasing fat accumulation and worsening fatty liver.

The researchers also identified changes in the composition of gut bacteria, altered liver gene activity, and elevated levels of pyruvate in the cecum among mice exposed to both reduced testosterone and fructose.

These findings suggested that the gut microbiome could play an important role in explaining why the combination was particularly harmful.

Further experiments helped the researchers identify a possible biological explanation for the increased liver fat.

"Upon examining this mechanism, we found that changes in the gut microbiota led to increased levels of pyruvate within the intestine. Furthermore, experiments using mouse-derived primary hepatocytes revealed that pyruvate acts synergistically with fructose to promote neutral lipid accumulation in hepatocytes," explained Takahashi.

In other words, changes in gut bacteria appeared to increase intestinal pyruvate, a compound involved in energy metabolism. Laboratory experiments with liver cells isolated from mice showed that pyruvate and fructose worked together to increase fat storage in those cells.

The discovery suggests that interactions among testosterone levels, dietary fructose, and gut bacteria may help explain how fatty liver develops and worsens.

Potential New Ways to Prevent Fatty Liver Disease

Understanding this relationship could eventually help researchers identify new approaches to preventing or treating fatty liver disease. In particular, targeting the processes through which pyruvate contributes to fat accumulation may offer promising possibilities.

"Going forward, we hope to clarify the mechanism by which pyruvate promotes triglyceride accumulation to pioneer the development of therapeutic drugs and establishment of preventive methods through dietary interventions," added Professor Harada.

Although the findings come from experiments in mice and isolated mouse liver cells, they provide new insight into how hormonal changes and diet may interact to influence liver health.

The study was published in American Journal of Physiology-Endocrinology and Metabolism.

Materials provided by Osaka Metropolitan University. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#1372. Man charged with assisting ‘foreign intelligence service’ after incident at UK base used for Iran strikes

The U.K. has said it had charged a man with an offense of assisting a "foreign intelligence service" over an incident at a military base used by the U.S. for strikes on Iran.

Mohmed Abdulkarim, 24, has been charged under the country's National Security Act "following an incident involving RAF Fairford," an air base in west England, prosecutors announced on Tuesday.

Between Aug. 31 and Sept. 28, Abdulkarim is alleged to have engaged in "conduct that would likely materially assist a foreign intelligence service in carrying out U.K.-related activities", the Crown Prosecution Service added. The foreign country was not named.

Prosecutors also charged 24-year-old Nouman Essghir with "entering a prohibited place for a purpose prejudicial to the UK".

The men are due to appear in court in London on Tuesday.

Five people were arrested on suspicion of explosives and terrorism offenses near RAF Fairford on Sept. 28. The base had been used as the U.S. Air Force's command outpost for operations from Europe and for American strikes on Iranian missile sites.

Announcing the charges, Frank Ferguson, a chief prosecutor for the Crown Prosecution Service's Special Crime and Counter Terrorism Division, said that they followed "a Counter Terrorism Policing investigation into a high-profile incident involving RAF Fairford."

"We will continue to work closely with our partners as this complex investigation continues," he said.

After the arrests, U.S. President Donald Trump said the U.S. had moved its long-range bombers out of the U.K. in response to a threat "linked to Iran."

Prime Minister Andy Burnham told lawmakers earlier this month that the incident was "highly likely to have been coordinated in Iran, almost certainly directed by Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard."

Over the summer, Iran's Revolutionary Guard warned it saw any military base involved in launching airstrikes on Iran as a legitimate target.

Tehran denied any involvement in the incident at RAF Fairford.

#1379. Blocco dei Tir, supermercati vuoti al Sud, ma è peggio del Covid

La mobilitazione degli autotrasportatori contro il caro carburante, che sta mettendo sotto pressione la distribuzione delle merci, merita più attenzione. La protesta non riguarda soltanto chi guida un camion o gestisce un’azienda di trasporti, ma chiunque faccia la spesa, lavori nella produzione alimentare o si occupi di ristorazione. Perché quando si interrompe il trasporto, il problema non è più soltanto di chi trasporta: diventa di chi produce, di chi vende e, infine, di chi mangia. Che trova i supermercati vuoti.

Non solo al Sud, in realtà: anche dal Veneto arrivano le prime avvisaglie.

Eppure il rischio è relegare la mobilitazione a una questione di categoria, una vertenza da seguire attraverso gli incontri con il Governo e le dichiarazioni delle associazioni di settore. Poi sono arrivati gli scaffali sguarniti, i reparti del fresco con disponibilità ridotte, le difficoltà nei rifornimenti di alcuni supermercati. E il problema è diventato improvvisamente visibile. Come se il lavoro necessario a far arrivare il cibo sulle nostre tavole esistesse soltanto nel momento in cui smette di funzionare.

Com’è possibile che chi lavora non riesca più, in alcuni casi, a sostenere economicamente il proprio lavoro?

Il caro carburante è il fattore che ha alimentato la protesta, ma il nodo è più profondo. Un’impresa di autotrasporto deve sostenere il costo del gasolio, la manutenzione dei mezzi, le assicurazioni, il personale, i pedaggi e gli altri oneri di gestione. Se i costi aumentano senza che le tariffe consentano di assorbirli, il margine si riduce fino a mettere in discussione la sostenibilità stessa dell’attività.

Non è normale che un lavoratore o un imprenditore debba scegliere tra partire rischiando di lavorare in perdita e fermarsi rinunciando ai propri guadagni. Non è normale che una funzione essenziale dell’economia venga considerata scontata finché qualcuno è disposto a sostenerne i costi. E non è normale che la fragilità di un’intera filiera diventi una questione pubblica soltanto quando produce conseguenze visibili per i consumatori.

Il punto non è sostenere che ogni richiesta di una categoria debba essere accolta senza discussione. È riconoscere che il prezzo di un servizio deve essere compatibile con i costi necessari a erogarlo. Altrimenti il mercato continua a pretendere efficienza da chi, economicamente, non è più nelle condizioni di garantirla. E i supermercati diventano scatole vuote.

La protesta degli autotrasportatori mette in evidenza una contraddizione che riguarda molti settori. Chiediamo a chi lavora di essere competitivo, puntuale e affidabile, ma spesso trattiamo le condizioni economiche come un problema secondario. Finché il camion parte, la consegna arriva e il prodotto è disponibile, il sistema sembra funzionare. Ma se per mantenerlo in movimento chi lavora deve assorbire costi insostenibili, quella normalità è soltanto apparente.

C’è poi una questione che in Italia non può essere separata da quella economica: la geografia dell’attenzione. La mobilitazione ha interessato diverse aree del Mezzogiorno, dalla Campania alla Puglia, dalla Calabria alla Sicilia. In alcune zone sono segnalate difficoltà nei rifornimenti, soprattutto per i prodotti freschi, che richiedono consegne frequenti e hanno tempi di conservazione limitati. Le conseguenze non sono uniformi, ma il disagio è concreto e riguarda territori nei quali la distribuzione alimentare dipende da collegamenti regolari con piattaforme logistiche, mercati e centri di lavorazione.

Eppure resta la sensazione di un Paese che non riesce a riconoscersi fino in fondo come un sistema comune. Il Mezzogiorno sembra dover arrivare all’emergenza per conquistare (forse) spazio nel dibattito nazionale. Le difficoltà economiche, le fragilità infrastrutturali e le conseguenze delle interruzioni logistiche diventano notizia quando producono immagini inequivocabili. Cioè un reparto vuoto, un mercato senza merce, una consegna che non arriva.

Il problema non è soltanto quanto spazio venga riservato alla protesta nei mezzi di informazione. È quanto le questioni che attraversano il Sud siano considerate questioni nazionali. Perché se una filiera alimentare si inceppa in Campania o in Puglia, non siamo davanti a un inconveniente circoscritto a quei territori. Siamo davanti a un sistema che mostra una vulnerabilità capace di propagarsi lungo tutta la catena di approvvigionamento fino ai supermercati vuoti.

Il Mezzogiorno non è una periferia economica che può essere ignorata finché il disagio resta confinato entro i suoi confini. È un territorio di produzione, trasformazione e distribuzione alimentare, con imprese e lavoratori che partecipano a pieno titolo all’economia nazionale. La protesta degli autotrasportatori dovrebbe ricordarcelo senza bisogno di aspettare che gli effetti arrivino altrove.

C’è un’altra contraddizione. Mentre in alcune aree del Sud i rifornimenti incontrano difficoltà e i supermercati sono vuoti, le segnalazioni descrivono una situazione meno compromessa al Nord. Nel frattempo, la grande distribuzione continua a basarsi su reti logistiche capaci di movimentare prodotti provenienti anche da Paesi molto lontani.

Non è una questione di contrapporre il prodotto italiano a quello straniero. Le importazioni sono parte integrante del sistema alimentare contemporaneo e rispondono a esigenze di mercato, stagionalità, disponibilità e prezzo. Il punto è: come può una filiera capace di movimentare merci da una parte all’altra del mondo diventare così vulnerabile quando si interrompono i collegamenti interni?

La domanda è rilevante quando riguarda frutta, verdura e altri prodotti freschi. Merce che attraversa confini e percorre migliaia di chilometri per raggiungere un punto vendita, mentre in un’altra parte dello stesso Paese il sistema di approvvigionamento rallenta o si blocca. Non significa che ogni prodotto importato continui ad arrivare regolarmente al Nord, né che le difficoltà del Sud dipendano soltanto dalla protesta. Significa, però, che la crisi invita a interrogarsi sulla resilienza delle reti distributive e sulle differenze territoriali nella capacità di assorbire uno shock logistico.

I vuoti sugli scaffali dei supermercati non dipendono soltanto da quanta merce viene prodotta. Dipende da come viene movimentata, da dove sono collocati i centri di distribuzione, dalla continuità dei collegamenti e dalla possibilità di sostituire rapidamente un percorso interrotto. È una questione economica, ma anche una questione di organizzazione del sistema alimentare.

Ed è qui che il confronto tra Nord e Sud smette di essere una contrapposizione geografica e diventa una domanda politica. Quanto è davvero integrato il mercato alimentare italiano, se una crisi che investe una parte del Paese può tradursi in difficoltà così evidenti nella disponibilità dei prodotti?

Nel dibattito gastronomico utilizziamo spesso parole come territorio, filiera corta, stagionalità, sostenibilità, valorizzazione delle produzioni locali. Rischiano di diventare formule vuote se non consideriamo le condizioni materiali che permettono ai prodotti di arrivare a destinazione.

Una filiera non è soltanto il campo in cui cresce un ortaggio, il caseificio che trasforma il latte, il laboratorio che produce pasta o il ristorante che lavora una materia prima. È anche il magazzino, il mezzo che trasporta la merce, la rete che collega produttori e distributori. È il lavoro di chi carica, guida, scarica e consegna. Senza questi passaggi, anche una produzione eccellente rischia di non raggiungere il proprio mercato. Infatti il Consorzio della Mozzarella di Bufala Dop ha annunciato il fermo della produzione. L’effetto non è solo nei supermercati con gli scaffali vuoti.

Per questo la sostenibilità alimentare deve comprendere anche la sostenibilità economica e sociale della filiera. Se il trasporto non è economicamente praticabile, l’intero sistema ne risente: il produttore rischia di non collocare la merce, il distributore di non rifornire i punti vendita, il consumatore di non trovare ciò che cerca.

Il problema riguarda anche il mondo della ristorazione. Un locale può costruire la propria identità sulla qualità delle materie prime, sulla stagionalità e sul rapporto con i produttori, ma non è immune dalle difficoltà della logistica. La disponibilità degli ingredienti, la regolarità delle consegne e i costi di approvvigionamento incidono sulla programmazione della cucina e sui margini dell’impresa. Il cibo che arriva al tavolo è il risultato di una catena di attività che raramente il cliente vede.

Parliamo molto di ciò che rende un prodotto buono, autentico o sostenibile. Molto meno delle condizioni che consentono a quel prodotto di arrivare sul mercato. La protesta degli autotrasportatori ci obbliga a riportare l’attenzione su questo passaggio.

Una mobilitazione non dovrebbe essere giudicata soltanto in base al rumore che produce o all’entità del disagio. Il fatto che una protesta sia civile non la rende meno importante; il fatto che non occupi ogni giorno le aperture dei telegiornali non significa che sia marginale. Al contrario, dovrebbe essere un’occasione per affrontare il problema prima che le conseguenze diventino ancora più pesanti.

Il l Ministero delle Infrastrutture e dei Trasporti ha annunciato risorse per il settore ma la tecnica sembra attendista. In Sicilia è stata annunciata una parziale revoca del blocco dei Tir, mentre in Campania, Puglia e Calabria la mobilitazione continua. Gli impegni istituzionali sono un passaggio importante, ma disponibilità di fondi ed effettiva soluzione dei problemi non sono la stessa cosa. Occorre capire se le misure saranno sufficienti a rendere sostenibili i costi e a ripristinare condizioni di lavoro compatibili con la continuità del servizio.

Il rischio è che si parli degli autotrasportatori soltanto per gli scaffali vuoti. E che il disagio dei consumatori venga considerato il problema principale, mentre le condizioni economiche di chi tiene in movimento la filiera restano sullo sfondo.

Gli scaffali vuoti sono l’effetto visibile di una crisi che comincia molto prima: nei costi che aumentano, nei margini che si assottigliano, nelle attività che non riescono più a sostenersi. Aspettare che il disagio raggiunga il supermercato ormai vuoto significa intervenire quando il problema è già diventato collettivo.

Il Sud non dovrebbe aver bisogno di scaffali vuoti per diventare una notizia nazionale. E chi trasporta il cibo non dovrebbe essere costretto a fermarsi perché ci accorgiamo del suo lavoro soltanto quando la merce non arriva più.

C’è la corsa a fare scorte alimentari: sembra di essere tornati ai tempi del Covid. Ma è peggio: il virus questa volta è sistemico.

Sembrava una nostra provocazione. Invece Coldiretti ha fatto un confronto proprio con l’emergenza Covid e ha chiesto all’Europa di mettere in campo un nuovo Pnrr straordinario per l’agricoltura, con risorse aggiuntive rispetto alla Pac. Fondi necessari per fronteggiare l’aumento dei costi di produzione, sostenere gli investimenti e garantire così la salute dei cittadini e la sopravvivenza delle imprese agricole. Secondo Coldiretti la crisi energetica e produttiva rischia di essere peggiore di quella causata dal Covid.

L’elaborazione del Centro Studi Divulga sostiene che se l’aumento medio dei prezzi dell’energia e degli input agricoli osservatonella prima metà del 2026 dovesse perdurare verrebbe a mancare dalle tavole una produzione di cereali pari a oltre 230 miliardi di pasti. Una cifra altissima che andrebbe a colpire soprattutto i Paesi più poveri.

Curiosa per natura, diffido dalle certezze assolute. Preferisco capire piuttosto che seguire, osservare piuttosto che giudicare. Non mi interessano le mode, mi interessano le idee. Osservo, faccio domande e cerco risposte. Credo che il senso critico sia il miglior ingrediente di ogni racconto. Se questo passa attraverso il cibo, tanto meglio.
