#1403. Lo storico ristorante di pesce di Roma che ora è ai Parioli: com’è

Ottavio, vecchia gloria della ristorazione di pesce a Roma, riapre dopo una lunga pausa e rianima un angolo di via Savoia, a cavallo tra Salario e Parioli. Stessa insegna, ma lontani dall’Esquilino, che ne aveva visto i natali. Prima come bottiglieria, poi mano a mano come uno dei punti di riferimento cittadini per una buona, solida cucina marinara di qualità e senza follie nei prezzi.

Il passaggio da Santa Croce in Gerusalemme, per Ottavio è anche un passaggio generazionale. Dai nonni fondatori, ai nipoti rifondatori con un guizzo di modernità innestata su una tradizione che, in questi anni di assenza, aveva fatto sentire la sua mancanza.

Una veloce scorsa al menu prima di raccontarvi questa cena stampa di Giorgia Basili e Giancarlo Loquenzi per darvi qualche prezzo verificato in loco ad ottobre.

Il menù è in gran parte lo stesso che nonna Anna cucinava ogni sera nel suo ristorante.

— Le ostriche (irlandesi, italiane o francesi) costano 5 o 7 € l’una— I Gamberi rossi di Mazara del Vallo, 16 € per 100 grammi— Polpo e patate, 24 €— Crudo di mare alla Mediterranea, 26 €— Linguine e mazzancolla, 32 €— Pescato del giorno, dai 100 ai 140 € per 1 chilo— Calamari e gamberi fritti, 18 €

Con tre piatti regolari – antipasto, primo, secondo – potete spendere meno di 80 euro.

C’è l’apertura trionfale con il Gran Crudo. Un tripudio di scampi, gamberi rossi di Mazara, gamberi gobbetti, tartare di gamberi e tonno Balfegò, carpaccio di pescato e calamari alla julienne. Non lo regalano, costa 85 euro, ma ci si mangia anche in quattro. Le pappardelle all’astice potrebbero aver viaggiato nel tempo tanto sembrano uscite dalla stessa cucina di allora e e con la stessa qualità della materia prima. L’unica cosa cambiata è il prezzo, 50 euro, ma potrebbe essere un piatto unico.

Lo stesso vale per gli spaghettoni alle vongole veraci (non sgusciate). A 24 euro riscattano da tutti quegli spaghetti alle vongole che ormai fanno anche nei bar e in pizzeria.

Non poteva mancare la Catalana di crostacei, pièce de résistance della cucina del vecchio Ottavio riportata pari pari nel nuovo locale di Roma. E’ un piatto della festa, un’occasione per celebrare, una gioia per gli occhi e per il palato. Astice, scampi e mazzancolle con patate, cipolla rossa di Tropea, pomodoro camone, pomodoro piccadilly e basilico. Più colori e sapori di così non si potrebbe immaginare. Anche qui il prezzo è di quelli che si ricordano, 150 euro per due persone. Ma in tre o in quattro non ci sarebbe comunque da lamentarsi.

Tutto questo e anche altro in onore alla memoria e alla tradizione, ma il nuovo Ottavio è anche un laboratorio di innovazione. Ferma restando la qualità indiscutibile della materia prima, il giovane chef Vincenzo Loffredo non scontenta chi vuole sperimentare.

Ho provato il suo risotto con qualche scetticismo – educato come sono all’idea che i risotti a sud di Firenze è meglio lasciarli perdere – ma mi sono dovuto ricredere. Il suo risotto con cozze, vongole, limone candito e tartare di gambero rosso non aveva niente fuori posto. Cottura del riso, cremosità, sapori e contrasti era tutta opera di precisione.

Da non tralasciare anche il pescato nelle varie cotture tradizionali. Da Ottavio perfetto grazie a quella specialità tutta italiana e non solo di Roma di toccare, cuocere o condire il pesce il meno possibile.

Insomma una cucina di pesce dal tono borghese, sostanziosa, senza effetti speciali, con lampi di innovazione, in un bel ristorante luminoso, al prezzo giusto.

Ristorante Ottavio. Via Savoia, 68, 00198 Roma RM. Telefono: 06 6549 2433. Instagram

Ci sono nomi che appartengono alla memoria gastronomica di una città e che, quando tornano, portano con sé una responsabilità precisa: non limitarsi a riproporre il passato, ma trovare il modo di farlo dialogare con il presente. È la sfida di Ottavio, ristorante di pesce che riapre a Roma con la terza generazione della famiglia.

A guidare la brigata è Vincenzo Loffredo, classe 1993, formatosi al Tino con Lele Usai. E in seguito passato attraverso esperienze in ristoranti stellati in Francia. E ha trascorso quattro anni accanto a Pierluigi Gallo da Achilli al Parlamento.

Il primo ristorante nasce nel 1955 in via Santa Croce in Gerusalemme, come trattoria di quartiere di Roma fondata da Anna Di Giacomo e dal marito Ottavio. Inizialmente propone una cucina tradizionale romana e accoglie i cosiddetti fagottari. Cioè le persone che portavano da casa le proprie pietanze e si accomodavano in osteria per mangiarle in compagnia, ordinando magari soltanto una minestra o un bicchiere di vino.

Dopo qualche anno, il locale cambia direzione e sceglie il pescato del litorale laziale. Negli anni Ottanta subentrano i figli Massimo e Berardino. Sono loro che rinnovano il ristorante fino a farlo diventare uno degli indirizzi capitolini più frequentati per la cucina di pesce. Oggi è il nipote Ottavio a raccogliere il testimone.

Partiamo con il benvenuto: un finger food che consiste in una focaccia fatta in casa con gambero rosso crudo e glassa di pomodoro. Accanto, una coppietta di tonno con una frollatura di 65 giorni — con finocchetto, timo, peperoncino, paprika, sale e zucchero —che riprende la consistenza della coppietta di maiale e rievoca la bottarga caramellata.

La memoria del ristorante torna innanzitutto nel Gran Crudo (85 €). Una composizione che rende omaggio alla vocazione marinara di Ottavio, tra i primi ristoranti a portare il crudo a Roma. In tavola arrivano scampi, gamberi rossi di Mazara e gobbetti, insieme alle immancabili tartare. Un battuto al coltello di tonno Balfegó e uno di gamberi. Completa il percorso il carpaccio di lampuga, pesce riconoscibile per la grande testa blu e la pancia gialla. Le preparazioni sono condite con salicornia, olio, sale e mandorle, lasciando spazio al sapore del pescato.

La Catalana di crostacei alla Ottavio (150 €, per due persone) segue invece la ricetta storica del ristorante di Roma. I crostacei e l’aragosta cotti al vapore sono adagiati su un letto di patate, pomodori — San Marzano, Pachino e Piccadilly — e cipolla rossa di Tropea. A completare il piatto, un tocco di aceto, sale Maldon e olio al prezzemolo.

Il menu conserva così alcuni riferimenti riconoscibili, ma lascia allo chef lo spazio per introdurre nuove idee. È il caso del risotto con cozze, vongole e tartare di gambero rosso (38 €). Nato dall’evoluzione del risotto classico di Ottavio e inizialmente proposto fuori menu ora è in carta. A renderlo particolare è la panura realizzata da Ottavio con squame di pesce sbollentate, essiccate e frullate insieme a erbe anch’esse essiccate.

Tra i secondi, il pescato alla griglia (28 €) segue la disponibilità del giorno e viene proposto con salsa BBQ e bieta. Nel nostro caso arriva il morone, pesce della famiglia della ricciola pescato ad Anzio. Vive vicino al fondale, si nutre di alghe e ha una carne grassa, adatta alla cottura alla griglia. La preparazione prevede una prima scottatura sul fuoco e una finitura al vapore. Il pesce è accompagnato da bieta e da una salsa verde ricavata dalla stessa verdura. Accanto, una salsa barbecue preparata a partire da cipolle bianche appassite, sfumate con aceto di vino rosso e aceto di lampone, quindi lavorate con la soia. La componente vegetale e quella agrodolce accompagnano il morone senza sovrastarne il gusto.

La conclusione della cena da Ottavio a Roma è affidata a due dessert, entrambi a 14 euro. Il Cannolo è una rilettura scomposta del dolce tradizionale.

Più articolato il Cremoso alle erbe, mini brownie e fichi, una creazione dello chef. La base richiama il brownie, ma la cottura dura soltanto sei minuti, così da lasciare il centro morbido e cremoso. La consistenza si amalgama con la namelaka alle erbe, una crema montata che richiama la tradizione tecnica francese e giapponese. In questa versione è preparata con dragoncello e basilico, le due erbe che Loffredo predilige. A completare il dessert, un fico in purezza, frutto scelto in base alla stagionalità.

La direzione del ristorante è affidata a Stefan Bujor, nato a Bucharest e con esperienze professionali in Italia (tra le ultime Numa al Circo) e all’estero, tra cui Londra (Social Eating House e altri). La squadra si completa con la sommelier Federica Persiani che, dopo la formazione AIS, ha lavorato per undici anni con lo chef Salvatore Tassa a Le Colline Ciociare, ad Acuto.

Anche gli spazi raccontano una precisa idea di accoglienza. L’interior design è stato curato dall’architetto Fabio Lacomara; colpisce in particolare l’aggetto della scaffalatura delle bottiglie di vino, elegante e spiazzante, quasi parallelo al pavimento. Al piano superiore, dove si trova la cucina, sono esposte le opere di Marina Mingazzini, nell’ambito di un progetto nato con il professore dell’Accademia di Belle Arti Eclario Barone che prevede un ciclo espositivo.

Il sito che vi parla di cibo, ristoranti, pizzerie, pasticcerie e di tutto quello che serve per un buon pranzo o una buona cena e colazione

#1405. Silicon Valley AI political groups turn on each other in the 2026 election

Silicon Valley's bid to dominate artificial intelligence politics has devolved into a fight with itself.

With one week until the midterm election, political groups favoring faster AI development and lighter, more uniform rules have spent roughly $8 million in general-election congressional races, besting groups pushing for stronger safeguards and more room for states to regulate that have spent about $6.9 million, according to a CNBC analysis of Federal Election Commission filings through Oct. 20.

In Florida's 25th Congressional District, that split has produced a direct face-off. During the primary, Think Big, an affiliate of Leading the Future, the main super PAC network pushing faster AI development and lighter regulation, spent $310,000 supporting Democrat Jared Moskowitz, whose district changed after Florida redrew its congressional map ahead of the 2026 election. On the other side, Defending Our Values, a super PAC favoring stricter safety guardrails and state-level authority, dropped almost $857,000 to boost Republican Scott Singer and an additional $740,000 to keep one of his primary opponents from being elected.

Now, Moskowitz and Singer face off in the general election.

It's a microcosm of the breakdown in Silicon Valley's bid to build a unified AI political machine. Both sides favor AI innovation and agree on the need for guardrails, but they remain locked in a costly tug-of-war over which candidates to back — and which will best align with their preferred deployment speed, regulatory reach and balance of state power.

Electing more allies could give either camp an edge in shaping AI policy in the next Congress, even as the feud risks weakening Silicon Valley's clout.

"Everyone supports some form of regulation. It's just a debate about how much," said Bruce Freed, president and co-founder of the nonpartisan Center for Political Accountability and a former chief investigator for the Senate banking committee. "Money is flowing in all directions to be in the driver's seat of what happens."

CNBC identified federal committees aligned with each camp and totaled their FEC-reported independent expenditures supporting or opposing congressional candidates. The analysis excludes state races and nonprofit advocacy spending.

This was not the plan. The model was cryptocurrency.

Fairshake and its affiliated pro-crypto super PACs, backed by Coinbase, Ripple and Andreessen Horowitz, spent more than $130 million during the 2024 election cycle, according to FEC filings. Candidates it supported won 53 of 58 races, a 91% success rate, according to crypto publication CoinDesk.

AI investors took note. In August 2025, Leading the Future launched with more than $100 million in commitments from tech heavyweights including Andreessen Horowitz, OpenAI President Greg Brockman and his wife, Anna, and Perplexity and Palantir co-founder Joe Lonsdale.

Co-led by Josh Vlasto, who worked for Fairshake last election cycle, the network deployed a Democratic PAC, Think Big, and a Republican PAC, American Mission, to support candidates aligned with faster AI development and opposition to a patchwork of state regulations.

The message was clear: Back AI's agenda or risk millions being spent against you.

"The AI industry announced last year that they were going to rerun the crypto industry playbook by coming in swinging with oodles of money in order to bully lawmakers into submission," said Sacha Haworth, founder and executive director of the Tech Oversight Project, a nonprofit watchdog that advocates for stronger regulation of Big Tech and AI.

At first, it worked. In the cycle's first major primaries in March, three candidates heavily backed by American Mission — Jessica Steinmann in Texas, Chris Gober in Texas and Laurie Buckhout in North Carolina — won their Republican contests after the group spent more than $500,000 supporting each, according to FEC filings.

But a rival infrastructure was already taking shape. Anthropic committed $20 million to Public First Action in February and another $20 million in July, giving the safeguards camp a major financial backer. Anthropic says its money is restricted to policy and public education and cannot fund candidate elections. Still, separately funded super PACs tied to Public First Action have spent millions advancing similar priorities.

The clash burst into view in New York’s 12th District Democratic primary. Think Big spent $8.3 million, according to FEC filings, trying to defeat state Assemblymember Alex Bores, who authored major state AI safety legislation. The Anthropic-backed Jobs and Democracy PAC countered with about $15 million to support him, while allied safety groups spent millions more, according CNBC's analysis.

Think Big and Jobs and Democracy spent a combined $23.3 million, about 40% of the two camps' primary spending nationwide, according to the analysis.

Bores ultimately lost to Micah Lasher, 39% to 35%, giving Think Big a tactical victory.

"They helped light a flame under the backlash that's now fueling so much of the midterm elections," Haworth said. "The race showed that spending against safety-first candidates could now trigger a counterattack from within the industry itself."

The fight has carried into the general election, but the pace of spending plummeted.

Safeguards-focused groups have spent $825,000 this fall opposing two Republicans who benefited from Leading the Future-aligned spending during the primaries, according to CNBC's analysis of FEC filings. The two races alone account for more than one-sixth of the safeguards camp's general-election opposition spending.

Guardrails Alliance reported spending $412,500 apiece, according to FEC filings, against Republican House candidates Jay Feely in Arizona and Aaron Flint in Montana, both of whom benefited from Leading the Future-aligned spending in their primaries. It also reported about $412,000 against Democratic Rep. Jimmy Gomez in California, whom Leading the Future endorsed but did not report spending to support, according to CNBC's analysis.

"The big AI groups still believe that their money can help influence elections even if it's just a couple in November," Haworth said.

Yet the overall flow of AI campaign money has slowed since the primaries.

Leading the Future's network reported roughly $26 million in primary independent expenditures, compared with about $8 million in general-election races. Safeguards-focused groups reported about $32.1 million in primary spending and $6.9 million in general-election contests. The groups reported another roughly $5.5 million in runoff and special-election spending.

Combined, about 74% of the roughly $78.5 million they have spent on federal candidates this cycle went toward primary races, according to CNBC's analysis.

Some of that decline reflects the smaller universe of competitive November races. But the slowdown has coincided with AI becoming a more difficult political sell.

A new CNBC All-America Economic Survey found 52% of registered voters said companies should pause development of advanced AI until Congress passes regulations, compared with 32% who favored moving ahead. Sixty-three percent said they would oppose an AI data center within 10 miles of their home.

“When evaluating risk versus reward right now, the backlash is just too big,” said Freed, of the Center for Political Accountability.

“AI executives and groups spent heavily in the primaries, so they likely achieved what they set out to do in most races. At this point, there's no real downside to scaling back,” Freed said.

The Brockmans gave $25 million to Leading the Future. But amid objections from OpenAI employees to the group's tactics, OpenAI's chief strategy officer acknowledged internally that the company was taking "reputational hits," according to Semafor.

The Brockmans later abandoned plans for another $25 million contribution, according to The New York Times.

Meta has retreated as well. Political groups it funded returned $25 million this summer — $22 million from the AI-promoting American Technology Excellence Project and $3 million from its California operation — according to IRS and state filings. The refunds cut its planned $65 million state-level political push by nearly 40%, to about $40 million. The Times first reported the refunds.

"Something's clearly not working," OpenAI CEO Sam Altman told Politico earlier this month. "I don't think spending money on politics is what's going to make people feel better about it."

#1406. Common drugs may help dangerous viruses spread through the body

Medications are designed to treat diseases and relieve symptoms, but some can also produce unintended effects that put patients at risk. While side effects are common with many treatments, researchers have identified a particularly concerning possibility involving drugs used to control inflammation.

Scientists at the Norwegian University of Science and Technology (NTNU) have discovered that a widely used class of anti-inflammatory medications may make it easier for certain viruses to infect cells and spread throughout the body.

"We have found a surprising and potentially serious side effect of a class of anti-inflammatory drugs. They can help viruses spread more easily in the body," says Denis Kainov, a professor at the Department of Clinical and Molecular Medicine at the Norwegian University of Science and Technology (NTNU).

Common Anti-Inflammatory Drugs May Help Viruses Spread

The medications at the center of the findings belong to a class called Janus kinase inhibitors, or JAKs. These drugs are widely prescribed to control inflammation, but their effects on the immune system may also leave the body more vulnerable to viral infections.

"Among the viruses that more easily affect the body with the help of these drugs are Rift Valley fever virus, influenza A, adenovirus and SARS-CoV-2, the virus that causes COVID-19," Kainov says.

These viruses can cause significant illness, making any treatment that potentially increases their ability to spread a serious concern.

Why Arthritis Drugs Can Weaken Antiviral Defenses

In a new study published in NAR Molecular Medicine, Kainov and his colleagues investigated how JAK inhibitors influence the body's ability to defend itself against viruses.

"JAK inhibitors are often prescribed for autoimmune diseases and inflammatory conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis," says Erlend Ravlo, a PhD research fellow at NTNU and first author of the article.

Although these medications can be highly effective at reducing inflammation, their benefits come with an important trade-off. By suppressing certain immune responses, they can also interfere with the mechanisms that normally protect the body from viral infections.

"In particular, the drugs suppress an important immune signalling pathway that helps protect healthy cells from viral attacks," Ravlo said.

This pathway plays a central role in coordinating the body's response when viruses attempt to infect healthy tissue.

Scientists Discover How JAK Inhibitors Disrupt Immune Protection

The research team found that JAK inhibitors, including the medication baricitinib, can reduce the activity of genes involved in fighting viral infections.

"These genes play a crucial role in the body's response to viral infections," said Aleksandr Ianevski, an NTNU researcher and coauthor of the new paper.

When JAK inhibitors interfere with this immune signaling system, they weaken an important layer of antiviral protection. Without the usual defensive response, viruses may find it easier to establish an infection and spread between cells.

To investigate these effects, the scientists combined advanced virology methods with gene expression analysis and organoid technology. Their experiments included cells from the lungs, eyes and brain, along with miniature organ models grown in the laboratory.

These approaches allowed the team to examine how the drugs affect antiviral defenses across different types of human tissue.

"Although JAK inhibitors are effective in the treatment of inflammation, this shows that they can pose a hidden risk for patients who have latent or active viral infections," says Ravlo.

What the Findings Mean for Patients and Future Treatments

The results highlight the importance of carefully considering the risks associated with JAK inhibitors, particularly when patients may already have a viral infection or when outbreaks are occurring.

Researchers suggest that healthcare professionals should exercise caution when prescribing these medications during periods of increased viral transmission.

However, the same immune-suppressing properties that create potential risks for patients could also offer advantages in certain research settings. Under controlled laboratory conditions, these effects may help scientists develop vaccines or evaluate potential antiviral medications.

The researchers hope their findings will encourage greater awareness of how JAK inhibitors influence the immune system and support further investigations into their safest and most effective uses.

"We recommend further studies to better understand how the drugs can be used optimally, especially during virus outbreaks or pandemics," says Ianevski.

Professor Magnar Bjørås of the Department of Clinical and Molecular Medicine provided significant scientific expertise and secured most of the funding for the research. Additional financial support came from the Central Norway Regional Health Authority, the South-Eastern Norway Regional Health Authority, the Research Council of Norway and the Swedish Research Council.

#1413. Israeli election draws tens of thousands of citizens flying back to vote

An extremely tight race into Israel's election Tuesday, has some citizens flying back into the country to cast their votes.

Israel doesn't allow votes from abroad, except from those serving in the country's diplomatic missions. As many as 80,000 Israelis living outside the country are expected to come back to vote in Tuesday's election, according to estimates from one group helping to organize citizens living outside the country. Israel has about 7.3 million eligible voters, according to the Washington-based International Foundation for Electoral Systems.

"While not a large block, the 80,000 that may return home to participate could make a big difference in the final count of a very tight election," said Yael Shomer, a professor of political science at Tel Aviv University.

In Israel's first election since 2022, Benjamin Netanyahu of the Likud party, who has served as Prime Minister for 18 years over three separate periods, is facing top challenger Gadi Eisenkot, the former chief of staff of the Israel Defense Forces, who heads the Yashar party. Both would likely need backing from potential coalition partners in order to win.

Polls are extremely tight heading into Tuesday's election. Issues like security, already a major decider for Israelis, have gotten even more contentious with the Iran war in full swing. The exemption of some ultra-Orthodox men from conscription is also causing a great divide in Israeli society, while Prime Minister Netanyahu is still working on a controversial plan that would give the governing coalition more control over the judiciary.

"All elections in Israel are energetic, but because this one will have such a meaningful impact on the future of the country it has been especially hard fought," Shomer said. "This election is really about how we see our future, voter turnout will be very high."

Voter turnout in 2022 was just above 70% according to Israel's Central Elections Committee. Pollsters believe it could reach as high as 87% this time. Among foreign service workers serving in embassies and consulates outside of Israel, voter turnout was 90%. According to The Central Elections Committee, that number is usually closer to 70%.

In order to help those living abroad come back to cast votes, an organization called Fly & Vote was set up by the America-Israel Democracy Coalition, a U.S.-based group which was originally created in 2023 to stop the effort by Likud to reform the judicial system.

While organizations and political parties are prohibited from paying for any kind of transportation for people inside or outside of Israel, Aid Coalition has found other ways to facilitate the voting.

Fly & Vote, which has been funded by private donations, chartered a flight for Israelis living in Portugal and bought blocks of tickets for flights from the New York area. Anyone on the flights had to pay for their own seats.

"Israelis who don't live here still have a stake in what we do, and we want to help them," said Ora Peled-Nakash, the group's co-founder. "We don't take a political position though and we don't tell anyone how to vote, we just help them cast their ballot."

Travelers will also have plenty of commercial options.

For decades El Al was the only Israeli airline to fly routes from the U.S. to Israel. Arkia started offering flights last year and Israir earlier this year. Legacy U.S. carriers United and Delta are also flying to Israel again after suspending flights due to the war with Iran. Germany's Lufthansa flies to Israel from Europe and British Airways is scheduled to re-start flights this week.

What's more, the price is in line with what it would be during normal times, Peled-Nakash said. There were still a few seats left on El Al flights from JFK or Newark airports ranging from $1,300 to $2,500 as of Sunday, according to research from CNBC.

After years of political instability that saw five elections between 2019 and 2022, Tueday's election result could help shape Israel's political, security and economic direction for years to come. But it also shows how politically divided the country has become.

#1414. Warhound wants to engineer and clone military superdogs—can they do it?

Warhound wants to engineer and clone military superdogs—can they do it?

The start-up is the brainchild of a founder of Anduril, the military tech firm, and Colossal Biosciences, a biotech company known for its de-extinction efforts

By Mary Randolph edited by Claire Cameron

Warhound officially launched on Thursday, though it’s been underway for more than a year and raised $200 million in funding.

A new biotechnology start-up wants to use gene-editing technology, cloning and advanced military technology to create a new dog optimized for combat. But does the science to back up its claims exist? And if so, can the company possibly deliver on the idea?

The start-up, called Warhound, is the brainchild of Colossal Biosciences’ Ben Lamm and Anduril Industries’ Palmer Luckey. Warhound intends to clone and genetically modify military service dogs to produce larger, more efficient working dogs for use in conflict zones and policing. Experts say that the science the company proposes is possible—but that it is also prone to error, inefficiencies and a slew of ethical concerns.

Warhound has already biobanked the genetic material from a group of elite service dogs, Lamm says, including breeds such as Belgian Malinois and shepherds. Warhound’s scientists intend to clone the cells of those dogs and edit the cloned embryos to produce new puppies. They’re expecting the first litters in early 2027.

If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.

Cloning dogs is not a new science. Research has shown that cloning service dogs produces puppies that have many of the same desirable traits. But the process can be harmful, says Lisa Moses, a veterinarian and bioethicist at Harvard University. The rate of successful live offspring remains low among the cloned dogs, and the process can put the surrogate mother in danger.

“It is by no means a perfect science, and by that, I mean it’s still a fairly inefficient process,” Moses says. “It requires a lot of dogs to have invasive things done to them and to be killed in order to produce one cloned puppy.”

Warhound intends to make several genetic modifications in its cloned embryos to make the dogs healthier, stronger and better workers. First, the company hopes to modify the dogs to reduce the risk of health conditions such as hip disease, vision loss and cancer predisposition—and, eventually, to optimize ideal traits for military dogs.

“The standard is that no dog enters service carrying a genetic marker known to cause a common career-ending condition,” Lamm says. “From there, we are working on edits specifically targeting additional longevity and health, as well as performance factors.”

Both scientists and private companies have genetically edited dogs before, and the research can “accelerate really fast because genomics in dog breeds already has a lot of data,” says Ben Novak, chief scientist at Revive and Restore, who works on wildlife cloning for conservation. Researchers have edited dogs to tweak genes for hip dysplasia, make them hypoallergenic and treat muscle disease, although the long-term health effects of these changes remain unclear.

But optimizing traits at scale and across service dogs could take time—and leave room for unintended consequences, Novak adds.

“It can be hard to figure out exactly what genetic element is creating a trait,” he says, “and some traits can be the combinations of hundreds or thousands of mutations across genes.”

Colossal Biosciences, which has a stake in Warhound and is providing much of the science, is no stranger to genetic engineering: last year the firm cloned and edited a gray wolf to create an animal that was genetically similar to the extinct dire wolf. The process for Warhound will look similar, Lamm says, but with modern dogs.

In its launch announcement, Warhound said it had raised $200 million in funding. Novak says that from a commercial perspective, the concept makes sense.

“For a biotech company, it is certainly a slam dunk idea: guaranteed military contracts, which is the most funded aspect of U.S. government science, with an actual potential to improve a sector of military use that I think everyone can agree is important.”

But from a bioethics standpoint, Moses says, involving man’s best friend in biotechnology can quickly become fraught.

“I’ve had lots of conversations about what Colossal Biosciences is doing and has done. But when you start messing around with dogs, people feel very differently,” Moses says.

Robert Lanza, former chief scientific officer at the Astellas Institute for Regenerative Medicine and a pioneer of cloning research, says the ethics and technique of Warhound’s premise are far from “black or white.”

“I think such goals are definitely achievable from a scientific perspective. But then again, it’s highly unlikely it could be done without many, many failures and defects,” he says.

Mary Randolph is a news intern at Scientific American and is based in New York City. Her work has been featured by Smithsonian Magazine, Pew Research Center, the Local News Initiative and various local newsrooms.

#1415. Ristorante Sadler a Casa Baglioni Milano: com’è il menu d’autunno

Il ristorante stellato Sadler, al piano rialzato di Casa Baglioni, in via dell’Annunciata a Milano, è una destinazione preferita da una clientela locale e italiana, ma anche per molti stranieri. Che scelgono questa tavola proprio in cerca del ristorante e del suo stile, anche quando alloggiano in altri hotel.

Nella sala molto ampia e luminosa le sedute sono una trentina. C’è anche una wine-cellar che funziona come una saletta-privata.

In sala, ai tavoli, due-tre-coppie e più tardi un tavolo per 8, cena d’affari. Interamente occupata anche la wine-cellar.

Subito evidente, fin dalle prime battute, l’armonia sala-cucina e anche sala-sala. Gentilezza non invasiva. Stile all’altezza della firma prestigiosa. Sbirciamo il menu d’autunno per questa nostra cena stampa.

Il menu della sera prevede piatti alla carta e due percorsi degustazione, quindi intesi per l’intero tavolo.

— Tradizione & Innovazione con 5 portate a 160 euro. — Creativo con 7 portate a 190 euro.

Ogni portata di ciascun percorso è ordinabile anche separatamente a piacere, ma non tutti i prezzi appaiono in carta (verificati in loco il 15 ottobre). Scegliendo alla carta 3 piatti – antipasto, primo e secondo – al ristorante Sadler spendete in media 155 €.

Il menu del Business lunch è più snello e conta 4 antipasti, 4 primi, 4 secondi.

Più una proposta di “Cucina milanese che vive nel tempo e nel futuro”

— Riso al salto (25 €) — Costoletta di vitello alla milanese (38 €)— Piatto unico, di ispirazione valtellinese, con tagliatelle di grano saraceno bietola Casera polpette di vitello e tartufo nero (33 €).

Lo regola non scritta da Sadler è fare la porzione degustazione al 70% del corrispettivo libero. Con pochissime eccezioni, come i tagliolini che, per la loro intensità, sono volutamente in porzione degustazione anche quando richiesti à la carte.

Trovo questo modus operandi trasparente. Specialmente se a confronto con altri percorsi degustazione con piattini non sempre giustificatamente microscopici.

Se fossimo una rivista di moda, diremmo che questo benvenuto è un fashion statement. Diremo invece che dettano la linea, preceduti e accompagnati da una bollicina Ferrari Trentodoc Riserva Lunelli 2016.

— Cannolo di riso al salto, citazione della celebre invenzione da passeggio dello chef Sadler. — Crescenza, crescentina, dragoncello – guscio leggiadro, ultrasottile e quasi podio. Simile nella forma ma diversi nell’esito, l’Airbag-bigné di patate, tartare di manzo (senza manzo nella versione per non carnivori) cipolla rossa, maionese fatta in casa.— Savarin alla pizzaiola, una miniatura da urlo. Primo sul podio.—Tartelletta di impasto udon alla barbabietola, robiola, mirtilli, fiori di sambuco, germogli. Strati sottilissimi e morsi di delicatezza.

E il cestino del pane: Grissini all’olio pericolosi – visto il ripetuto refill, Focaccia barese pomodorini-origano e Shokupan con cipolla rosa dentro impasto, spennellato di miele e cosparso di sale Maldon. Come una nuvola, come di dovere.

Con pagnotta lievito madre arriva l’olio extravergine Trinacria etichettato Sadler, pomodoroso e ancora di medio-alta intensità all’assaggio in purezza.

Siamo due commensali, amiche con gusti diversissimi. Scegliere piatti individuali senza doppioni racconta meglio il menu d’autunno.

Per me, Sashimi di ricciola dello chef Lovato (in carta a 55 €) impiattato a bocciolo, con foglia di shiso, mela verde, cetriolo e completato al tavolo con latticello e olio alla verbena. In una parola, l’oltresashimi. Nel calice Verdemare di Mezzanotte Verdicchio dei Castelli di Jesi 2023, fresco e balsamico.

Dal menu degustazione Tradizione & Innovazione, Capasanta alla plancia con carciofi alla giudia e spuma di dragoncello. Inatteso. Nel calice, Nascetta delle Langhe Castello di Perno. È la seconda volta che bevo questo vitigno, dopo la Trattoria i Bologna a Rocchetta Tanaro. E comunque, piatto gaudioso.

Conclusione trionfale, la Padellata di crostacei (in carta a 110 €) grande classico di Sadler. La mia porzione-degustazione non è affatto piccola, è uno spettacolo. La accompagna una salsina erbacea e titillante. Nel calice, il potente Catarratto Lunarìa di Sergio Genuardi del 2023.

La mia commensale opta per un super autunnale Carpaccio di cervo estratto anche questo dal menu degustazione Tradizione & Innovazione.

Un Kloster Eberbach Crescentia, Riesling Secco Rheingau del 2022 è il pairing perfettamente in grado di reggere la carne rossa.

Seguono i Tagliolini 40 tuorli cotti nel brodo di cipolla e finiti con caviale Asetra, stavolta dal menu degustazione Creativo del ristorante Sadler. Nel calici, Champagne Cossy Cuvée Origine Premier Cru Extra Brut. Intensità.

Il Trancio di rombo alla plancia, salsa di scamorza affumicata, indivia belga, olive taggiasche, acciughe del cantabrico e polvere di capperi (in carta a € 65) è forse il più sobrio dei piatti. Ma solo all’apparenza. Lo completa in pairing un Nebbiolo Sommoclivo Torre San Quirico Azzate.

Al posto del dessert, Orologio di formaggi: Ubriacone affinato nelle vinacce di Amarone, Montebore abba giovane caseificio Guffanti, Castelmagno, Blue Cheese, Gorgonzola. In abbinamento, Champagne, su consiglio della sommelier accettatissimo: Rosélie Rosé de Saignée di Roger Coulon, un Pinot Meunier 100% Vecchie Vigne rosa carico Extra Brut Pas Dosé.

Vermouth Bianco Dorato etichettato Sadler, frutto di una collaborazione chef-sommelier per un commiato dalle sfumature foliage. Si conferma l’amore di Claudio Sadler per le spezie.

Se parliamo tanto di valorizzare la sala, valorizziamola. Ho apprezzato molto vedere al piede del menu di Sadler, i nomi dei singoli professionisti impaginati come se fossero i solisti di un’orchestra sul programma di un concerto.

Giacomo Lovato, executive chef in stretta connessione con Claudio Sadler, ma portatore anche di precedenti esperienze Cracco che vuol dire anche eredità Marchesi.

E i suoi sous-chef con le loro specialità: ladies first, Alice Locatelli, poi Samuele Corti agli antipasti, Jordan Chuquillanqui ai primi, Matteo Sanvito ai secondi. Pamela Pettinari sommelier curiosa e provocatrice. Ci siamo messi felicemente nelle sue mani per i pairing al calice.

Mihai Dragan e Francesca Renda intorno a noi con attenzione, con senso del fluire del servizio e con il sorriso, tutto il tempo. Lo chef Lovato che si è seduto al nostro tavolo a chiacchierare. Quando una persona ama il proprio lavoro, si vede.

Ristorante Sadler. Via dell’Annunciata 14, Milano. Tel. +39 02 5810 4451. Instagram

Milanese, trent’anni di copywriting e comunicazione aziendale. Le piace che il cibo abbia le parole che merita: è cultura. Parlando molto e mangiando poco, non si applica nel suo caso il “parla come mangi”.

#1418. James Webb discovers a scorching lava planet with a “giant sunscreen”

Astronomers have discovered surprising evidence that a scorching planet covered in molten rock may be protected by a reflective layer of clouds that acts like a giant sunscreen. Scientists previously believed that the planet's extreme conditions would make it nearly impossible for an atmosphere to survive, but new observations suggest otherwise.

An international team of researchers, including Dr. Anjali Piette, an astrophysicist at the University of Birmingham, reported the findings in The Astronomical Journal. Using the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), the scientists monitored a rocky exoplanet called TOI-561 b, located approximately 280 light-years from Earth. Over 37 hours, they observed nearly four complete orbits around its host star.

The observations indicate that TOI-561 b may be surrounded by a substantial atmosphere, although its conditions would be far too hostile for life as we know it. This atmosphere appears to help the planet reflect much of the radiation coming from its star. One possible explanation is a layer of highly reflective silicate clouds that prevents the surface from reaching the extreme temperatures expected on an exposed rocky planet. The atmosphere also appears to move heat from the permanently illuminated dayside toward the nightside, further reducing temperatures on the star-facing side.

A Lava Planet With an Atmosphere That Should Have Disappeared

Scientists still do not know exactly which gases make up the atmosphere of TOI-561 b. One possibility is a thick layer of carbon dioxide, resembling the atmosphere of Venus but under much hotter conditions. Another is an atmosphere dominated by sulfur dioxide, a gas released by volcanic activity on Jupiter's moon Io.

Dr. Anjali Piette, Assistant Professor in Astronomy at the University of Birmingham, said: "Our discovery challenges current theories. We would expect a heavily irradiated rocky planet like TOI-561 b to have lost its atmosphere billions of years ago.

"Instead, the evidence suggests it still has a significant atmosphere today. This raises major questions such as whether the planet started with an unusually large supply of gases or if the ocean of molten rock covering its surface, acts as a planet-wide volcano that is constantly feeding its atmosphere."

James Webb Reveals Why the Planet Is So Reflective

Earlier measurements revealed something puzzling about TOI-561 b. Its dayside was significantly cooler than researchers predicted for a dark, rocky planet orbiting so close to its star. That unexpected temperature suggested that much of the incoming energy was either being transferred to the nightside or reflected back into space before it could heat the surface.

To investigate, the team observed the planet throughout its orbit, allowing them to examine its nightside for the first time. Because the same side of TOI-561 b always faces its star, the nightside receives no direct starlight. However, the measurements showed that this darker hemisphere was not warm enough to explain all the missing heat.

The findings instead indicate that TOI-561 b reflects approximately 75% of the starlight reaching it, a remarkably high proportion comparable to Venus.

To determine what could produce such strong reflectivity, the researchers compared the telescope measurements with computer models of the planet's climate. Their simulations suggest that clouds containing silicate minerals, including silicon dioxide (SiO2) and magnesium silicate (MgSiO3), may form over the dayside. If present, these clouds could reflect incoming radiation before it reaches the surface, functioning as a natural sunscreen.

Professor Lisa Dang, who led the project at the University of Waterloo in Ontario, Canada, said: "We measured how the planet's brightness and heat changed throughout its orbit. This technique, known as a phase curve, revealed that the planet reflects a significant amount of light from its star, and that heat is being redistributed around the planet instead of only on the sunlit side. Together, these point to the presence of an atmosphere."

Could a Global Ocean of Lava Keep the Atmosphere Alive?

The new findings strengthen earlier evidence gathered by Professor Lisa Dang, Dr. Anjali Piette, and their collaborators that TOI-561 b has a thick atmosphere that may be continually replenished by gases escaping from its molten interior.

That possibility could help explain how the planet has maintained an atmosphere despite enduring intense radiation from its star for billions of years. Rather than simply losing its gases to space, the planet's vast reservoir of molten rock may be constantly releasing new material into the atmosphere.

Researchers now hope to determine whether TOI-561 b is more like an extremely hot Venus or a much more intense version of the volcanic moon Io. Additional observations with JWST at longer wavelengths could reveal important details about the atmosphere's chemical composition and help resolve the mystery of its long-term survival.

Professor Dang added: "The next big question we will seek to answer is whether TOI-561 b's atmosphere resembles Venus or an extreme version of lo. Observing the planet at longer wavelengths with JWST could give us insights and help explain how a planet this hot has held on to an atmosphere for billions of years."
